en: Oṃ, homage to Śiva.

Triumphant on this earth are the words of Rāmakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa— whose form was equal to that of Vidyeśvara and who was as delightful as the rays of the moon for flooding the entire ocean of the nectar of established doctrines.
From him, indeed, [this work] was both received and heard through the arrangement of the jewels of knowledge.
I shall declare the Bhāvacūḍābheda and the Vidyākaṇṭhasaṃgraha.

For here, just as the means for the worship of Śiva and so forth was told by Maya— the direct disciple of the former Self-born Lord— to the sages, so too does his disciple relate it to his own disciples.

"At the back is the Himavat," and so forth; by this, the sages situated at the front of the Himalayas, near his feet, beheld Maya seated. Thus, even though the verse was composed for the purpose of illustrating the grammatical formation (*prakriyā*), it has been explained [in this manner].
"The knower of all sciences."

One who knows the fourteen branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*); the fourteen branches of learning consist of the Vedas together with the *purāṇas*, the *smṛtis*, *mīmāṃsā*, the *dharmaśāstras*, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), which are the fourteen bases of knowledge and of dharma; as well as all crafts and artistic skills.

The specific distinction among them is that he is the impeller; by this, his status as the Architect of the Universe (*viśvakarman*) is established. He is one whose mind is solely intent on Śiva, the supreme devotee of Maheśvara, and who is devoted to the grace of his followers. Furthermore, from the two scriptural readings, "the teacher of others also" and "by means of the rays of awakening," it is understood that [his eyes] are filled with joy and agitated by those endowed with splendor.
"By this [means], those whose descent of power (śaktipāta) has been inferred through supreme purifications such as faith and self-restraint,
he— Viśvakarman— having paid homage to the Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, the introducer of the scripture, spoke to Marīci and the others who were endowed with splendor," and so forth. "O God..."
The sacrifice to the Divine (devasya yajanam) is the primary goal, depending on its constituent parts and having multiple bases for that [sacrifice].

Among those, the sacrificial components are meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the state of being fully composed, distinguished from the other limbs of yoga; and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the restraint of the mind within a desired location.
And so says Patañjali:

"Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a single location. Meditation (*dhyāna*) follows internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), or for its sake, consists of the contemplation of the Supreme Lord as a single object within a specific part of the body, such as the heart. Thus it is said in the venerable *Kālottara*, consisting of three hundred and fifty verses: "One should meditate on Īśvara in the forehead. Recitation (*japa*) is said to be either whispered (*upāṃśu*) or mental (*mānasa*).
The recitation of mantras according to a prescribed number; *bhāva* refers to a pure state of being such as devotion (*bhakti*) and so forth;

and *tapaḥ* (austerities) refers to practices such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), as it is said: "Breath control is the supreme austerity," and "Then the supports in one's own form," and so on. In that context, the word "having established his presence" (*kṛtasannidhau*) [is used].

The phrase beginning with "in one's own form" (*svamūrtau*) and ending with "moving" (*cala*) is to be connected with each [of the preceding terms]. In that context, since worship (*yajana*) preceded by the ear (*karṇa*)—that is, proximity (*sannidhi*)—has been mentioned, [it follows that] "worship is superior to these [other supports]; [it is] in the *liṅga* alone": that is, among the aforementioned substrates (*ādhāra*), worship is performed in the substrate which is more distinguished, namely the one consisting of the *liṅga*.
The meaning is "it is excellent. And so, in the Mahābhārata and other texts, the venerable sage Vyāsa said:
"Having known Bhava to be the form of all, he who worships the Lord in the *liṅga* [attains the goal]."
The Bull-bannered One bestows upon him exceeding affection.

"What is its nature? means: what is its material cause (*prakṛti*), what is its instrumental cause (*kāraṇaka*)? And "the various ritual procedures pertaining to it" refers to the connection with what will be said later: "explain the other injunctions concerning the *liṅga*. "Firm foundation" (*āsthā*) means stability; "established in the hope for auspiciousness" (*śubhāśāmāsthitam*). This is in reference to this Śaiva scripture.

In rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), auspiciousness belongs only to the four directions—east, west, north, and northeast—and this follows one's own intention. For instance, one should stand in whichever direction accords with the purpose of the desire;
for example, one who wishes to cause distress to another should go toward the southeast (*āgneyī* direction), while one who wishes for [another's] death should go toward the south (*yāmyā*).

One who desires to inflict disease and the like should [direct it] toward the eastern direction; one who effects eradication (uccāṭana) toward the southern direction; and one who effects [it] toward the northwestern direction, and so forth. Now, the definition of the teacher (ācārya): he is the supreme guide (daiśikottama). "Born in the Ārya country"—the Ārya country is where there is deliberation on the meaning of the scriptures and their correct practice; he is one who has arisen from such a place.

"Pure" (*śuci*) means one who is free from desire for the property of others. And so says the *Smṛti*: "He who is pure regarding his purpose is truly pure; one who is merely pure by means of earth and water is not pure.
"Dexterous" (*dakṣa*) means one who is skillful in all matters, such as one's own duties, initiation (*dīkṣā*), and exposition.
"Concentrated" means one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), devoted to the performance of rituals, and has completed the *ācārya-vrata*.
Regarding the *ācārya-vrata*, it refers to the conduct prescribed for the teacher in other scriptures which is practiced after the consecration of the teacher (*ācāryābhiṣeka*),
as stated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva* [Tantra].
Then the preceptor himself should indeed observe the excellent vow of the preceptor:
sleeping on the ground for two fortnights, eating only at night, and always consuming sacrificial porridge (caru).

"One who observes silence and bathes at the three periods of the day," and so forth. "The learned one" (*vidvān*) means a scholar, not a fool; as it is said elsewhere: "A king's brother-in-law, one who is suspicious, and a teacher devoid of devotion [are not to be relied upon]. And "in the lunar mansion" (*nakṣatre*) refers to the moon, stars, and so on.

The purity of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is established by its being situated in the first, third, sixth, seventh, tenth, or eleventh position. As those learned in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) have said:
"That which is based on the birth [sign], the third, the sixth, the seventh, and likewise the tenth..."
The Moon situated in the eleventh house accomplishes all the goals of men.

Thus, having attained birth as Tārā, through the avoidance of the third, fifth, and seventh lunar days, there is purity from Nārā; by the inclusion of "etcetera," one is also free from the eleven inauspicious [days] such as Kāladaṇḍa and others, even when there is purity of the yoga. As it has been said:
In the illustrious Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa].
"One should abandon those yogas indicated by their names, as well as the eleven [inauspicious ones].

By this, it is meant that even if a *pluta* yoga is not explicitly mentioned, it is excluded by the mention of *viṣṭi*, *vṛddhi*, *vyatīpāta*, and so forth, as well as by the description of them as "terrible" (*dāruṇa*), "fierce" (*ugra*), "cruel" (*cara*), and so on.
The "terrible" asterisms are Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla, which are used for rites such as killing.
The *ugra* (fierce) asterisms are Maghā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, and the two Pūrvās; they are for the accomplishment of rites involving cremation grounds, vetālas, and the like.
The *cara* (wandering) asterisms are Svātī, Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj; they are for [rites] such as elevating and so forth.
The *kṣipra* (swift) asterisms are Hasta, Puṣya, Abhijit, and Aśvinī; they are for the accomplishment of tasks requiring speed.

The constellations Dhruvāṇi (the fixed stars), Rohiṇī, Sraṅ (Ārdrā), and the three Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā) are for rites such as initiation (mokṣa). The soft (mṛdu) constellations—Citrā, Anurādhā, Revatī, and Mṛgaśiras—are for actions of a gentle nature. Regarding the phrase "at the rising of the eastern [signs]" and so forth: the term *lagna* (ascendant) refers specifically to the signs beginning with Aries; in that context, it refers to those signs that rise with their head first (*śīrṣodaya*).
The six signs that rise head-first (śīrṣodaya) are Gemini, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Aquarius, and Scorpio;
the five signs that rise back-first (pṛṣṭhodaya) are Aries, Taurus, Cancer, Sagittarius, and Capricorn; while Pisces rises both ways (ubhayodaya).
These houses, beginning with the third house, are not [visible] to Mercury; they correspond to the positions of the limbs of the person known as Time (Kālapuruṣa).
Their collection is the *cakra*. When that is pure, its purification is as follows:

the planets are situated in their own favorable positions. As they say: "Jupiter is in the seventh, ninth, and twelfth houses; Saturn and Mars are in the sixth and third. This is according to the *Sadaiśika* [system].
Regarding the conception of the ninth-parts (navāṃśas) and so forth: whichever sign and whichever ninth-part possess auspiciousness, one should be joined with that;
for example, the first ninth-part of Aries is the Aries-ninth-part itself, and likewise for Cancer.
The first ninth-part belongs to Cancer, and that is auspicious for it. This is the meaning of "its own lord" (svasvāmī).

The lords of the twelve signs, beginning with Aries, in order, are: Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Jupiter, and Saturn; [alternatively] Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mars, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Yama (Saturn), and Jupiter are the lords of the signs. When [the sign] is aspected by that [planet], it is for the planet.

And the aspect is as follows: from the position where a planet is located, it aspects two positions—the tenth and the third—with one-fourth of its aspect; the ninth and the fifth with half its aspect; the fourth and the eighth with three-quarters of its aspect; and the seventh with its full aspect. As it is said in that very same [text]:
"In the tenth and third, the ninth and fifth, and the fourth and eighth [houses], they behold the wife and likewise bestow their fruits.
Regarding "its friend" (*tatsuhṛd*): the meaning is that it is aspected by the lord of the sign that is a friend of that [sign] or by its friend. From the friend of that...
These have already been stated according to the words of Varāhamihira; here, however, they are stated in general terms:

the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Moon [are the lords] of the Moon; the Moon, Mercury, and Mars [are the lords] of Mars; Jupiter, the Moon, and the Sun [are the lords] of Mercury; the Sun and Venus [are the lords] of Jupiter; and the Sun, Moon, and Mars [are the lords] of Saturn.
Mercury and Saturn [are the aspects] of Venus; for the Sun, they are Venus and Mercury. Regarding "aspected by a benefic":

the benefic planets are Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and the Moon; however, Mercury is considered malefic due to association with malefics, but not inherently so. As they say: "The waning Moon, the Sun, and Mars are malefics; by them..."

"Joined with a benefic" (*saṃyutaḥ saumyaḥ*) is again a qualification of the ascendant (*lagna*). "A man endowed with vigor" (*vīryavannaraḥ*): the state of the ascendant being endowed with vigor is as follows: when it has a conjunction with its own lord, or is aspected by a benefic planet, or has a conjunction with a benefic planet, or is aspected by its own lord.
As it is stated in that very same [work]:
"The sign which is conjoined with or aspected by the Moon, or observed by Mercury and Jupiter, becomes strong.
Regarding the phrase "in the third part of a clear mind," the "third part" (tryaṃśa) refers to what is known in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra) as the decan (drekkāṇa).
A specific deity was seen, who was delighted by whichever *rāśi* [it belonged to]. As it is stated in the *Vṛhajjātaka*:

"Adorned like Varuṇa, possessing many jewels, wearing a quiver and armor, armed with a bow, and skilled in the arts of dance and music—he is a composer of poetry at the end of the sign of Pisces. And another [verse]:
A woman, pure and with her hands holding the ends of a freshly washed white garment, having raised a water-pot from her shoulder, proceeds toward the temple;

she speaks of a maiden who has reached the final third [of her life]. In that state, there is hope for such a condition. The seventh case (locative) should be explained as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇya*). [This refers to] one whose mind is not serene.

The Drekkāṇas therein have also been specified; they are not displayed here for fear of making the book too voluminous. Furthermore, it is indeed possible for a certain zodiac sign to be endowed with a vessel of jewels, as it is stated in that very same work:
That Kambala, whose body resembles that of a *kiṃnara*, is equipped with quivers, a bow, and armor;

he carries a pitcher filled with jewels upon his shoulder, and the sign of Capricorn follows behind him. Furthermore, with hands occupied by golden vessels mixed with pearls, gems, and conch shells, he is adorned with ornaments.
"For the adornment of one's wife, a great treasure; a boat for one who has fallen ill, like a fish [caught] by a hook.

When the Drekkāṇa is likewise situated as such, it is indeed established as the Ascendant (Lagna). Being "exalted" (urjita) when conjoined with a Drekkāṇa is also specifically stated there: "In that case, the human-faced one has a body equal to a dog."

"Standing in the hermitage, having taken up a drawn bow, you must protect the sacrificial materials used for the rites while performing austerities; let the bowstring be one-third the length of the bow. Furthermore, it has the form of a horse.

That man bears a crest of pale-white garlands and wears a black antelope skin as his garment; difficult to approach like a lion, he stands in the midst of the lords of beasts with a bow in his hand and a nose curved like that of a deer.

Thus, when such powerful *drekkāṇas* as these occur in my hand-held *lagna*, the gods—or the words [of the text]—are "poisonless" (*nirviṣāḥ*); or, in another sense, it means one should proceed from a *drekkāṇa* that is free of poison (*viṣāda*).
For even those [planets] that possess poison (*saviṣāda*) may occur in those very same [positions]. And so it is said:
"Resorting to me, joined with a serpent upon my head, harsh as a female snake, she cries out while dwelling in the forest;
and having taken refuge on a branch of the *palāśa* tree, she stands in the midst of the sign of Cancer. Furthermore:
"Stationed in a garden, clad in armor, bearing a bow, carrying arrows and missiles, and having the face of Garuḍa."

He performs deliberation for the sake of action within the net of his playful self, thinking, "This is the middle of the couple. Or, "in accordance with the task" means that this matter is accomplished according to the purpose of what must be done; likewise when the ascendant is joined with a decan (drekkāṇa) consisting of such [a purpose] for the sake of cruel rites like malevolent magic (abhicāra).

The accomplishment of the desired object certainly occurs; likewise, such [omens] have been taught there in the presence of Śruti: "O Serpent, a man whose limbs are entwined by snakes, stripped of his garments, with his inner soul distressed by thieves and fire in the forest, having reached the lowest state, cries out for a fish."
And furthermore:
"The first is the Makara, having a body resembling that of a boar, with bristles on its back, makara-like fins, and tusks; it possesses a harness, a net, and a headband, and has a fierce face."
Furthermore:

"A man wearing the form of a monkey, carrying a golden quiver and armor, stands in a forest adorned with jewels, terrifying the deer with fruits and meat; he is described by the Yavanas as being at the end of the *tulā* [scale]."
Furthermore:
Above a *śālmalī* tree, a vulture, a jackal, and a monkey, accompanied by one wearing soiled garments, cry out while separated from their mother and father; this is called the "Lion-form."
The connection with the subject at hand is that one should act "in this manner" for the sake of achieving such results as those described above.
Thus, the designation *horā* refers to half a zodiacal sign (*rāśyardha*) as being "facing upwards.
It is of three types according to its orientation: upward-facing, horizontal, and downward-facing. As they say:

"Upward, downward, or oblique—this is the *hora*. Among these, when one [the *lagna*] has been consumed by the Sun with its face upward, that [subsequent *hora*] presided over by it should be traversed with its face oblique; O virtuous one, it is said that they are "released, traversed, and arrived" in sequence. From among those, [the term] "release" (*mukti*)...
The omen facing upwards is considered auspicious; in other compendiums (*saṃhitā*), it is called "the charcoal-less" (*anaṅgāriṇī*).
For the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), that which faces downwards is known as "the smoke" (*dhūmā*); this is established there according to the *Śākuna* (treatise on omens).
Thus, the desired result is brought about by hearing the cries of auspicious birds such as the *kapiñjala*, the *laka*, the *kokila*, the peacock, and others.
Having recognized that the omen yields a result, even the *Śruti* says:
"O Kapiñjala, speak auspiciously before us, and speak auspiciously behind. The great poet Kālidāsa also says:
"This Cātaka bird speaks sweetly on the left," and not otherwise. Suddenly, it was proclaimed by a single person...
The entry [into the practice] is by means of expressions such as "victory," "merit," and "well-being. The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative:

either by restraining the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), or by lengthening the *prāṇa* and *apāna* through experience, or by desiring to know the flow [of the breath] through either of the two nostrils—the left or the right.

And this is the purpose of that inquiry: even if the aforementioned omens are favorable, one should proceed only if the vital breaths flow through the *amara-dhra* (the fontanelle); the word "api" (even/also) has the sense of an alternative, meaning that one should go after performing a rite for peace (*aśānti*). This is the connection with the subject at hand.
Now, the examination of stone:

"having a smooth sound. Those that do not produce a harsh noise, being smooth, non-rough, and white-colored, as well as those of red and yellow colors—these three types are for a Brāhmaṇa; however, for a Brāhmaṇa specifically, it is the white color. Likewise, for a Kṣatriya, [the stones are] yellow and black in color.

The red [garment] belongs indeed to the Kṣatriya; this restriction is made in relation to the Vaiśya and Śūdra, but not in relation to the Brāhmaṇa, because for him, that [red garment] has already been prescribed previously in reference to his specific case. Even so, the black-colored [garment] belongs to the Vaiśya, while the yellow belongs to the Vaiśya alone, whereas the black-colored [garment] belongs to the [Kṣatriya].
This is the meaning here regarding the Śūdra. And it is stated in the venerable Kāmika:
"These four [initiations] are for the Brāhmaṇa; three for the King (Kṣatriya); two for the Vaiśya."

"By the rule for the Śūdra, [the image] is one-faced; it has a hidden shadow. This means its splendor (*chāyā*)—its beauty—is hidden, profound, and immovable. Regarding the statement "the perfected one is downward-facing": with the intention that a facial mark should be made on the base portion (*budhnabhāga*) out of a desire to fashion the *liṅga* as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one should apply a mark there.

In the case of a pearl that is "mukta" (released), it is "ūrdhvamukhī" (upward-facing) or "uttānamukhī" (face-up); its release consists in moving upwards precisely because it possesses few lines (*hīnarekhā*).
If the lines of a white-colored pearl are red, yellow, or black, then—according to the connection with what is to be stated later—that pearl is not desired for a Brāhmaṇa. And likewise:

In the *Śrīmat Piṅgalāmata*: "That which has inferior lines is called 'inferior'. If there is a white line for one who is red-colored, she is praised as being of the Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya [castes]; in this same way, it should be understood for the others as well.
As it is said in that very same work:
A white line at the top is auspicious; a pale-white line resembling crystal causes the destruction of tools such as chisels and the wares of metal artisans. And it is said in the Paitāmaha:
"A pale-white line that resembles crystal brings about the destruction of many metals."
Make it firm with stakes; the "adhesions" (*śleṣāḥ*) are clusters of lines resembling water-waves;

the "shells" (*puṭāḥ*) are of the form of oyster-shells; the "drops" (*bindavaḥ*) consist of phonemes; and those which are parts of the aforementioned lines are associated with pure, stone-like [substances]. Thus, each of the stakes and so forth is [described].

It should be applied [to the image] of wicked beings such as serpents, monkeys, crocodiles, and so forth; that which has its parts or fragments (*śakala*) oriented toward the north— that is, in the northern direction—
on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) upon the ground, by whichever teacher Śivabhaṭṭāraka has been worshipped, he is thus described.
"Hutāgni" means one who has performed the fire-ritual; "with the common mantra" refers to the seven common mantras. As it is stated in another Saṃhitā:
The Praṇava, Mātṛkā, Vyomavyāpin, Ṣaḍakṣara, Prasāda, and Bahurūpa—

these are remembered as the seven common [mantras]. For the sake of success through one of these, artisans, those who live by their craft, and those who have taken up vows are accepted as assistants, having been made to resolve upon the mantra to be accomplished.

Restraining his disciples who are related to the Guru, with speech and mind controlled and senses unwavering, he should meditate upon Maheśa. Likewise, muttering the *svapnamānavaka* mantra, he should sleep.
Thus it is said: "At the end of the night, one sees a dream—whether desired or undesired—with a steady mind."
Regarding the term *gartā*: for one who obtains curd (*dadhi*) in other regions, its non-consumption is excellent.
Regarding the term *viṣṭā*:
by obtaining excrement and other impurities (*mala*), excluding excrement, it is excellent as a fan (*vyajana*).
"Free from obstacles such as palm-leaf fans" means without doubt; "for the sake of breaking the rule" means for the purpose of subverting the ritual procedure;

"having accomplished his task" means being without further purpose; "he should strike" means he should strike slightly after first marking it with lines of signs by means of dividing it into three parts, starting from the *brahma-sthāna*.
With respect to liberation, but with respect to worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), however, it is said that "one travels from the station of Rudra" by means of vehicles such as chariots and the like;
this refers to the presiding power (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) over them. Having emitted the power of Kāmīśvara who presides over the trees, because she is always present everywhere, it is stated elsewhere:
There is a certain pervasive power of Śiva (śivakalā) that abides within two continua, consisting largely of *nāsā* [the nose], for which no presiding deity is found.

Thus, having honored that tree with the mantra to be recited hereafter and having dismissed it, and having restrained the conscious self (cidātman), since the utility belongs only to that living being, it is "substantial" (sāravat); thus there is the well-known designation for the wood of a tree that has been struck as "sāradāru. A milk-tree (kṣīradruma) is such as the Palāśa and others; [it possesses] sweetness (mādhurya).
"Endowed with the quality of fragrance," and so forth. That which is produced from a tree endowed with the quality of sweetness bestows good fortune (*saubhāgya*).

The meaning is that that which is produced from a specific tree endowed with the quality of fragrance bestows fame (*kīrti*). "Surāhvā" refers to *devadāru* (deodar); "śāka" refers to a specific tree named *śāka*, which is well-known in other regions.
The meaning is that those [objects] made from trees beginning with *devadāru* and ending with *bilva* are "bestowers of all [desires].
The *piśāca-tree* is known as the *vibhītaka*.
The *kolākṣi* is a particular bird that produces the fruit of the *bhedu* tree; those [places] which abound in such [birds]...
And "with roots" means: those devoid of roots; "root-turning" refers to the *aśvattha* and other such trees;
"hollow" refers to those whose core consists of a large cavity, or those whose very essence is moist;
"pitcher-watered" refers to those grown from a mound of earth (*valmīka*)—a heap of soil accumulated by ants and increased through human effort—from which they have arisen.

"Madhupākṣi-kṛtālayā" means those whose dwellings have been made by honey-bees—specifically, by those birds known as "gaṇas" who are famous in other regions. This implies they are not well-known to the local people; thus, no one knows that the Vedas have been brought to a state of systematic arrangement (caturaśratā).
Regarding the phrase "mānonmānādi": *māna* is measurement across the sides; *unmāna* is vertical measurement;

by the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), *pramāṇa* (circumference) is also included, as it is measured on all sides with a cord. That desired mountain-form [image] is of the highest of the high quality, measuring up to nine cubits (*hasta*). And by the force of the word "ca" (and), the *liṅga* is also made of stone or earth.
The "highest" [size] is as previously stated. The phrase "beneficial for men" refers to the *niṣka* measurement. Regarding "reduced by one-third":

from the aforementioned measurement of nine cubits, reduced by one-third, the wooden [image] of six cubits is the "highest of the high. This connects with what is to be said later: "the metal [image] is half of this."

Following this, the most excellent [type] made of iron is said to be three cubits in measure, which is half of the six-cubit [standard] previously mentioned. That too is deficient; for that which was described as the most excellent, rising by four constituent parts (*catuṣprakṛti*), is also considered "middling" when it is deficient by one-third in relation to each [individual part].

By the word "foremost" (*agrya*) which is about to be mentioned, the word "supreme" (*uttama*) is indicated; thus, a six-cubit stone is the supreme medium, and a two-cubit metal [image] is the supreme medium—up to the point where it is divided into three parts. This measurement of the supreme medium applies to all four [materials].

Having divided it into two parts according to the state of the composition, the best of compositions is half that measure. By that [measure], for stone and earthen [liṅgas], there are two types: the middle and the superior, measuring two cubits and three cubits respectively; the wooden [liṅga] is two cubits, and the metallic one is one cubit—this is the meaning. "By their own three parts" means these same three types of liṅgas are to be applied according to each respective material.
These are divided ninefold by their respective three parts each. This is the meaning:
with respect to the *uttamottama* (highest-of-the-high) category, the *madhyamottama* (middle-of-the-high) possesses a three-part status;
and by the proportional calculation of those three parts, [the categories are distinguished] from the *uttamottama*, *madhyamottama*, and *kanyasottama*.
There are six other types of liṅgas. In this way, through its own three parts, a ninefold division arises.
Thus, for the stone and earthen materials, starting from the *hasta* and so on, they are multiplied by nine up to that point;
they remain established as nine times nine.

For a wooden [liṅga], starting from the highest of the high at sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and decreasing by one aṅgula for each subsequent interval, there are four types of liṅgas—namely, the middle and the low. Together with the previous ones, there are thus seven; and below the highest of the low, two more are likewise established.
Thus, there are nine types of wooden liṅgas, even in the case of the "Lion" (mṛgendra) measurement.

"By sections of sixteen finger-breadths"—thus it is also by an eight-finger-breadth proportion for the metal [image]. Regarding that, it is also stated: "The metal image is of the best kind when its internal parts consist of eight portions. Having thus described the liṅgas measured in cubits, those measured according to the previously established dimensions of the temple are now described.
"From the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) of the temple," and so forth.

This is the rule for the alternative measurements of the ten [types of] temples that increase by five [cubits each], beginning from four cubits and ending at thirty-six cubits; for each of these nine temples, the dimensions arise from the measurement of their respective inner sanctums. Thus ends the procedure for the alternative measurements.

Since it will be described as being common [to all], this [specific detail] is indeed unnecessary; thus, the highest [type of] height is three-fifths of the interior of the temple intended for the prakṛti, and likewise,
the middle-middle [type] is five-ninths, because of the mention of the internal subdivisions to be described later.

In the same way, by virtue of that inner essence (*garbha*), it is the youngest (*kanyasa*); and by that very scripture (*śruti*), it will become the "youngest of the youngest" (*kanyasa-kanyasa*). Regarding the phrase "by its internal division" and so forth: among those three, there are two in the intermediate region; therein is the division, and by the one who bestows the three threads, there are six.
The liṅgas become designated as superior-superior, superior-middle, superior-inferior, middle-superior, middle-middle, middle-inferior, inferior-superior,
and inferior-middle; thus, for each temple, the liṅgas are like the measurements of the sanctum (garbha)— this is the meaning.
It is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa* and other scriptures:
"When the [length of the] womb-bearing [linga] is divided into five parts, one part constitutes the smallest linga;
when divided into nine parts, three parts constitute the best linga."
With five [parts], the middle liṅga becomes the middle-middle;
above and below that, the womb (garbha) should be divided into three parts each.
Thus, in the womb, the signs occur according to their application in a number of nine.
By the reasoning established in the passage beginning with "the eldest of the eldest," even though there is a multiplicity of signs,
this [sign] is the eldest of the eldest, the eldest-middle, and the eldest-youngest.

The meaning is that there are exactly nine [temples] due to this distinction consisting of "middle" and "eldest," and not many. Regarding the designation "eldest" and so forth: this designation of "eldest of the eldest" and so on remains applicable even with respect to temples (*prāsāda*), depending on their [relative] characteristics (*liṅga*); this will be explained therein.

Regarding the nine [types of] liṅgas, ranging from four cubits up to thirty-six cubits, it is established by the logic that will be explained below through the vehicle itself: just as for a nine-cubit liṅga, which is of the highest-of-the-high grade due to its measurement, a thirty-six-cubit temple is likewise of the highest-of-the-high grade; and so on.

It is established that for the smallest of the small (kanyasakanyasa) hand-measurement, a temple of four cubits remains as the smallest of the small. However, with respect to the linga according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha), the designations of "largest" and so forth are applied to each temple, even within the ninefold system.
This is the meaning:

even in the case of a temple measuring thirty-six cubits according to the measurement that will be described hereafter, it possesses the status of the "smallest of the small" (kanyasakanyasa) because it serves as a support for a liṅga of the smallest of the small size, measured according to its own internal dimensions; thus it remains so.

The meaning is established that the measurement of four cubits for the womb (garbha) constitutes the "most excellent of the excellent" because it serves as the basis for the most excellent of the excellent lingas. Regarding the phrase "and of the lingas compared to the temples," this is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. And regarding the phrase "and of the pedestals (pīṭhas)," by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that the pedestals also receive the designations of "eldest" (jyeṣṭha) and so forth in comparison to the temples; thus, they are designated in that very same sense.

Due to the variety of terminology, the measurement of the *pīṭha* (pedestal) is established from within the *prāsāda* itself by the phrase "the foremost by three parts of the arrow" (*śarāṃśa-tritayena-agryam*). This means that between those two— the best of the best and the smallest of the small—
by means of the middle measurement, it is the middle [size].
The phrase "it becomes the middle pedestal" is the completion of the sentence; this refers to what was stated regarding the prescription for the *liṅga*:

"the middle one is made with nine or five parts. Regarding the phrase "those others": other than those [three], there are six pedestals like the *liṅgas*; having previously mentioned the three *liṅgas*, these others are the six according to their internal subdivisions.

The meaning is that the pedestals (*pīṭha*) are likewise produced. Regarding the phrase "measured according to the size of the *liṅga*": although it has been stated here that "the foremost [pedestal] is by three parts of the arrow," which establishes the measurement of the pedestal, nevertheless, this [measurement] pertains to the *prasāda* (temple) in accordance with the measurement of the *liṅga* that will be described later. Thus it is in those three [cases].

The *āyati* of the *liṅga* is its length; the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is extended according to that measurement. As far as the length of the *liṅga* extends, so far is the width of the pedestal. Since the height will be described later, for those *liṅgas* with unmanifest faces, the width is equal to the height.

And regarding the manifestation that is dissimilar, [one should consider] its internal depth, height, and width; by this, [the distinction of] "eldest," "middling," and so forth would be purposeless, as they would yield equal results. However, if one intends to distinguish between results, then the classification into "eldest," "middling," and so on is established. As it has been said:
The installation [should take place] in the supreme Lord.
It has been stated that because of the greater number of constituent parts (*aṅga*), there is a greater abundance of fruit here;

this will also be explained in this context. For those who know the *pratiṣṭhā-liṅga*, the fruit is that they enjoy the results for as many thousands of years as there are atoms in it. These are the higher and lower [attainments]: enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

The higher enjoyment (*parābhukti*) is indeed pure piercing (*śuddhavidha*), while the lower enjoyment (*aparābhukti*) consists of the ninefold experience; likewise, the higher liberation (*parāmukti*) is the attainment of the elixir of mercury and the opening of the cavities, which is approved by Śiva, whereas the lower liberation (*aparāmukti*) is the state of being a Vidyā or a Vidyeśa. And so it is said:
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.

The Guru [bestows] the immediate knowledge of light (*jyotirvidyā*), the state of a Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśatva*), and the liberation while living (*aparāmukti*). Here, "equality with Śiva" (*śivasamatā*) is the supreme [liberation]. These two—the supreme and the non-supreme—yield the fruits of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). This is established by scripture; that is to say, it is observed in the scriptures. Regarding "mahānīla": *indrānila* (sapphire), *vajra* (diamond), and *vajramaṇi* (diamond-gem) are well-known as *heruka*; such is its nature.

The division into Jyeṣṭha and so forth is determined by the *liṅga*; the meaning is that whatever is common to all qualities, temples, and pedestals (*pīṭhas*) is appropriate for them. This applies even though Bāṇaliṅgas, self-manifested (*svayambhū*) ones, and others may serve as the support for all types of pedestals.
Regarding the phrase "preceded by the object of proof" (*sādhyapūrva*): having first worshipped the object of proof (*sādhya*) and subsequently,

after its dismissal (*visarjana*), introducing another mantra— thereby never incurring the fault of *mantra-saṃkara* (confusion of mantras)— this statement refers specifically to the case of a manifest (*vyakta*) Bāṇaliṅga.
Since the mixing of mantras is indeed possible elsewhere through the word *liṅga*, and so forth;

that which is the cause of wonder by being the cause of the creation and dissolution of all categories of objects—that the wise call by the word *liṅga*. Even the ten etymological derivations (*nirukti*) belong to those very same entities.

Because [the soul] dissolves right there during the dissolution (saṃhāra), for that very reason there is a coming back at the time of creation; and therefore, that state or place is imperishable and indestructible, unlike how it is described by other ordinary people using the word "liṅga. Thus, whatever is the designation of such a Blessed One, that is His true name, as has been explained and established immediately above.
The meaning is that when that state of "expenditure" (*vyaya*) is being established by means of the definitions to be stated hereafter,
the word for it is used figuratively (*bhākta*) or metaphorically (*upacarita*) because the individual instances residing therein serve as its basis; thus,
it is of three kinds in the manner that will be described, and it is supported by that [threefold nature].
The mouth-linga; [this is] the length of the linga.
Regarding the desired length of the *liṅga*, by calculating sixteen parts of it,

the width (*viṣkaṃbha*)— that is, its breadth— is determined by four, five, or six of those parts. And this width excludes the *sādhanā-liṅga* which consists of the *lokapāla-liṅgas* to be described later.

Each of these [elements] is established in its own proper occasion by what has been stated; thus, when that [universe] is joined with the expansion of Māyā, having attained a certain magnitude and an extent in the four directions,
the squareness of the lower portion, which consists of the Brahma-region, is indeed established.
"For the purpose of turning the middle portion, by abandoning the other half of its diagonal"—here, "that" refers to the square;
that is, the two diagonal corners of the square which are manifested by the placement of a cord. This has been stated elsewhere as well:

A thread extending from corner to corner is called the "diagonal" (*karṇa*). By means of half of that [diagonal], one should produce an octagon; the remainder of the instruction is that one should cast eight marks at the four directions along the lines for producing the square, and by discarding the other half [of the diagonal], one should generate the octagon.
There is another method for producing an octagon:
when that square has been divided by the sages into seven parts, one should omit the portion at each corner, and so forth; or else, by excluding two portions, one should make it octagonal.

Above that, from the eight-sided [base], the portion belonging to Rudra—which is above—should be brought to a circular state, a state of complete roundness, by revolving it from the central region of the Brahma-place. One should bring it to a circular state through the process of eliminating the corners. There is also another method for producing this circularity. From the eight...

First, by producing sixteen sides for this very [base], there may be a sequence of displaying thirty-two sides, or else the process of reducing the sides (*śrilopa*) may occur; and that [reduction] is of many kinds through the methods of turning the head (*śirovṛtti*), such as the *chattra* and so forth. Regarding the fourfold nature of the *chattra* itself: that which is the eighth part of the head (*śiras*) consisting of wooden sections—this is the [first type].

When that *kāṣṭhāṃśaka* is divided by four, there arise four varieties of the *chatra*— namely, the *puṇḍraka* and the others— corresponding respectively to the rotation of the first, second, third, and fourth parts,
for the sake of attaining distinct results. However, the *kukkuṭāṇḍa* arises from the rotation of the fourth part of the head.

The *trapusa* (cucumber) shape is formed by turning one-sixth of the head itself; the shape known as *bālacaṇḍa* is formed by turning one-third of that same head. Thus, the twenty-one varieties resulting from the three types of width (*viṣkaṃbha*) multiplied by the seven types of head-turning (*śirovartanā*) are established.

Regarding those nine new *liṅgas* mentioned previously for each temple according to the common procedure (*sādhāraṇavidhi*): having worshipped these in the common procedure for the sake of liberation, those whose primary focus is the divine (*daivapradhāna*) attained their respective desired abodes. Likewise, "in one or another" means in one of the ten directions.

One should fashion that *liṅga*—which is worshipped by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) for the sake of attaining mastery over the directions through illusion (*māyā*), or which serves as the cause for paralyzing, scorching, creating enmity, and so forth among enemies—as previously described. Now, regarding the *liṅgas* of the world-protectors, it is said: "By means of four [units] and four half-sixths, this is its width (*viṣkaṃbha*)."
Having thus divided the length of the Brahma-portion into twelve parts, its thickness shall be one-third of that;
this applies specifically to all uniform liṅgas as stated in other scriptures. As it is said in the venerable *Pratiṣṭhāparameśvara*:
"Thickness and length [should be] equal on all sides, with the thickness being one-third [of the length] on the linga.
"Like the middle [linga], the eight-angled [linga], and so forth" means as described for the mokṣaliṅga.
"And circular as before" means the circular portion is one-eleventh (rudrabhāga) just as before; however, this linga is of the Indra type.

From the [measurement] named Śatrumardana; with two [parts] each for the east and west at the top of the umbrella (chatraśiras), and one each for the north and south; thus it is provided with seven corners (aśris). "By five [parts] of its own half":
from its own half divided into eleven, by five parts, the square (caturaśra) width (viṣkaṃbha) [is formed].

"From the portion of Brahmā" means up to that point. The center is a circle as before; however, for the *hautasa* [altar], one's own direction is adorned with seven-pointed [figures] and likewise divided into eleven parts. Having done so according to the reasoning to be explained later, one should fashion the shape of a *śakti* on both sides by drawing three lines each, using nine parts.

Regarding the phrase "by five [parts]," the word "half" (ardha) is to be understood here as well: having divided half the length of the Yāmya-liṅga into nine parts, one should fashion the back with five of those parts, the chest with five, and both sides with three parts each.
In the illustrious *Piṅgalāmata*:

"From half of nine parts, two [sides] are formed by three; the thighs and the back are formed by five. Thus, the Brahma-section is characterized by its width (*viṣkaṃbha*); the eight-sided figure, however, results from the reduction of nine-sixths.

There, having divided the back and chest into nine parts, one should perform the carving of the sections. Having likewise divided both sides into six parts, by the very carving of these sections, the broadness is manifested in the region of the chest, while the reduction [in width] occurs at the two arms. In the place marked for the arms, on both sides, one should make them circular by removing the angularity.

Because it diminishes three out of every ten parts, as will be explained later, this is called the *daṇḍa* [breathing technique], which is half [of the full cycle]. And having performed this, the venerable Lord Yama attained the power to bring about the complete destruction of all [impurities] and likewise achieved the yoga that bestows omniscience. This is the *āgneya* [fire-related practice].

The portion for Brahmā is to be expressed by means of a division into twenty-two parts; just as five parts constitute the center of the Āgneya [fire-altar], so too is the portion for Viṣṇu. In this very manner, its circular form is described according to the characteristics that will be stated hereafter, as he will say: "In its own share, the rim is one and a half parts. This refers to the top.

Divided into seven parts and excluding one and a half parts, it takes the shape of a sword from the northeast (īśāna) direction to the southeast (āgneya), and from the northwest (vāyu) direction to the southwest (nairṛta). Its head, which is auspicious, consists of exactly five [parts] and belongs to the southwest. By this, O Supreme Lord, he [is established] in the state called liberation.

He attained yoga and knowledge characterized by the attainment of the causal sign (*nimitta*) and bondage; [the measurement is] four and a half, meaning a span of four and seven-eighths for the width, while for the middle part there is no other definition than what was previously stated. Its head remains exactly as it is.

By placing [the linga] at one-third from the top, like the crescent moon, the Śravaṇa-liṅga is indeed honored; by this, he indicates that it is indeed the Yakṣa-liṅga. However, the distinction is that one should make that Yakṣa-liṅga have a "secret anus" (gududara) by omitting one and a quarter parts from the head out of five divisions.

Furthermore, this "Gadāśiras" [mantra] is for the sake of prosperity (bhūti), while the Vāruṇa [mantra] is for the sake of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi). Incidentally, that which was stated regarding the Yakṣa-mantra is also mentioned here in sequence: "by seven parts of one's own half-months. This means that when the Linga is worshipped by Vāyu, the Brahma-portion is the "Viṣkambha," derived from one's own half divided by twelve and multiplied by seven.

By calculating nine parts and reducing three, it becomes an eight-sided figure divided by Viṣṇu. The Rudra-circular portion is as previously described for the initial fashioning of the liṅga. As for its head, other than the umbrella-shaped one, among the three types beginning with the *kukkuṭa*, that which is most pleasing should be made.
One should perform that [rite] for the eradication of enemies and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by six, by eleven, and by half":

when divided by eleven, the half-measures consist of six parts; this is the extent [of the area] when Īśāna is worshipped. The *viṣkaṃbha* (width) is the portion of Brahmā. Then, for the destruction of worldly existence, it should be divided into eleven parts on both sides.
One should make it octagonal by omitting a third part on each side. The head should be at the north, adorned with three triangles on both sides in the east;
its head should be fashioned with nine planets, using the remaining two-thirds [of the space] by dropping [lines] on both sides across six parts.

This form shaped like a hen’s egg is another method for fashioning the head of the *kukkuṭāṇḍa*; by means of this, knowledge (*jñāna*), yoga (*yoga*), as well as sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) and the status of a Lord of Kings (*rājarājeśitva*), are accomplished. It is said to be "shaped like a lotus bud" for those worshipped by Prajāpati and Viṣṇu.
By resorting to other characteristics for the two *liṅgas*, that [designation] is not applied according to the previously stated definition; rather,
one should fashion the head of the *prājāpatya* in the shape of a lotus bud, while that of the *vaiṣṇava* should be made in the form of a conch and marked with a discus and a lotus.

Now, the characteristics of the Thousand Liṅgas: "Its [height] divided by eleven. Regarding the word "its" (*tasya*), having divided the height of the image intended to be made as a thousand liṅgas into eleven parts according to the directions, one should first establish one form at the front; before that, by the designation of "planets" (*graha*), there is the number nine.
Having thus set aside [the remainder], one should then divide the image of the side-direction equally by ninety-one parts. In this way, there are one thousand and one lingas.
Regarding the phrase "with unequal quarters," it means that between two lingas, the linga is on the back part, and not [on the front].

By this ritual placement (nyāsa), one should mark the primary linga and the secondary linga; whether one does so or not is according to one's preference. And it is said that one obtains all desired objects through the enumeration of its divisions, which is equal to that of the previously mentioned lingas.
Now, the marking of the earthen linga (pārthivalinga).

Regarding "flowing with oceanic merit": it refers to specific types of earth from the ocean, as well as from the Puṇyasaravatī, the Puṇyakṛtī, the Gaṅgā and other such rivers; and from sacred fields (*puṇyakṣetra*) such as Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, and so forth. The clay brought from these places should be collected along with unctuous substances such as black gram (*māṣa*), wood-apple (*vilva*), and *asvattha*.
The connection is with what will be stated later: "having fashioned that [image] by means of that [clay] joined with those [pigments], and having established it in Brahmā.

By the rule stated in the section on the examination of stones, the meaning is that for a Brāhmaṇa it is with white clay, and likewise for a Śūdra it is with black clay. And that [image] should be uncooked, according to one's preference.

One should prepare a dried-up vessel with a diamond-like coating (*vajralepa*) consisting of lime (*sudhā*) mixed with a special variety of *makola*. Once this has been baked, one should fashion the *liṅga* from it; then, as for "Suratā’s womb," gold, silver, or copper should be placed within its interior. These [metals] are to be inscribed with the first syllables of their auspicious names.

These are technical designations intended to demonstrate brevity of composition. Regarding "hemadhāra": *hema* is gold; *tāra* is silver; *aruṇa* is said to be copper; *pītala* is brass (*rītaka*); *jyeya* is known as lead (*kṛṣṇāya*); and that which originates from it is tin (*śrīmaram*).
Or, for the purpose of destroying an enemy, one should act according to the characteristics of the Yāmya-liṅga;
by implication, this means using an object made of tin (*trapu*) or lead (*nāga*), as these two are known to serve that same purpose of the enemy's destruction.
Likewise, in the task endowed with the characteristics of the Yāmya-liṅga, it was stated at the outset that [the image] may be made of three or more metals.

The *liṅga* produced from the three metals—consisting of gold, silver, and copper—is the *liṅga* for the purpose of attaining the *mātṛsiddhi*. Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing any one of the *guhyakas* or *yakṣas*, it may be made from other metals such as iron; that is, apart from gold, silver, and copper, it may be made from something else.
"From the five metals, when one [is present], it is born, that is to say, produced"—this is the sense of the locative case *janau* (in the sense of "born").

Having thus described the metals as stable, the mobile ones are now described. Likewise, in the phrase "mādhūkaraṃ" and so forth, the word *tathā* refers back to the nature of the metal; it refers to the conduct (*vṛtta*) related to the *madhukaras*, that is, the bees.

This is the movement [of the iron]. For those ascetic practitioners who have gone elsewhere from here—those desiring to see the deities, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and other such sites—the iron remains stationary; yet for them, that iron is mobile and excellent. It is beneficial not only for them, but as long as they remain devoted to the practice of mantras (*mantra-sādhana*). And for those intent on the propitiation of mantras who seek liberation (*mumukṣu*), [it is likewise beneficial].

For them, as well as for householders, it is declared that [an object] made from the six metals with the addition of tin and lead in their houses leads to prosperity; that is, for the sake of wealth. Excluding tin and lead, and with gold as the supreme, there is another manifestation of power consisting of objects made from the five metals, excluding gold.
Thus it has been stated that [the object] possesses the nature of being an objective domain (*viṣayatva*). Now, the signs of the jewel (*ratnaliṅga*).
"Arising from all jewels," and so forth. Regarding "vajra": the jewel known as *heruka* arises for the destruction of enemies;
other gems such as *puṣpa*, *nīla*, and so on, are to be understood only from their experts.
*Jyotīrasa* is a specific kind of crystal; that which is born from the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) is for the attainment of splendor; [the gem] is for the destruction of death.

Sphaṭika (crystal) bestows all those desires that have been mentioned as arising from candrakānta and those which are yet to be mentioned; likewise, the śūlamaṇi is established in the world for the same purpose. Arṣamaṇi, also known as arṣāhara, is a specific type of stone. By means of these two—
That which was produced as the *liṅga* under discussion was for the destruction of enemies;

likewise, the *pulaka* was created for the sake of the *sasyamaṇi* for the attainment of crops; and the *bhujaṅgamaṇi* was made by the Goddess for the sake of those supernatural powers (*siddhis*) pertaining to the gods.

The emerald (*marakatamaya*) is a gem renowned in other regions for those desiring freedom from disease; likewise, that which is called *mahāvarta* and red iron (*raktāyaskānta*) should be understood as being of the same nature. These are produced there for the sake of minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*), and they belong to the class of mantras for those very minor accomplishments. As for those [mantras]...
The classes of mantras are those very ones; by means of them, there are other consecrations (*saṃskārāntara*), and that which is consecrated by them is "established" (*pratiṣṭhita*).
This is to be inferred from its qualities (*guṇāt*). The classes of jewels belonging to the Supreme (*parā*) have not been mentioned;
their fruit should be inferred from their qualities. The meaning is that because of their association with excellent qualities, the fruit is auspicious. This is stated in the *Varṇābhidhāna*.

The word "viśeṣa" (distinction) is connected with the three [factors] beginning with color. Therefore, from the causes consisting of the specific designation of the particular color and the particular configuration, the teacher who knows those [causes] must infer the fruit: whether it is a separate seat or one with a base. And that [fruit] arises from gems and jewels.

In the *Samuccaya*, it is stated that the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) should not be performed above nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), whereas in this case it is twelve finger-breadths; this is the distinction. As it has been said:
"A wise man should make [the pedestal] one finger-breadth [in height], whether made of gems or crystal."
Beginning from one finger-breadth up to twelve finger-breadths.
Thus: that pedestal (*pīṭha*) is separate; its base (*pīṭhikā*) is three finger-breadths, the interior (*garbha*) is six, and as he will state regarding the carving (*carcā*):
"With two parts [is] the carving for them; the cavity for the pedestal (*piṇḍikāvaṭa*) is one-third."
In that regard, it has been stated:
The *liṅga* is divided into five parts, and the pedestal (*vāsa*) is divided into three;
one should then place a single auspicious white portion upon it.
Two or three parts of the *susumā* should be joined with the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), with no distinction made for the pedestal itself.

For the sake of accomplishment, the portion of the image (*arcā*) should be shown as exactly three finger-breadths; one may also make it according to the measurement of the *vācaṇaka*, but one must not make it smaller than that. This is its own proper place.

It is beautiful and well-arranged; if it is also radiant, possessing an excellence of luster, then even with such abundance, it would not be a cause for fault—this is the distinction. They state that the production of the size of a chickpea is possible. Regarding the phrase "subtle and having a single purpose," in that subtle jewel, there is only one quality of this kind.

One becomes powerful by that [attainment] whose characteristic is that all defects have been overcome by the living being. And so it has been said: "That by which the price of a fragment of stone is made small upon the earth—that is the manifestation of splendor whose pride has not set."
"May he bestow the Brahman," [he says].
From one cubit up to the limit of another cubit, stone liṅgas have been prescribed; however, below one cubit, they are not seen anywhere.
For what purpose is this prohibition? It is for the sake of ensuring that [liṅgas] smaller than a cubit are not made.
If, by some chance, someone were to make one of the dimensions to be mentioned later out of aversion to it, [then this prohibition serves to prevent that].

One should perform [the rite] for the sake of accomplishing fierce deeds. However, there is a prohibition regarding his favor and the like; that mountain which is diminished by the hand, its strength should not be made firm in favor. Likewise, for the sake of the attainment of prosperity and abundance in the houses of householders, it is not sown; thus, this non-performance of it [is prescribed].
It has been established; therefore, he says: "That [is] in the Raudra [chapter]."

In fierce and terrifying rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like, one should make the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) marked with barley and larger than [the usual] measure. Since it was not previously stated by what measure that [pedestal] should be when its excess is required, he says for that very reason: "by two parts among them," referring to the plural [number].
In all *liṅgas* characterized by the singular number and prescribed for fierce rites (*raudrakṛtya*), the self-rule (*svayaṃvidhi*) applies:

the worship consists of two parts, and one part is placed in the cavity of the pedestal (*pīṭhāvaṭa*). That [portion] should be measured as being below the hand (the cubit) and installed within the cave for the eradication of various regional afflictions.
When the demarcation of the site has been performed according to the procedure to be described, there are no [need for] the temple, the house, the spear, or the staff.

These threads—the red lines for the heads of the world-protectors—have already been explained in that context with reference to other matters. That which is of two kinds is the *kukkuyaṇḍa* (the egg of the cock).
This is for that purpose. The previously mentioned Āiśāna [mantra] should be employed for higher goals such as liberation (mokṣa) and so forth;

the Raudra [mantra] mentioned immediately after is intended for those who are inferior or middling, for the attainment of inferior or middling results. This is the distinction, according to the sequence of one, two, or three [mantras].

From the measurement of the *liṅga*, in the sixteenth part of the *kṛti*—since the products (*kārya*) consist of modifications (*vikāra*) which are characterized by the number sixteen, as the Sāṃkhyas say: "The sixteenfold is the modification"—when that [measurement] is divided by six: [The following verse follows: "Six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, twenty-two, twenty-four, twenty-six, twenty-eight, thirty, thirty-two, thirty-four, and thirty-six; these are the measures of the *liṅga*. In this [verse], the first half consists of the measures of the *liṅga*, while the second half consists of the measures of the *pīṭha*. Among these, the first measure is the smallest, and each subsequent one increases by two units. The first measure is the smallest because it is the root of all others. The second measure is larger than the first by two units, the third is larger than the second by two units, and so on, up to the last measure, which is larger than the one preceding it by two units. This is the sequence of the measures of the *liṅga*. Now, regarding the measures of the *pīṭha*: the first measure is the smallest, and each subsequent one increases by two units. The first measure is the smallest because it is the root of all others. The second measure is larger than the first by two units, the third is larger than the second by two units, and so on, up to the last measure, which is larger than the one preceding it by two units. This is the sequence of the measures of the *pīṭha*. Thus, the total number of measures for both the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha* together is sixty-four. Since the total number of measures is sixty-four, when one subtracts the four measures of the base (*vartana*), the remaining sixty measures are divided into six parts. Each of these six parts is called a *kṛti*. Thus, there are six *kṛtis*. When these six *kṛtis* are divided by six, they yield ten. The distribution of those sixteen parts of the six parts begins from the portion of Brahmā: one part in the portion of Brahmā, two parts in the portion of Viṣkambha, and three parts in the portion of Rudra; thus, as will be described for the sake of warding off defects such as the *dhvaja* and others, there is an additional half-finger in the case of a *liṅga* measured in cubits.

The mouse has the form of a king-bird (nṛpakṣi) Garuḍa; "jīvajīvakādi" means that it is distinct within that [form]. "Of mixed form" means having many shapes.
"Upon the completion of the formation," meaning upon the finishing of the construction, [it is described as] "joined with vermilion when washed," and so forth, by means of milk from the *āvi* (ewe).

Having applied a paste of vermilion (siṃdhūra), on the following day, in whatever place the vermilion does not move after washing and so forth, there exists a "womb" (garbha); this is the collective meaning. As stated in the scriptures taught by authoritative persons: *kākṣī* is *kāyusa*, *tāla* is *haritāla*, *hayārāti* is *aśvamāraka*, *karavīra* itself, *pathyā* is *harītakī*, and *piśāca*.

The pair of external [substances] was mentioned previously; *vajra* (diamond) and *sudhā* (nectar) have also been mentioned. *Chanda* refers to the leaves of the *sūraṇa* plant and so forth. *Sudarśanā* is marked with wheels. *Amla* is *ambilikā*. The fruits are those of *raudrī*. *Ruṇyājaṭā* is *bhūtajaṭā*.
*Āvikam* refers to the milk belonging to pregnant women (*garbhikā*). *Vāṣyasruti* is a flow of heat.
Foam is a mass of water-bubbles; the reflection of limbs is the manifestation of the parts of the specific forms to be described hereafter;

"one whose limbs are perfected" refers to one whose form is complete; "praised" means lauded, while its opposite is "blamed"; the mark or sign is to be observed; and the *sārasa* is a particular species of bird.

By the phrase "Śakra, etc., Indra’s bow, Bhaga, etc.," and so forth, other auspicious components are understood by themselves; the meaning is that these are all praised for the sake of the success of every deity. Now, regarding the term *taditamaṇikabandhakāka*: *kabandha* refers to a headless torso, and *kaścit* refers to some kind of bird.

The specific distinction is that other letters which are modified (*vikṛta*) are not desired, nor are they to be praised. Those belonging to Agni consist of the letter *ra*; those belonging to Vāyu consist of the letter *ya*, and these are not praised. That which is known in the world as "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) may be inauspicious (*amaṅgala*) in its actual application, and vice versa. Furthermore, whatever is well-known in its established context—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious—is to be understood accordingly.

For the sake of establishing its auspiciousness, it should be accepted in this manner: following the description of the unmanifest (avyakta) linga—which consists of the five primordial elements (prakṛti) together with the jewel-lingas—this [text] states the ritual service (upakarma) of the manifest (vyakta) linga after concluding that section. Thus, in the verse beginning "iti vaḥ śaile," it was taught by means of words alone through a brief enumeration (uddeśataḥ). It was not...

The word "uddeśa" (enumeration) is employed here for the sake of brevity; thus, in the phrase "atraca uddeśataḥ," the suffix *tasi* is explained as having the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārthe*).
[Thus ends the chapter on the Unmanifest Sign in the Śrī Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi.]

Now, regarding the definition of the manifest (*vyakta-lakṣaṇa*), it begins with "the threefold measurement" and so forth. There are three types of vertical measurement (*ūrdhva-māna*) and horizontal measurement (*tiryag-māna*). As they say:
"Vertical measurement is indeed [one form of] measurement"; therefore, that which belongs to the manifest is specified as being threefold.

The manifest [icon] is of three types of measurement: this refers to the threefold installation (*pratisthā-samuccaya*) by means of the measurements of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), doors (*dvāra*), and cubits (*hasta*).
Thus, the image (*pratimā*) is threefold according to the measurement of finger-breadths, doors, and cubits. He states the measurement of finger-breadths: "From the eight directions," etc.

This rule applies to any one of the three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) mentioned in other scriptures as the standard measure; as stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara*: "When eight auspicious barley grains, which are equal in size and well-purified, are placed together, that is called the largest (jyeṣṭha) finger-breadth."

Seventy is declared to be the middling [number], and with six it is desired as the smallest. Therein, the number consisting of the Vasus (eight) is first to be placed; before that, again, the number consisting of the directions (ten) is deposited. Thus, the number consisting of one hundred and eight is formed.
One applies [the calculation] to those directions starting from the east, because there is no decrease; by subtracting twelve each time,
one perceives two other groups consisting of ninety-six and eighty-four respectively— thus,
within such groups.

The meaning is as follows: just as previously, when the primary elements (*prakṛti*) were present, the subtle (*avyakta*) and the *liṅga* expanded through the measure containing grace (*prasādagarbha*), and thus the six gross elements (*tattvas*) were produced; so too here.
From the first primary element, which consists of one hundred and eight units and measures three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
By increasing [the measurement] in increments of three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula), there are three types: one measuring one hundred and five [finger-breadths] is the highest-middle;

one measuring one hundred and two is the highest-lowest; and that consisting of ninety-nine finger-breadths is the middle-highest. Likewise, from the measurement of ninety-six [finger-breadths], that which is ninety finger-breadths [is the lowest-lowest].

The middle *nyāsa* is ninety finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the small (*kanyasa*) with the largest [proportion] is eighty-seven finger-breadths, and the small with the middle [proportion] is likewise; thus, by means of these three which correspond to the natural state (*prakṛti-sthānīya*) and the intermediate group of six, there are nine measures of finger-breadths. Immediately following this measurement, another measurement will be described as "according to the measurement of the temple" (*prāsāda-mānata*).
In that same manner, according to the measurement of the temple, regarding the door which has been divided by fire—that is, divided into three parts—one should set aside one part;

then, by the measurement of the remaining two parts, the image along with its pedestal is [the size] of the smallest of the small. In that very same door, when divided by the Vedas (into four), likewise by setting aside one part from the remainder...

From three parts, the middle [type] is the *madhyama*; when the door is divided by nine planets beginning with Rāhu and Ketu, the *uttamottama* is formed by the remaining eight after discarding one part. Having thus described the three types of temples, the measurement of the images for the three superior [types] is according to the measurement of the temple door.

This division does not apply to those names that are about to be mentioned, because a prohibition regarding them will be stated later by the rule "not in *jyeṣṭha*, *budha*, *masu*, and *tri*. Therefore, the phrase "that" (*tat*) refers back to the three bases (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, whatever internal subdivisions exist among those three, they too are included within the six measures (*māna-ṣaṭka*).

According to established convention (*prasiddhi*), it has been stated that the subject matter is an image measured at six *māṇava* finger-breadths; that must be produced according to that very convention. For example, according to the measurement to be described for a temple (*prāsāda*), from a door-measurement of two cubits (*dvihasta*) divided into three parts, by discarding one part, there is one [unit] consisting of thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The smallest of the small (*kanyasakanyasā*) nature arises from the reduction of one part out of a measure of four parts.
The middle of the middle (*madhyamamadhyamā*) second [nature] is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), by means of a nine-part division; it is eight parts, less a third of a finger-breadth.
The third [measurement] is the "eldest-eldest" (jyeṣṭha-jyeṣṭhā), which consists of forty-three finger-breadths (aṅgula). Therein,

that which is immediately below the eldest-eldest and above the middle-middle— by means of applying three threads and so forth— is designated by the names "eldest-youngest" (jyeṣṭha-kanyasā) and "middle-eldest" (madhyama-jyeṣṭhā).

Having produced three measures, then, in the interval between that which is below the middle-middle and above the small-small, one likewise applies three threads and so forth; thus there are three [measures]:
the middle-middle, the small-small, and the great-small, as well as the small-middle. In this manner, [the nine measures are established].
That group of six is the constituent part as described for the *prakṛtis*.

The meaning is that the constituent parts (*aṅgakas*)—which are the very parts previously stated for the three *prakṛtis*—are the sets (*rāśis*), first [by the method of] proportion (*anupāta*) and then [by the method of] the triple-set (*trairāśika*), according to the sequence demonstrated. This applies by way of general rule to all eighteen as well.
When the measurement of the image is obtained according to the measurement of the door of the temple, there is a rule regarding the proportions;

this division is made by means of the three abodes, Meru and the others, among the three superior abodes. He states the measurement of the image in *hasta*s: "three groups of five," meaning three times five, which is fifteen *hasta*s.

They exist. Since it will be stated right here that "hands" [are the unit], the smallest-of-the-smallest image is measured by that [unit]; thus, the division called "measured" (mānākṣipta) consists of fifteen doubled, which is thirty, and fifteen tripled, which is forty-five—these are the three [sizes]: the middle-of-the-middle and the largest-of-the-largest.

The hands are of natural proportions; regarding them as well, the procedure previously shown applies—meaning that, through internal subdivisions, it consists of the sixfold material requirements, just as in the case of images measured by finger-breadths (aṅgula) or door-measures (dvāra).
Now, for the sake of perfecting the limbs of whichever of the aforementioned image measurements is chosen, [the measurement] by finger-breadth (aṅgula)...

Regarding the characteristics of the illusion (māyā) and so forth: whether measured by the span of a hand, by the measurement of the door, or even by nine finger-breadths (navāṅgula), that which is ninety-six finger-breadths long is considered the medium-best (madhyamottama).
For it, one should calculate a finger-breadth by dividing its own height into one hundred and eight parts; and by means of that [unit], for it—
The division of parts has also been stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "Whosoever is being measured, divided into nine parts;
one-twelfth of one of those parts is considered to be an *aṅgula*. Other designations for the *aṅgula* and so forth exist for the sake of common usage.

"It is deficient" means that for that very [unit] there is the designation "deficient" and "half a *kalā*"; for this very reason, the measure of a *kalā* is double that. A pair of spheres (*golaka*) is indeed a *kalā*. As long as three parts of a *kalā* remain, it is called a "star" (*tāraka*); that too, doubled, is a "segment" (*khaṇḍa*).

The six *yugma-nitālas* consist of two fingers and two-thirds [of a finger]; *nāmatāla* and so forth are its synonyms according to tradition (*saṃpradāya*), that is, through the lineage of the gurus. "The Lord" refers to Sadāśiva and so on.
Only the highest form is multiform (*virūpa*). Among those, the Lord Sadāśiva deserves the highest of the high measurements.
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), beginning with Ananteśa, are of superior and middling [grades].

This applies to those seeking enjoyment and liberation other than for specific desires (*kāmya*). However, in the case of desire, the situation is otherwise: within the sphere of Māyā, starting from Kalā, the Yogimaṇḍalīs and other Vidyeśas are worthy of middling and superior measures; others are even beyond that.

The *piśācas* and others are entitled to the "younger" (*kanyasa*) and "elder" (*jyeṣṭha*) portions according to their actual status; thus, in view of their respective positions, because they are the younger, it is said "the younger," meaning that one may optionally choose between the younger and the middle portion. Furthermore, at the end [of the sequence], even the *daityas* and *ādityas*, for the sake of pervading the paths, are likewise [included] up to the humans. This is the sense. [This applies] to the *anuṣaṅga-pratiṣṭhās*.

And this measurement applies to the installations [of the deities] as the retinue of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva—these being installed in front, at the sides, and in the rear—but not in the case of those [deities] who are independent and have not attained the status of a retinue; for in their case, all of this measurement is the "eldest of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhajyeṣṭha*). As it has been said:

Regarding the phrase "born of its own level" (*svabhūmija*): because that which has the greatest pervasion within its respective sphere is the primary one, it is the most excellent of the excellent by way of its result. The crown (*mauli*) is eight *kalās*; that whose height is eight *kalās* is a crown measuring sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The head-ornament (*śirobhūṣaṇa*) is a single peak, namely, the single crescent moon (*ekacandrakoṭi*).

It should be made; however, here it is the head. For therein is established that which is seen in the Pārameśvara and other [texts], because there is no internal space within the hollow center of the crown. It is mentioned separately.
Nevertheless, he will state later: "The distance between the ears is one and a half tālas, and from the line of the eyebrows it is double that. Here...
That elevation is implied by the sense itself. The face is six *kalās* [in height] and twelve *aṅgulas* [in width];
it consists of three fields (*kṣetra*), which are the three parts consisting of the forehead, the nose, and the chin. These are two *kulās* each. As it is said:
"The forehead is two *kalās*, and likewise the nose, the bridge of the nose, and the mouth. From there follows the neck (*grīvā*).

The two *golaka*s (spheres), the four-finger-width neck from its base, the heart, and the navel-circle—these [four] are [one *tāla* each]. The abdomen and the region below the navel—these three are to be made the measure of one *tāla*; this is the remainder [of the proportions]. This applies to the supreme (*parā*) form of the Jyeṣṭhā [form], excluding the specific modifications regarding the positions and so forth.

Thus, with thirteen *kalās* in the twenty-six-fingered knee-guard (*jānupālī*), two *golakas* each in the shanks (*jaṅghā*) which are eleven *kalās* and twenty-two fingers long, and four fingers in the ankle (*gulpha*), the image known as *parā* consists of a measurement of one hundred and eight units. As it has been said:

"Indeed, this [length] of one hundred and eight finger-breadths is for the *parātatu*," according to the *Citrasūtra*. Having stated, "The *haṃsa* is of that same measure," it is further said: "The *bhadra* has a trunk (*nasta*) of two finger-breadths; the *mālavya* is four finger-breadths; the *rucaka* is deficient by eight finger-breadths."

Regarding the phrase "with twelve finger-breadths" (*dvādaśāṅgulaiḥ*): in that [other system], such as the *Kiraṇa*, the height of the thighs and shanks is measured from the knees to the forehead; here, however, it is measured from the shanks. The specific detail regarding the height above is "one *kalā* for the upward height. He states the measurement of the side: "deprived of two *kalās*" means the stake (*śaṅku*) is reduced by four finger-breadths, being one-third [of the total].

It is eight finger-breadths long, including one-third [of the width], measured by the lateral side-measure. At the base of that forehead, the two eyebrows should be made three finger-breadths away, not touching it by even one finger-breadth;
they should be one finger-breadth in thickness at the middle portion, but thinner at both the beginning and the end than that.
