The foot [of the chariot] should be half that measure; for this very reason, the two eyes should be sharp-pointed and cool, measuring two finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the side, or extended by two-thirds of a finger-breadth. Likewise, their front and back ends should be shaped like a grain of barley, and for this very reason, they possess the appearance of a fish’s belly.

Regarding those two, according to their form as described by what will be stated later—starting from "eight barley-corns wide in the middle"—the measurements for the stars are determined by a fifth part of that *tāraka* measurement; thus, intervals between stars (*tārāntara*) of that size are auspicious. However, in the central region, they are naturally eight barley-corns wide, measuring one *aṅgula*.
Because, by its very nature, it is an object suitable for a gentle likeness. As it is stated in the Citrasūtra:
"The eyes of one who is changeless are praised when shaped like the belly of a fish.
However, he describes the different types of eyes according to their distinct meanings, beginning with "the bow," "the lotus petal," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by three, six, nine, one, and more": because there is an addition of one to nine, it amounts to ten;

thus, according to this numerical sequence, the yogin should fashion a net called *cāpa* (the bow) with a width made of three types of grain—rice, barley, and wheat. As it is said in that very same [text]:
The eye should be shaped like a bow for the observation of the power of yoga.
For lovers, it should have the luster of an utpala petal and measure six barley grains; as it has been said:
"The eye of lovers should always be known as resembling an utpala petal. With nine [barley grains], however, it has the luster of a lotus (padma).
The procedure for one who is angry [is as follows]: with ten [units]. "The *śāra* is the eye," as they say:

"with ten increased by nine and one. Furthermore, it is stated even in the *Citrasūtra*: "And that eye which has the form of a *śāra*, it should be twelve *yavas* in length. He states other types of glances: "Equal and gentle," and so forth. And of these...

One should learn the characteristics of dance and so forth from the treatises of Bharata and others; or alternatively, one should know them through experience, since their application regarding images is strictly in accordance with the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*). As it is said in the *Viprasūtra*:
"From constant observation, [one knows] the changeless [state], and always [the distinction between] the flawed and the flawless."
Raudrī belongs to the one whose nature is fierce (raudra) and who has attained the desire for Brahman.
That same [expression] is considered to be the *asūyā* (envy) of the Lord of the Quarters when he has manifested anger;
it is dispassionate, resembling the half-moon, and devoid of harshness.
For one who is weary of distance, desirous, devoid of the power of tranquility,
and full of distress, the gaze should always be made contracted.
For one who is attached to meditation, his activity regarding worldly duties becomes as if unmanifest;
for the deluded man it is like a bud, but for the heedless man it is well-known [to all].
And the Lord should be depicted as squinting for one who is miserly and of low birth;
as smiling with a laugh for one who laughs, and with a gentle smile for one who weeps.

For one who is virtuous, that very same gaze should be employed; for one whose life is ruined by perversion, it should be cast downward; and for one who is arrogant, the gaze should always be made sidelong.
The speech of one afflicted by painful sensations is turbid; that of one whose limbs are sluggish and whose vigor is stolen away is dull;
that of one filled with wonder is full of amazement; and that of one who is serene is indeed tranquil.
For one who is affectionate toward those who are affectionate, who is self-controlled through restraint,
and who is gentle toward all beings, compassion is praised.
To him who was already ashamed by his own modesty, yet looked longingly at his beloved; to him who enjoyed the blissful rest of his gaze, its pupils half-visible due to the intensity of his purpose.

She should be made red at the extremities, as if drowsy, and appearing to be fast asleep; she should be made timid for one who is jealous, and distressed for one who desires what ought not to be done.

The gaze of one who is indifferent (*nirlobha*) is directed upward; likewise, the gaze of one who is to be acted upon (*kāryya*) is [downward]; the gaze of one who is asleep is [fixed] on the ground; and the gaze of one who is arrogant (*dṛpta*) is circular (*maṇḍala*). Among these, two gazes—namely, the gentle (*saumyā*) and the compassionate (*anukampā*)—are prescribed for the subject matter of the deity;
the others are to be employed according to the specific purpose. As it is said in that very same [text]:
Their pupils were heard to be moving up and down, drooping, dejected, and distorted;
they were overwhelmed by fierce, harsh, and agonizing pain, and were agitated by fainting and delirium.
The views beginning with "Manda" and "Duṣṭa," which have been censured,
[bring about] the afflictions of night, fear, agitation, famine, calamity, and confusion.
These [doubts] may arise through delusion regarding the names of the deities;
therefore, these should not be performed by a wise person under any circumstances whatsoever.

Having thus stated the incidental characteristics of the [facial] views, the subject at hand is now described. "Again, indeed, raised... means that in front, at the tip, the nose should be made two finger-breadths high; however, in the region of both sides, it should be increased by one *kalā*. At its own base, in the vicinity of the eyebrows, it should be less than the measure of the pupil (*tāraka*).

The reduction [in width] occurs gradually from the base to the tip according to the proportional sequence; however, at the nostrils, in the region of the base, the reduction is equal to one-third of a *kalā* on all sides and upwards. As before, the distance from the eye to the middle of the ear is two *catur-aṅgulas* in measure, and the ears are likewise.

The two auditory globes (śabdādvigolaka) are four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) in length; however, their specific distinction from the measurement of the eyes (apāṅga) is that they exceed [the eyes] by one barley-corn (yava). Their width is half of their length, and the ear-lobes (śravaṇa) of these two are elevated.
The circumference is by a fourth part of a finger-breadth, and the two conch-like structures (śaṣkulī) are measured by a quarter-finger-breadth.

The *śaṣkulī* is the circular rim within the cavity of the ear. The *khalva* is the circular rim outside the cavity of the ear; its meaning is that it should measure one, two, or three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width. The slightly elevated region beyond the *khalva* is designated by the term *śakunī*. It should be made with a width of half a finger-breadth.
Indeed, near the very edge of the outer corner of the eye,
that part known as the *tuṭaka* appears as if entering the ear;
each of those two ears has a circumference of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) at its base, while their tips are irregular.

The two [jaws] are called *pāśau*. May those two be beautiful; they are covered with appropriate ornaments and decorations. The region below the root of the ear, immediately beneath the chin, is designated as the *hanu* (jaw). Both of those jaws measure six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length; that is their very connection.

The junction-region (saṃdhipradeśa) should be two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula). The mandala of the two cheeks (gaṇḍa), which is spherical in its entirety, measures two finger-breadths; it is not false, being neither too elevated nor too depressed, and for that reason it is very beautiful.
The region of the mouth (āsya) is four finger-breadths.
Then, by one-eighth of the length-measure—that is, eight *aṅgulas*—it is broad.
It is unextended (*avyāta*) and unaltered (*avikṛta*). That [lower lip] is three *aṅgulas*; the lower base (*budhna*) is eight *aṅgulas*.
The upper lip is half an *aṅgula*; the mouth is a quarter [of that]; and the upper lip is placed with a fourth part of the measurement of the upper lip.

Between the lower lip and the upper lip, there is a depression known as the *araṭyā*. By the word *sṛkviṇī*, the two corners of the mouth are denoted; in that regard, its measurement is the same as that of the *gojī*. The lower *gojī* is the region between the middle of the upper lip and the chin; it is measured according to the *gojī*.
He speaks of the double-folded facial thread (*dviguṇāmukhasūtra*). The two corners of the mouth (*sṛkviṇī*) are at the ends of the face;
likewise, the two *jyotiṣī* [points] are at the fifty-star mark. Between those two is the "single maiden" (*ekumārikā*), which is well-known in the world.
These two must be made equal by taking the thread from the center; that is the meaning of "having equal threads. The poet [says] near the bridge of the nose between the eyes.

In the case of a mouse-faced [image], with a measurement of one and a half mustard seeds, the thread should be aligned equally through those two nostrils, the center of the earth, the tip of the nose, and that lower part which is the chin; these three points must be made to fall on the same line. The space between the ears is the measure for the middle of the head.

The eight directions are eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) each. This same measurement doubled is thirty-six finger-breadths from the middle of the eyebrows to the hollow of the nape of the neck (kṛkāṭikā). Up to that extent, the neck is eighteen finger-breadths in width according to its transverse measurement; its circumference is double that of its palm.

Twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). This will be made clear later by the passage beginning with "In all cases, the circumference is three times [the width]," and so forth. The shoulder (*skandha*) is six finger-breadths in length; at the end of that shoulder is the binding, which is sixteen finger-breadths. The two upper arms (*bāhu*) are sixteen finger-breadths each.

The two *upabāhus* (forearms) and the two *aṅkas* (upper arms) are each eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) in measure; the joint between them is likewise, as is the space between the two arms, namely the region of the forearm (*prakoṣṭaka*). That too is of that same dimension. The reality (*tattva*) is indeed the finger-breadth; the middle of the hand is seven finger-breadths in length from that [wrist].

And transversely from the center, it is likewise five finger-breadths [on each side]. That which is the middle finger is exactly five finger-breadths long. The finger near the thumb is the index finger (*tarjanī*); the one between the middle and little fingers is the ring finger (*anāmikā*). Both the index and ring fingers are on either side of the middle finger.
According to the measurement, [the middle finger] is three and a half finger-breadths less than those two;

that is to say, it is three and a half finger-breadths for the smallest [finger]. The thumb is raised by three finger-breadths below the base of the index finger; this is how it should be positioned. Furthermore, [the thumb] touches the tip of the first joint of the index finger.
He who touches the position of the fourth part is characterized by two joints; he states the measurements of the joints as follows:
the first joint of the middle [finger] is two finger-breadths less one barley-corn (*yava*);
that same [measurement] less one barley-corn is the middle [joint]; the other, the third [joint], is the same.
The meaning is "three and a half finger-breadths. Regarding the two fingers, the index and the ring finger:

having excluded one-tenth of each joint (*parva*), those two—the index and the ring fingers—each having three joints, possess three joints [total] because they are similar to the *aṅgula* in terms of their measurement, just like the three joints of the little finger. Those...

The ring finger is one-fourth less than the mountain (the middle finger); those [fingers] situated between the joints should be made [smaller] in that same sequence, but I have not stated [the measurement] for the fingers themselves. At the base, he spoke of the middles.

It is three and a half finger-breadths [in width] at the middle, and it is exactly that same measure at its end, but it is less by one *yava* and devoid of three *yavas* at the edge (*paryanta*). Regarding other [types of] *sūcī*, it is said: "The length (*āyati*) is less by a tenth part from the middle measurement; and likewise, by a tenth part. This is the meaning. Just as the length is less by a tenth part from the middle measurement, so too [is it] by a tenth part.
The circumference at the base of the thumb is equal to the length of the ring finger and the index finger combined;
that is, the circumference is the same as the length of the little finger.
At the point of origin, the circumference is six finger-breadths. Then, at the joint on the back [of the hand], it is...

At the initial commencement of the base (*budhna*), it should be five finger-breadths (*pañcāṅgula*); at the middle of this very joint (*parvan*), it should be four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) due to a slight reduction. Just as that joint is slightly less at the junction of two joints, or as something is four finger-breadths [less] at its end, so too is it reduced in sequence at the root of the arm (*bāhumūla*), in the region of the base of the shoulder (*skandha*).

The width at the end of the arm, near the forearm, is three *yavas* less than the previously mentioned width; thus, it is five *aṅgulas*. Near the forearm, the width is four *aṅgulas* at the region of the wrist (*maṇibandha*). In the middle, it gradually tapers down in sequence.

The circumference is three times the diameter; this is the girth below the region of the throat. In the two seasonal periods (*ṛtukalau*), having extended twelve finger-breadths beyond, the nipples are at the tips of the breasts with a space of seven [fingers] between them.
The distance between those two is likewise six finger-breadths; thus, the measurement of the thread there is in the form of a triangle.
It is established: on the sides of the flanks, the two wings are six *aṅgulas* [in width]; for the two nipples, there is a circle two *yavas* outside.
From both sides, by four *yavas*, the center of the circle is exactly one *yava* in measure; thus, the diameter at the region of the navel becomes five *yavas*.

The width at the base is eighteen finger-breadths; from below the navel, it measures twenty-one finger-breadths; the generative organ (upastha) is four finger-breadths. From its commencement downward, the two testicles are to be made two finger-breadths [in length]; at the root region of the generative organ, the width is two finger-breadths. Of that—

Furthermore, the general rule is that in all cases [the measurement] is threefold, including one finger together with a third part of a finger at the tip. This is an exception to the triple circumference that would otherwise apply to the ears, cheeks, and so forth; thus, by the phrase "excluding the ears, cheeks, etc.," the ears, cheeks, nose, and nails are intended.
"I do not admit that it is not possible. [This refers to the following: The two thighs are characterized by a width of twelve finger-breadths at their commencement;

from there, they taper gradually until reaching the upper limit, which is the root of the knees, where the width is six finger-breadths, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) in reference to the base of the shanks (*jaṅghā*).

The width at the region of the back of the shanks is exactly half a *tāla*; at the region of the knee-joint, the measurement is the same, but with an increase of one *kalā*. This half-*tāla* is further increased by one-quarter of an *aṅgula*, which consists of two *yavas*.
It must indeed be made. In that regard, the measurement for its width is eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and two barley-corns (*yava*).

"The covering is threefold" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. In the middle of the shank, there is the part known as the *jaṅghālava* (the calf), which is well-known in this world. Therein, the thirteen *kalās* amount to twenty-six finger-breadths; the covering is threefold.
The circumference of the ankle joint is equal to that of the calf; half of that [is the measurement] for the region of the instep.

With thirteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), one-third of that is the circumference, and by one-third of that is the width—this is established. The two feet are fourteen finger-breadths in length; what is known in the world as the heels and the toes are four finger-breadths each.

In terms of width, the two feet at the root region, below the ankles, should be five finger-breadths wide; near the point of origin of the toes, they should be six finger-breadths wide, which is beneficial. Beyond that, the big toe (aṅguṣṭha) should be made three and a quarter finger-breadths wide, and the finger adjacent to it is known as the fore-toe (pradeśinī).

That [middle size] should be made measuring half a finger, one finger, or more by a barley-corn; from that, the remaining [sizes] are explained as being diminished by a quarter-part, that is, by a quarter-part at each step.
Excluding that [largest], those diminished by a quarter-part, measuring seven barley-corns, become the smallest [size].

Let us set aside for now the comparison with the image of a Great Being (Mahāpuruṣa). Even in the case of people like ourselves, the little finger is seen to be two finger-breadths longer than the others. Therefore, the previous explanation is the correct one. And it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*: "The index finger should be slightly longer; the others should be less by a sixteenth part."

Thus, at the base of the big toe, the circumference is five finger-breadths (aṅgulas). In the middle, it is the same, minus one finger-breadth. At the tip, extending to the very end, it is four and a half finger-breadths respectively; and the circumference of the index finger at its base is progressively smaller.

Near the throat it is three finger-breadths [in circumference], and two finger-breadths plus one barley-corn at its front. For the other fingers, a reduction of one-eighth part each should be made. This is the meaning: starting from the stated circumference of the index finger, there is a decrease of one-eighth part for each of the [subsequent] three fingers.

It should be fashioned at the base of the nails. At the site of origin, they are praised when slightly depressed; and in front, they should be somewhat raised. Furthermore, whatever other limbs of the cow there may be, those too one should fashion according to what is beautiful. As it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara*: "The body hairs..."

The teeth and hair, as well as the protrusion of the teeth, the joints, and the petals—one should cause these to be fashioned so that they are beautiful. Measurement consists of the characteristic of width (viṣkaṃbha), height (unmāna) from above, and circumference (nāhātmaka). Therefore, according to the stated proportions, one should not make it either less or more.
One should perform [the rite] so that it may yield auspicious results. For those whose bodies are turned slightly by way of pride,

or likewise for those whose bodies are turned halfway, whether engaged in the performance of ritual acts according to the rules for optional rites while standing or sitting, or likewise while rising halfway— whatever measurement [is applied] to them is considered unreal (atāttvikatayā).
Therefore, because it is not ultimately real regarding the attainments of enjoyment and liberation, that [image] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it is said in that very same work:
"An image endowed with those measurements and beautiful in all its limbs should be known as praiseworthy; for [in such a case], the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is not recommended."
The types known as *rijvardhagata* and *rijvākhyam*, as well as *sācīkṛtam*,
*chāyāgatam*, *sarvākhyam*, *bhittikam*, and *ardhabhittikam*.
"The cast-off, the turned-back, and the standing pose—thus ninefold it is proclaimed.
Now, he describes the female image:

Regarding the passage beginning with "yavādhika" and so forth: with reference to the supreme image among all images, two additional parts (upacaya) are to be made. As for "yavādhika": having taken two *yavas* from the height of the nose, one should add them to the width of the eyebrows. Having taken a sixteenth part (*kalā*) according to the measurement of the face, one should apply that very same [portion].

One should likewise provide [the measurement] for the two eyes above the mouth for the sake of superiority; that is, by three *yavas* less one-third. In reality, the two eyes are longer by two *yavas*, and their width is greater by half of that, which is one *yava* more than half of those two *yavas*. The pair of shoulders [is greater] by a *kalā*.

In the case of a male image, a reduction of four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) should be made. Since the nigolaka has already been mentioned, one should take one finger-breadth from the width of the neck and apply that same measure accordingly to the back of the feet and the expansion of the buttocks; in this way, the slender-limbed form of a female image is also clearly manifested.
Also, according to the doctrine of the illustrious Nandikeśvara:

"One should fashion women with slender limbs"—this refers to all the fingers as well. According to the male proportions, the width, the height, and the circumference should be made one-seventh less; likewise, from the length of the shanks and the length of the thighs, both should be reduced by one-sixteenth (a *kalā*), and the hips (*kaṭi*) should likewise be devoid of that *kalā*.

"Side and middle"—by the word "and," both [of these] are free from blemish (*vigata-kalaṅka*). That which consists of the side and the middle should be made; by means of these three parts (*kalā*), that pair is again "solid" (*ghana*), meaning fleshy (*māṃsala*) and rounded (*parivartula*).

The task [is as follows]. As it is stated in that very same place: "Exceeding [in beauty] the breasts, thighs, shanks, and hips. The *aśvattha* is the *vaṭa* tree; the secret [mark] has the shape of its leaf. It is made possessing all splendor. The ellipsis is that it becomes a bestower of desired results. Now, regarding the dwarfish [type]: "the staff-like arms" (*dordaṇḍau*). The two staff-like arms consist of the upper arms and forearms.
Having subtracted three *kalās* from those two, the width of the chest region should be produced by that same measurement.

Having taken a fourth part from the length of the hands and feet, there is an increase of that same measure at the head; thus they are properly disposed. The pair of faces is set apart from the length of the shanks and thighs by one *vitasti*.

And those who possess both [of these defects]: for those with stunted bodies, the navel and buttocks are enlarged by measurement, as are the sides and the region of the hips, according to their respective proportions.
Now, those of hunchbacked form:

"Raised from the heart-measure," and so forth. Having subtracted two units (*kalā*) from the measure of the heart, [the measurement] increased by that amount is to be applied to the chest. Having subtracted one unit from the middle between the navel and the fist, the back region is marked with a curvature (*kujjā*)—that is, a raised mark—made according to that measure. In this way, it becomes curved (*kujjā*). And "those others" refers to other [measures].
And having ascertained from observation that those with deficient or excessive limbs, such as the lame and so forth, possess a [corresponding] physical constitution, one should act accordingly.
Now, the Guhyakas.

"By half a *kalā*" and so forth: a *kalā* is one *aṅgula*. Having taken [this] from each of the thighs and so on, the width (*viṣkaṃbha*) of both sides is increased by that; likewise, the width at the chest and the navel is by two *manus*, that is, twenty-eight; and the width at the abdomen is by [two] *manus*—the word *manu* signifying fourteen.
The name [is used] because it denotes [the deity]. For the image of Rudra, the belly is said to have a width of twenty-one finger-breadths;
however, for these [other deities], it is twenty-eight finger-breadths, as in the case of the mace-bearer (Gadī) and so forth. Vaiśravaṇa means the king whose vehicle is a man (Naravāhana).
Now, the Vetāla.

From the measurement of the shanks, the thighs, and likewise the arms, one should take a sixth part; at that very location, a length of that same measure should be applied. Their mouths should be made distorted and wide open. The *anuvartakas* are the attendants.
Now follows the description of the iconographic characteristics of the image of Bhairava.
"Vaktram," and so forth.
The face is eight parts [in height] and sixteen *aṅgulas* in width, and the eye is likewise even;
as it is stated with indignation in the *Citrasūtra*:
"The eye of one who is angry is indeed shaped like an arrow (*śāra*)."
The "blood-eyed" (śārekṣaṇa) has already been described. Furthermore, there is the "protruding-mouthed" (prasṛtāsyaka) and the "open-mouthed" (vyāttāsya).
One should make the open mouth with three finger-breadths (aṅgulas), as it is said: "The open mouth is three finger-breadths.
[This refers to] Bhairavanātha, whose head is adorned with severed human heads, a serpent, and a fierce snake.

The natural proportions: his chest is six *aṅgulas* wider than the standard measurement; the hips are ten *aṅgulas* wider; and the breadth of the thighs is four *aṅgulas* greater. Regarding the knees and calves, which are well known here as "the crushers" (*kuṭṭaka*), it should be understood that these two must be made two *aṅgulas* larger.

In the middle region of the shanks, they increase by one and a half *kalās*. This means that at the top of the shanks, near the ankles, there is an increase of one *aṅgula* due to a third part; thus is the meaning. Those two feet are slightly elevated and turned upward at the base of the arms, at the root of the shoulders.

The two forearms (upabāhu) are each two fingers more than one kalā; by name they are indeed [the same as the arms], and at their ends, in the region of the wrists, they are established and well-known through proportional sequence.
With the measurement of fingers, the two fangs should be made protruding, sharp, and set; in this manner one should fashion that body.
And by means of a great trident, the great Asura was lifted up; the rest is clear. Regarding the phrase "fivefold" and so forth: the Maheśānas, the Vidyeśvaras, and Hara have ten arms each.
These ten arms of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva were not mentioned previously, but they too are established by this very same prescriptive statement.
They are to be fashioned. Regarding the "vimānas" (vehicles): Gaṇas, Gaṇeśas, Skanda, and so forth. Śikhī is a peacock;
Vṛṣa is the bull, whose form will be described below, and its two testicles are to be fashioned [separately]. Bhṛṅgī has a body consisting mostly of bones.
Tryakṣa is mounted upon a lion. Gaurī’s Gaṇeśa is Gaṇapati, who has the form of a dwarf and a royal countenance.

With the mantra *svadaṃṣṭrādharohita*, he grants desired objects; with the fourth hand, [he is] "the Bestower of Fearlessness" (*abhayakara*) through that gesture, by which the three-eyed one (Śiva) and the Vidyās were created. Likewise, the Vidyēśvaras, headed by Aṅguṣṭhamātra, as well as the hundred Bhavas—all these belong to the eight beginning with Ananta.

They should be fashioned in imitation of Vidyāmaheśvara and the others, possessing qualities superior to those of the world-protectors (lokapālas). Indra, the god, should be depicted as chosen by his presiding deity, the Thousand-eyed One (Sahasrākṣa). Agni should be mounted upon a ram made of wood. Yama should have a spear in his hand.

Śāranetra should be depicted with a staff in his hand; likewise, Kāla is mounted upon a buffalo and holds a noose. Śakra, on account of his wrath, is naked and without clothing, yet possessed of his attendants; thus he is surrounded by the Pitṛs. Those Pitṛs are seated upon Darbha grass mats, each upon a lotus, together with the Piṇḍas and accompanied by their vessels.

Diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) and others, which possess forms corresponding to Time itself, are made the retinue of Kāla; likewise, Varuṇa—the one with a terrifying, fierce, and formidable appearance, who performs a dance, holds a noose, and is surrounded by aquatic creatures such as tortoises, frogs, and crocodiles—is likewise created. Kūrma, kacchapa, makara, and so forth [are his attendants].

He is surrounded by aquatic creatures; he has a deer for his seat, holds kusha grass in his hand, and is Sadāgati (the Ever-moving). Vāyu (the Wind) should be depicted as having a pair of curved eyebrows and being a friend of Rudra. Vaiśravaṇa has been described in the section on the characteristics of Yakṣas, beginning with "Vaiśravaṇa is the lord of the city," and so forth; thus, he is associated with the Yakṣas.

The Blessed One has a retinue of yakṣas and wears a snake as a sacred thread; Kūṣmāṇḍa and the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) hold the weapons mentioned [in scripture], and he likewise holds those same weapons. He is "surrounded by various hosts" means he is surrounded by hosts of manifold forms. Thus said the Blessed Vyāsa Muni in the Mahābhārata and other works.
Some were dwarfish, matted-haired, or shaven-headed; others had short necks and large bellies, while still others possessed great energy, massive bodies, and enormous ears.
With distorted faces and feet, and with ears fashioned like those of horses,
Mahādeva was thus worshipped by such hosts.

Regarding "padmāsana" and "of the padmāsana": there is an optional distinction; he may sometimes be mounted upon a bull, or else situated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), or established in the leftward posture known as the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
The definition of the lotus and half-moon postures is declared in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*.
Likewise, with the two *nyāsodūrvā* [postures] facing one another, one foot and then the other;
this is declared to be the *padma* [posture], and after that, the *ardhacandra*.

In the same way, having placed the soles of the feet together with the toes interlocked, it becomes the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) posture. Regarding the term *kūrca*: by the inclusion of the phrase "bearing a beard, *kuśa* grass, and so forth," the *brahmākārya* is one who bears the sacred thread (*pavitra*) and the rosary (*akṣasūtra*). *Śrīkaṇṭhanātha* possesses the form described for the *vidyeśa*.
The meaning of the alternative is that he stands upon a bull with a body that is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara),
or else he is naked (digvāsas), bearing an erect linga, having entered the Devadāru forest; such is the intended sense, or rather—

He is made to stand in the posture of dance (*nāṭya*). At that time, he should be provided with a full ensemble of musical instruments, such as the *muraja* drum and others; or alternatively, one may represent him in the form of Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa.
Now, the rosary (*akṣasūtra*).

"Or from the lap": the meaning is that both [Viṣṇu and Śrī], joined together with Nārāyaṇa, are to be worshipped for the attainment of all desires. Here, Viṣṇu should be made one-faced, three-faced, or four-faced;
Garuḍa, the lord of birds, is situated there, or he may be made as the one reclining on the waters (Jalaśāyin); in that case, he is joined by Śrī upon the serpent Śeṣa.

The Lord (Bhaṭṭāraka) should be depicted as seated upon a couch that serves as his bed; furthermore, he is accompanied by the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) mounted upon that lotus which was mentioned as being bent down, and [the Lord] is the Fish (Matsya). According to the ritual requirements and the instructions for the rite, the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa) may be the Fish, the Tortoise, or the Boar. As far as...

Or he becomes Kalkī. And therein, the portion belonging to Bhāgavata is presented in brief; from that, the definition [of the manifestation] whose opportunity has arrived is set forth. This means that which was indicated by the name occurring within the "Ten Manifestations" (*prādurbhāvadaśaka*) as the "Great Pride" (*mahāmada*).

Now, the characteristic of the "fish" (matsya) is as follows: "Having made it four-cornered," and so forth. When a square has been made and its sides are equal on all four sides, the drawing of the fish must be performed. Regarding the width, he prescribed the exclusion of one part; that is, in the matter of width, one part [is to be set aside].

The meaning is that one should erase it. Immediately thereafter, [one should take] a cord equal in length to one's own *yāma* (span). That cord which is even is the *āyāma*; in whichever direction its half has been set aside by the removal of a portion, one should rotate the second [cord] with a cord of equal measure to that.
From the limit of the two parts, one should let the length-measuring cord fall downward;

there, having established the lower part, one should rotate it according to the sequence of a half-moon. Then, by means of the formation of a fish-tail (*matsya*), one should turn it around from the opposite side. In this way, on both sides—

By excluding four parts, there remain three parts; that is to say, from the remaining portion belonging to the group of seven. "From the three parts due to error" means: both halves on each side of that [central part] constitute a single *kalā*. From the measurement of those side-*kalās*, one should fashion two slender [limbs] of that same dimension.

The word *tanūja* (son) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indicator). The meaning is that it should also imitate other well-known fish, such as their mouths, tails, and so forth. As it is stated in that very same work: "And the hands and feet of the twice-born [should have] lines; thereafter, from the junction of two revolving lines..."

One should form the head and the tail at two points. Thereafter, by observing the remaining lines—excluding the middle line, the two side lines, and the lines indicating the division of the head—the manifestation of the fish is revealed. This is the worship of the Fish-form of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.

Even at the time of the dissolution of all beings, it is indestructible; one enjoys its inexhaustibility. The manner of this [process] and its conclusion should be understood from the manuscript. Now, the method for drawing the tortoise-grid (*kūrmavartanā*): "Half the diameter" (*vyāsārdha*) means that half of the diagonal line (*karṇa*), which is the cord from corner to corner of the field's width (*vyāsa*), is the specific dimension.

Since it is restrained outside the field, by means of the three-part division of that which has been led outside and the relinquishing of one part on all sides through rotation, and likewise by the relinquishing of the spherical [portion] in the lateral region,
the entry is seen as being like a tortoise due to the abandonment of its circularity according to the measure of the two remaining parts.

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. What is it like? To this he says: "With four feet" (*sāṃghricatuṣṭaya*); that is, at the location of the four corners of the square field, there is a line of circumambulation (*bhrama-rekhā*) joined externally by four feet.
And by that, the length of the neck (*kaṃdharā*) is double the previously established portion.

"Likewise for the neck": the measurement prescribed for that [the body] is indeed applied to his head. "With ears as eyes" means that all parts such as the ears and eyes should be fashioned appropriately for this tortoise, who consists of a specific type of living being. And he is established in his own power, situated in the capacity of Nārāyaṇa.
On this earth, he is the support of the ground, the bearer [of burdens], and worshipped with mantras;
having attained a presence that bestows desired sovereignty, he even brings about the perishability of the imperishable,
and his form is to be understood from the concluding leaf.
Now, the procedure for the boar-shaped altar (varāhavartanā).

"The face" refers to the length of the face, which is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas). Above that, the two jaws (hanu) are each seven finger-breadths, because there are two corners of the mouth (sṛkviṇī) [on each side]. Thus, by repetition here, there are indeed two jaws.

It has been established that [the face] is seven *aṅgulas*. Regarding the phrase "the face as before": as previously stated, this face is to be fashioned by means of a three-part division. Then, by the measure of one part, one should fashion the region of the forehead (*thalāpradeśa*) as a substitute for the brow, and by two parts, the bridge of the nose (*ghoṇāpṛṣṭa*); such is the meaning.
The opening of the nostril—that cavity—is what is meant by "in that [nostril]. Its measurement is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Also in the *Śrīpiṅgalāmata*, it is stated:
"The nostril opening is two finger-breadths. When the fangs have emerged and protruded to the extent of three finger-breadths, [the following occurs].

In the work [of iconography], when the eyes are slightly curved from the starting point toward the ears, which are like a representation of Rudra, they then become beneficial and beautiful; the two ears should measure four finger-breadths in length and height, and the distance between their sides should be exactly half that measurement from the ear-hole to its end.

The height from the middle of the ear is eight *aṅgulas*. Regarding that height from the middle of the ear, as for the other [features] of Varāha, whatever other characteristics for the formation of the facial parts have not been stated, those should be made according to the form of the boar itself, such as when he was grasped by the tip of his tusk during the lifting of the ocean.
The ground is beneficial.
Now follows the movement of Nṛsiṃha. Regarding "the mouth":
it means that it should be as wide as the mouth of a boar, specifically sixteen finger-breadths in length.

"Extended" means that it is equal in its dimensions on all sides; that is to say, when established in sequence, its measurement is two fingers at each step, meaning the sequence is by the measure of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The shoulders are twelve fingers [in width]; the eyebrows are curved, meaning the face is intensely arched. The mouth is the opening of the face.

"Vyānta" means expanded; "bhīṣaṇīya-jihvam" means having a terrifying tongue; and "samudbhūtānudbhūṣitā-vṛtta-talaḥ" refers to one whose palm is thus characterized—round and adorned with protruding [lines]. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the other three [emblems] as well, since it is said: "The two hands bear the discus and the mace, while the other two are upon the chest of the great Daitya."
The meaning is that he has two great arms dripping with blood. Thus, his four hands are described as having the aforementioned forms;

furthermore, all other measurements regarding the limbs and minor members, even those mentioned by Bhairava, apply to him. His garland (*vanamālā*) is woven from fresh leaves; O Rāma, these are the ornaments of the Blessed One, and [he holds] an axe (*kuṭhāra*).

The axe (*paraśu*). It serves as the defining characteristic of the first Rāma. "Another too" refers to the second, who is indeed of the form of Jāmadagnya; however, he is Paraśurāma accompanied by his axe (*saparaśu*), while this [third] is Dāśarathi. Thus, there are three Vijayas. "Buddha," and so forth.

One whose ears and long lobes are like those of a Buddha, and whose robe is distinguished by its specific arrangement, who has previously performed the imitation of the eyes of the one named Padma, and for whom the palms of the hands and soles of the feet bear the mark of the lotus— when this very [practice] is performed while established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is called Mahāyoga.

"Kalkī bestows [it]," and so forth; this is clear. "Brahmeśa," and so forth. "Its support" refers to the vehicle of her previously mentioned form, Vārāhī, who has the face of a boar. As it is stated in the *Śrī Piṅgalāmata*:
"Vārāhī is the one with the face of a boar, the long-tongued one, and the pot-bellied one. She is Bhairavī, whose form is terrifying.

Thus, from the word "Cāmuṇḍā," the Goddess Cāmuṇḍā is also [described] by Bhairava as having the form of Bhairava, both in terms of dimension and appearance. However, she has withered limbs. Regarding the words "the Sun" and so forth:
"Anūru" is Aruṇa, and "Soma" refers to the specific seat called the Half-Moon (ardhacandra), which was mentioned previously.

Aṅgāraka (Mars) is deep red; Budha (Mercury) is a boy at the onset of youth; Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) has a form resembling that [of a teacher]; Śukra (Venus), the son of Bhṛgu, is neutral and possesses a gentle form; he is called "Kānta" because he is very radiant;
and [the Sun] is "Kāṇa" because his eye is crooked—this is the remaining meaning of the word *kāṇa*.

Because [the term] is not established as a synonym for "beloved" (kānta). Sauri is Śanaiścara (Saturn), who is always intent on gazing at the earth with his eyes; Rāhu is called Candramardana because he crushes the moon, being primarily the cause of its crushing. Otherwise—

"From the crushing of even the moon and sun, the comet born of Viriñca bears the mark of smoke. Regarding "on the left thigh": those whose left limbs, beginning with the left thigh and extending to the left arm, are positioned [in that manner];
likewise, by those who have displayed fear raised with the right hand; and the passage beginning with "mālā" (garland) and so forth is clear.

The *piśitāśanas* (flesh-eaters) are the *rākṣasas*; "Durgā" and so forth is clear. Regarding "Gaurī": she is in the form of a young girl (*kumārikā*), meaning she has the appearance of a maiden who has reached five years of age and is performing ascetic penance (*tapasyantī*). "Vāgīśī" and so forth is clear.
With a steady gaze (*niṣkaṃpadṛṣṭi*), meaning an unflinching gaze, he is established in Brahman, possessing a peaceful form and remaining indifferent (*udāsīna*).

Among them, Vasiṣṭha, together with his wife, remains undisturbed. Nārada is a yogi who likewise desires the Lalitā-vidyā. The intention is that he, Nārada, should make his knowledge of Brahman firm and well-established. Thus, the passage beginning with "the seven ṛṣis" is clear. Regarding "Revarda":

Below, the Lord Revatīdhara; and below at the base, the divine physician Dhanvantari, who is joined with Apratihāra. Bheṣaja and Auṣadha, as well as the two Aśvins, are likewise to be represented in the form of Dhanvantari. The word "sravaṃtyaḥ" (the flowing rivers) includes [these deities] by way of conjunction.

The flowing rivers should not be made double. Of what nature are they? They are "possessing lotuses" (*ambujavatyaḥ*). To this he says: just as there are water-born creatures (*jalajāni*) in the midst of the water, so too, due to the commonality of the word "water-born," the lotus (*padma*) is also present upon the backs of the mounts as their support; thus [the group] beginning with Gaṅgā was created.

Various groups of attendants were dancing; others performed various kinds of playful movements, singing songs such as the *Itihāsas* for the gods. Their appearance was that of barbarians with curly hair, resembling dwarfs; these servants were seen within the stream for the purpose of forming a retinue.

These are specific classes of attendants (*gaṇa*) with broad circular bellies; by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that the *kṣetrapālas* are also of this same nature. Being thus established, they become accomplishers of the fruits mentioned in both cases.
This quality of being an accomplisher of the stated fruits is just as it is for the *kikaras*, who achieve success according to their desires.

The meaning of "being a procurer" (*saṃpādakatva*) is "being a protector of the field" (*kṣetrapālatva*). For whichever group of deities—whether mentioned or even unmentioned—one intends to perform the rite today, their form as established by their own ritual manual (*svakalpa*) is to be worshipped for the attainment of the fruit; this is clear from the passage beginning with "in front," and so forth.
[The second chapter in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, concerning the characteristics of images.]
Now, the characteristics of the *pīṭhas*. Regarding the word "atha" (now):

The power of action (kriyā-śakti) belongs to the Lord, the Blessed One, whose nature is the power of consciousness (bodha-śakti), and it resides within His embrace; likewise, the sacred seat (pīṭha) which is of that same nature is what is presided over. For the sacred seat, which is the object of the Lord—the presiding subject—who exists in the form of the Liṅga, is essentially of the nature of action. Therefore, because it pervades the entire half [of the universe], the sacred seat is mentioned first.
This should be reflected upon regarding meditation and so forth,
as it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇa:
"Therefore, the seat (pīṭha) should be conceived as being devoid of all paths. "The union of those two" means that the union of those two powers—knowledge and action—is characterized by identity.
That reality, consisting of vision and action, is like Nṛsiṃha: although it possesses a dual nature, it is indeed one.
"Without foundation" (*apratiṣṭhā*) means that very [state] which exists when those two are joined;

and when there is the presence of a particular foundation, it is the installation of the mantra denoting the Supreme Lord upon a support such as a *liṅga*, just like [the installation of] a deity. Because it is thus, for that reason, the *pīṭha* (seat/foundation) is to be understood; furthermore, it is both "common" (*sāmānya*) and "other" (*itara*). "Common" [refers to...]

Regarding enjoyment and liberation (*bhukti-mukti*): for that purpose, whatever is performed—whether by name, such as *Āmā*, *Payodharā*, *Pṛthvī*, *Yakṣī*, and so forth; or by measure (*māna*), in the same way as will be described as consisting of nine [units] beginning with *Aghnastā*; or by meaning (*artha*), which is the fruit (*phala*) in the very same manner.

Regarding what was stated previously— that the interior (*garbha*) of the temple to be described [is the standard]— and that for temples as well as for *liṅgas* and pedestals (*pīṭhas*): therefore, the pedestal which is intended to be made according to the measurement of the interior of the temple,
in its nine varieties such as the *iṣṭha* and so forth (excluding the *liṅga*), is primary for the sake of success.

"That which was taught for the sake of enjoyment (bhoga) subsequently becomes for the sake of liberation (mokṣa), because the installation (pratiṣṭhā) performed by the agent results in liberation at the conclusion of enjoyment; this is indeed heard [in scripture]. And so it is stated in the *Rurusaṃhitā*:

Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time, they become endowed with the ranks of celestial women, their longing dissipated, and they come to possess the sovereign power of the state of Śiva; thus it is said, "from the hand" and so forth. Those pedestals (pīṭhas), however, which are measured from the hand up to the *liṅga*, serve for the sake of liberation, while enjoyment occurs as a secondary consequence.

By the application of the ritual procedure, even for those seekers of liberation who possess such [qualities], the desired goal is indeed attained through the performance of sacrifice preceded by vows and other rites at the sacred seats (pīṭhas) such as Piṭha and others.
This is evident because of the clarity of its own radiance and its great length; the seat (pīṭha) is equal to its own extension and half of that on all sides.
In this context, regarding the pedestals for the images, one type—both broad and high—is mentioned; however, elsewhere it is described in many ways.
As it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
The measurements of the pedestal (pīṭha) are said to be its own proportions, starting from the eyebrows, nose, chin, shoulders, armpits, heart, navel, and private parts, down to the knees.

And of what nature is that task? To this he says: "The Vedāśra. This means that for complete temples (*prāsāda*) as well as for *liṅgas*, one should perform both types [of measurement]. The word "should perform" (*kuryāt*) is an expression used for the prefix. As for the one who, having imagined a variant reading such as "just like all temples and *liṅgas*," [interprets it as] from the measurement of the temple to the measurement of the *liṅga*...

Regarding the statement "one should make two pedestals," [the author] explains that its meaning is already established by the previously mentioned passage: "between the temples and the liṅgas, and between the liṅgas and the pedestals. Thus, there is the fault of redundancy;
furthermore, this demonstrates a faulty variation in the reading and the fault of ignorance. And so it has been stated by our own teachers.
Whether this reading here is correct or otherwise, it is not fundamentally different; however, because of the confusion of students, demonstrating that [other version] would be ignorance.
Now, if one were to examine the reading quickly extracted from the manuscripts, it is indeed correct.

"It is to be accepted" means that it is not contradicted by the virtuous. "Applicable to all genders" refers to what was previously mentioned; because of the commonality of gender, even in the case of images, when a circular pedestal (*piṭha*) is obtained, there is an exception [to the rule]. "For one's benefit" means that, excluding the rules regarding destruction and so forth, one should not make a circular pedestal for images. "The earth," etc.

The earth and the other [elements], beginning with water, serve as the pedestals for the sake of prosperity and for the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*). Having described those powers individually according to their names, characteristics, and lack of characteristics, they are now being explained. As he will state: "The earth is square and level, in the case of pillars and so forth," and so on. Other than these, there are eight [others] beginning with *padyā*.
The common fruit is that which is called worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), while the specific fruits are [powers such as] the ability to paralyze (*stambha*) and heat (*tāpa*);

they exist for the sake of those [fruits]. However, the [elements] beginning with Earth are for the sake of *siddhi* alone. Regarding "Padma" and so forth: although there is a commonality in the circularity of the three named Yakṣī, Pūrṇā, and Raudrā, [the distinction applies] to Pūrṇā.

The specific characteristic of the fifth girdle is that it is Raudrī; it should be understood that for Raudrī, the specific characteristic is the mark of a trident. From the half-measure between one corner and the corner-thread, by shifting [the center] by an eighth part, circularity is achieved in succession.
Regarding the phrase "by a sixth part":

Taking the Brahma-line of the field and leading it outward by a measure of one-sixth to both the front and the back, then fixing the cord from that increased portion and applying six cords in the four intermediate directions by means of four "fish" (geometrical intersections), thus the assembly hall becomes a regular hexagon with a central nave.

And because it is hexagonal, it is the Vajrā; and because it is sixfold, there is another way [of classifying] the Vajrā. Since it will be described as being placed in front of the Vajrā, it is called "southeast" (āgneyī). Regarding "having four corners":
when it is square, that which is its half, and further, that which is the work to be done upon that—by the exclusion of one-eighth of that, it resides in both corners.

"Successively from its own field likewise"—the intention is that this refers to the entire field. Having drawn the Brahma-thread forward with a measurement of one-eighth [of the side], one should effect a junction from the point where the two extended threads meet at the ends of the two circles on both sides. [The direction] starting with Kārṣāṇavī is the southeast (Āgneyī).

Regarding the southern direction, he says: "From half of the sun," and so forth. Because of a movement of twenty-four [units] in number through both [sides], and because of the circumambulation of half the field from the starting point (*avadhi*), it is said to be "not complete in its sequence. For this very reason, the southern direction (*yāmyā*) is like a half-moon, located to the south of the city.

Standing for the purpose of seizing the arrogant enemy, or standing in the cremation ground (śmaśāna), she indeed effects his destruction; thus she is called Rākṣasī. Regarding the phrase "in three parts" and so forth: having divided the Brahmasūtra into three parts on both sides within a square field, two fish-diagrams (matsya) are formed near the two intermediate directions (vidiś).
Likewise, by producing a third fish at the end of the portion increased on one side, this [mandala] thus has three widths.

Thus, the nine [mandalas] beginning with Pṛthvī were previously mentioned; because the measurements, names, and results are identical, he states all that regarding the [mandalas] beginning with Padma in the same way, starting with "In the body, the wings," etc., meaning in the field of the *pīṭha* within the body.

The ellipsis is "when [the area] is divided fifteenfold. And here, one-third becomes the *khāta* (excavation), and the sixteenth part of these is the *mekhalā* (girdle). This is because, according to the general rule (*utsarga-vākya*) that will be stated later, one must exclude a sixteenth part from the top of the entire *pīṭhaka* (pedestal) field, and [the girdle is made] from the remainder.

From the center of the field, toward the upper direction and the horizontal directions, one should mark those [stones] with as many [lines] as are indicated for each respective portion. Having thus fashioned the pedestal (piṇḍikā) endowed with the eight characteristics, according to the very rules for the characteristics of the breasts in the venerable Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara;

One should fashion that water-fillet (*toya-paṭṭa*) with a width and height equal to seventeen parts; one should arrange that [portion] above the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). By means of that, one should have the water-fillet made according to its width and height. Thus, when the body of the lotus has been marked with fifteen parts from the top, [one proceeds] toward the side directions.
According to the statement to be explained, in the middle portion resting upon the *liṅga*, excluding one-third, it is marked with exactly fifteen [divisions] on both sides.
As it is said in that very same place:
Having divided the Brahma-pīṭha into sixteen parts diagonally, the piṇḍikā [is formed];
one should then divide the space above those two sides into sixteen parts.
On both sides of the Brahma-portion and on both sides of the Liṅga-portion,
two parts each are situated there on both flanks.
Thus, having consumed [the world] in sixteen portions, upwards, across, and downwards;
this too will become clear further on.
Having abandoned the support of the *liṅga* in the center, one should thoroughly cultivate the form alone.

And by this [rule], at the time of defining the *candrakalā* (moon-digit), the specific girdles (*mekhalā*) beginning with *pada* are assigned according to their respective order under the designation "Indra" (*indra-saṃjñayā*). In that case, there is one *indu*. Such designatory terms as these are well-known.

Thus, one should construct those [elements] in the number stated by her; four [of them] from the upward movement (udgama), that is, from the upward progression, and from the entry into the parts (aṃśapraveśa). Furthermore, in the upper part above the lintel (kaṭa), there is the so-called pericarp (karṇikā); and by means of two [parts] according to the direction of the projection (nirgamana), as well as by the part called the lotus (abja), there are the water-receptacles (jalādhāra).
As before, below the section for the exit of the water here, one should fashion the girdle called *pāda*; likewise,

above the two girdles of the one named *abja*, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*), auspicious lotuses facing east and west should be fashioned on that very girdle named *abja* belonging to the *padma*.
Now, he speaks of two [sections] concerning the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) called *vāpī*, which possesses the characteristic of being mentioned once:

"In sixteen parts," and so forth. Here too, the word "body" (*deha*) is to be supplied. By the reasoning previously established, the area of the *ābhya* field is likewise divided into sixteen parts from its emergence.

And by way of entering the divisions: one should fashion the specific parts beginning with the *pada* and ending at the neck (*kaṇṭha*) using twelve parts. Regarding the projection (*nirgama*) of the pond (*vāpī*), it is said that there should be four; thus, above the neck, exactly four fillets (*paṭṭikā*) should be made. However, in the venerable *Kiraṇa* and other texts, there is a distinction, as three are prescribed.
"Just as with a *vāpī*, so too with a *payastri* [is measured] by its dimensions. A *vāpī* is square.
"With clearly defined characteristics" means that it is a *vāpī* only when its proportions are clearly manifest. Now, regarding the measurement of the *vajrāpīṭha*, and so forth.
Regarding measurement: first, having determined the sequence for the vertical measurement, when it is divided by twelve;

likewise, when the horizontal measurement is likewise divided sixfold by that same logic—then, by the designation of "one" (rūpa), there is one part called the *mekhalā* (girdle) and the eyes (*locana*), making two; by that [designation], the neck (*grīvā*) is formed.
And the northern altar (uttaravedi) should be made on top of the mat, hexagonal in shape, by one part for one who desires sovereign power;
now follows the crescent moon (candrakalā).

"Middle," and so forth. Having set aside the middle of the three-fold *liṅga*, when the remaining portion of the field is divided by eight along two directions, there are two parts designated as "Yama"; by that, the "throat" (*kaṇṭha*) is formed.
From the phrase "due to upward movement" (*udgamāt*), because of the upward movement, there is an "emergence" (*vinirgama*) by means of two parts.
From the two upper portions of the neck, there are exactly two fillets (paṭṭikā) for the exit of water;

however, its third fillet consists of sixteen parts and is indeed established as such. And this [third fillet] is provided with a girdle (mekhalā), is sharp-edged, and is square, if it is so intended.

Then, for those desiring nourishment (*puṣṭi*), there is the digit of the moon (*caṃdrakalā*), which is nectar-like and circular with a single girdle (*mekhalā*). Now, the *saṃvarta* [measure] begins with half a sun and so forth. And here, in the middle, it is established that one should exclude the support of the *liṅga*.
Therefore, half of the measurement (*unmāna*) is marked by six girdles and so on, according to the observation of the six parts.

One should divide the side of this very noble [base] into eight parts each by means of six girdles (*mekhalā*), as otherwise their existence would be impossible. In this manner, one should apply the six girdles by entering from below upwards, proceeding part by part in the cardinal directions. This is what is meant by "the neck and lip consist of two parts."

Above that, having consumed the second half from both sides by four [parts] and likewise from the height by four parts, the neck of this [image] should be made according to the measurement of that one part which is the tooth-portion of the entire field.

From the remaining three parts situated horizontally, three other girdles (*mekhalā*) emerge by successive increments of one part each; thus, a fourth is indeed made from the sixteen-part portion provided for the purpose of the water emerging over the *kaṭha*. This is known as the *nandikāvarta*, according to the opinion of Piṅgalā, and is called *devābhyūhā*.
Because its definition is as follows: that [definition] has not been stated here, as it is seen in some *svastika* diagrams but not in all;

therefore, it has not been explained. Likewise, since it is found within the root-text (*mūlagrantha*), that root-text is written here by the scribe, beginning with "above, taste" (*ūrdhve rasa*) and ending with this [point]. The portion beginning with "mutually" (*anyonya*) and so forth is omitted for fear of breaking the continuity of the text.

The many *pīṭhikās* (foundations), which are intermingled with mutual distinctions, are not defined by name because of their great number; they are described as being well-known by such designations as "superior," "middling," and "inferior" according to the division into triads and so forth, and for the sake of attaining various fruits and minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "the three parts" (*tryaṃśa*) and so on: of all these [pīṭhikās] indeed...
By a third part— that is, by a one-third portion according to the direction of measurement—

which was indicated at the time of explaining the characteristics of the *candrakalā*, having abandoned the middle which is the locus of the *liṅga*, there is again the three-eyed one with six limbs; furthermore, the girdle (*mekhalā*) is the water-holder (*jalādhārikā*).
Also in the illustrious Piṅgalāmata:

Regarding what was stated concerning the provision of the sixteenth part for the purpose of a water reservoir at the very time of the specific characteristic (*svasvalakṣaṇa*) of each [unit], that was not demonstrated here because it was scattered [in other contexts]; therefore, it should be understood from those [very sources], as well as the excavation (*khāta*).

The part known as the *liṅgāśraya* (the base of the liṅga) extends from the edge of the pit up to the *brahmaśilā*; the area for the drainage channel (*praṇāla*) where the water flows out is well-known by the name *nāṭaka*. And that [base] is like the *arcā* (the image), because its height and lateral measurement will be described in the same manner as the *arcā*. "In the north" means in the northern direction.
Regarding temples for *liṅgas* facing east or west, it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara*:
"In a temple facing east or indeed facing west, the water-channel (*praṇāla*) should always be constructed in the north; this is the rule. Furthermore:
The liṅga should be installed and the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be installed in such a manner that the praṇāḍuka is situated to the north of the pedestal.

Now, this is its characteristic: "svāgrahī na" and so forth. This means that from the very starting point, it is not [straight] at the end of the fire-altar; rather, it is diminished by half its measure. "This is otherwise by proportion" means it should be performed according to the sequence of the rule for reduction. He states the measurement of the excavation for this very [altar]: "fifty," and so forth, from the base-line.

The meaning is that it should be such that there are two parts of five [units] from the middle, two parts of seven from the edge, and two parts of ten according to the measurement. Of that water-channel (*praṇāla*), the excavation—
the path for the exit of the water— is double the depth from the root region (*mūlapradeśa*) toward the front.

"By which [measure] water should be prepared very quickly, together with one and a half parts," and so forth; "in all three places, the pedestal (pīṭha) of that [liṅga] is the girdle (mekhalā) with one and a half parts," and so forth. And for all of that which has the form of a deity, the pedestal is the substratum (adhikaraṇa), which is well-characterized.
To whatever extent there is pervasion across the path, it is characterized and delineated by that very extent of the path;

just as [the domain] of the Lord Paramaśiva is characterized by the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), that of the god Śrīkaṇṭha extends up to the summit of the Guṇas, and that of the gods beginning with Brahmā extends as far as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Thus it is.

The pervasion (vyāpti) is to be established by the preceptor. Regarding the qualities and defects of the seat (pīṭha) and so forth, the meaning is that its merits and faults are to be discerned— just as in the case of a liṅga— by means of the application of unguents and other rites as prescribed in the scriptures, according to the logic already stated.
[Thus ends the section on the Pīṭhas in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi. May there be auspiciousness!
"Then," and so forth. "One should strive" means one should apply effort. "That which is all," and so forth. *Asṛk* means blood;
by the word "its color and taste," it is called "sweet. "Astringent" refers to the blood of a wound, such as that from *harītakī* and the like; the meaning is "the scent of that. *Bāṇa* means arrows.

The regions of the earth are pervaded by clusters of *amṛtā*, *guḍūcī*, *kāśa*, and specific types of *darbha* grass; their dust is [light] like that of the clouds, etc., as stated in the passage beginning with "plava" and so forth. By the mention of "east" (*prācī*), the eastern direction is understood. Thus, in the *Kiraṇa* and other texts: "It flows toward the northeast"; therefore, those lands which slope toward the northeast are established as the most excellent and well-endowed.

Those lands that are beset with the mire of the Kali age are likewise [unproductive] fruits. The "caves of beasts" (vyālabilāni) are the holes of serpents, the anthills previously mentioned, and saline wastes; as for sands, they are a thick mire primarily consisting of putrid manja. Lands that have been excavated, possess water, and have the qualities of a lamp are commended.

In that regard, the examination of the excavation (*khātaparīkṣā*): Just as in an excavation, that soil which is more abundant than the earth of the surrounding area is excellent; that which is equal is middling; and that which is less is inferior. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "A span deep, prior to filling the pit, [the soil] is auspicious if it is more [than the surrounding earth]; if it is equal..."

The middle [quality] is to be known as that which does not fill the small [vessel]; that in which the water of the lotus quickly comes to rest is auspicious, and that in which it does so without delay is excellent.
This is the examination of water (*vāri-parīkṣā*). The examination of the lamp (*dīpa-parīkṣā*) is as follows: [it is performed] with an uncooked jar filled [with oil] and likewise [prepared].

In the alms-bowl (śarāvaka), having ignited the wicks—white and so forth—which have been consecrated with the mantras of the faces in the sequence of the directions starting from the east, whichever of those wicks remains burning for a long time is auspicious.
This same meaning is also stated in the venerable Piṅgalāmata; it is said therein: "There, the unbaked jar..."
"Beyond this," and so forth. That which is free from the aforementioned [faults], wherein there is tranquility, is indeed excellent;
otherwise, it is impure—in such a manner [it is described]. "Among these," and so forth.
Among these, when all qualities are not present, whichever ground has fewer faults and more qualities is that which is free from the fault of the thorn (*śalya-doṣa*).

It must be purified for the sake of removal. Regarding the phrase "in the field to be purified" and so forth: having mentally constructed the body of the dwelling within the field to be beautified, one should recognize the thorn residing in its limbs through signs and marks. He states this very point in the verse beginning with "evil" and so forth.
Any one of those previously mentioned malefic planets, having entered the *horā*, indicates a structural flaw (*śalya*) in the building;

that is, it declares its presence. By the term *horā*, the ascendant beginning with Aries is meant here. If a malefic planet is not at some time situated in the ascendant, he asks whether such a flaw exists or not by saying "in a quadrant or a trine," and so forth.

By the term "kendra" (quadrant), one refers to the fourth, seventh, and tenth houses from that [ascendant] time and so forth. As it is stated in the *Sūkṣmajātaka*: "The four kendra positions, along with the ascendant, the seventh, and the tenth, are designated as 'kaṇṭhaka'. A malefic planet situated therein indicates a thorn or a structural defect located in the house. Or else:
He himself, situated in the triangle, makes this known; by the word "triangle," the ninth and fifth houses are intended, as it is stated in that very same place:

"Navapaṃcame trikoṇa" means that if it is either adorned by or conjoined with the lord of the sign (rāśīśvara), then it bestows its own [results]; this is the connection. The lords of the signs have been explained previously.
Having thus understood the state of the decans (drekkāṇa), he says "drekkāṇa" and so forth in order to explain its specific characteristics. This...

Two verses: At the time of the expansion of the text, if a Drekkāṇa with a weapon rises, one should know that it is an iron modification, an iron splinter (*lauha-śalya*). The eight [metals] beginning with gold are expressed by the word "iron" (*loha*). And the Drekkāṇa with a weapon was described by Varāhamihira in the *Vṛhajjātaka*.

When the *drekkāṇa* is Sārgala, the man has his waist girt with black cloth; he is fierce like the god Kṛṣṇa intent on protecting, and he wields a raised, terrible axe. He has blood-red eyes. That very same [result] is a thorn when accompanied by a fetter (*nigaḍa*), and that same result is ashes or glowing coals when associated with fire (*agni*). When it is associated with a noose (*pāśa*), he is...

A fragment of leather is the splinter; that is said there to be the sign of the Pāśa-drekāṇa. As it is said: "A woman, stripped of garments and ornaments, approaches the shore from the great ocean; fallen from her place, her limbs entwined with resentment—such is the beautiful Scorpio ascendant. In the presence of a staff, the splinter is made of wood.
One should recognize a wooden splinter as being accompanied by a staff; and the staff is described by the Yavanas as follows:

"Clad in blue garments, with a blue body, fierce, armed with a staff, wearing a blue crown and garland, his limbs marked with folds like lattice windows—this third [deity] is like the Kali age. [This applies to] gems, gold, and so forth.

When [the weapon] is joined, one should understand that the shaft (*śalya*) made of it consists precisely of gems, gold, and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), necklaces of jewels and pearls are included. Furthermore, its being joined with gems has already been stated: "Varuṇa was previously adorned with many great gems," and so on. Regarding the term *kravyāda*: *kravya* is raw meat; they eat that.
When such a person eats [the meat], it should be understood that there is a bone-thorn (*śalya*) originating from the carcass.

Furthermore, a carnivorous animal (*kravyāda*)—such as a lion, a jackal, or the like—is also indicated at the outset by the sign of Capricorn (*mṛga*), which is indeed a killer of men and is associated with poison. And if that [sign] is seen in the ascendant (*lagna*), so says Yavaneśvara:

"A violent man wearing a golden armor, skilled in the application of [subterranean] passages, knows the nature and value of treasures hidden in pits; he is soon robbed along with his companions. Thus, he describes the recognition of the arrow-head in another manner.

"By the *āyas*, etc. [means]: "The banner (*dhvaja*), smoke (*dhūma*), likewise the lion (*siṃha*), the dog (*śva*), the bull (*vṛṣa*), the bird (*khaga*), the elephant (*gaja*), and the crow (*dhvāṅkṣa*)—these are to be known as the *āyas* by those learned in the scriptures, categorized as stationary (*sthira*) and moving (*cara*). Thus, it should be understood by means of the *āyas*; but by what [means] are they determined? To this he says: 'by the certain movements of the sun (*ādityagati-niścitaistathā*)', such as being ablaze (*pradīpta*), smoky (*dhūmita*), and so forth."

Regarding the word "sthair" (by the stars): we do not know the true meaning of these two and a half verses—beginning with "ādityā gata niścayam," "eteṣāṃ buddhyā," and "atha vā kiṃ bahunoktena"—because, for the most part, they are ignorant of the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). As for the passage beginning with "śvamṛgādayaḥ" and so forth... [the word] "ādi" (and so on).

From the mention of "grahaṇāt" (from seizing), it should be understood that there are twenty small creatures, consisting primarily of cats, mongooses, and mice, [that occupy] the field. Furthermore, after the full knowledge of the thorns (śalya), [the text says] "then, by its heat," etc.; at that time, the preceptor, the patron, or the artisan—whichever among them is established in the instruction—[relates this] to that Vāstupuruṣa.

The southern direction is the right, and the northern is the left. When [the deity] is situated therein, whatever slight itching or pain one might experience in that body or physical frame, know that to be a thorn lodged in the limb. To clarify this very point, he says: "From the head," meaning from the upper half of the Vāstu-puruṣa.
The phrase "at a distance of slightly less than two cubits" is connected with what will be stated later.

Furthermore, bone constitutes a *śalya* (foreign body). Regarding "wood" and so forth: now, when the mouth is being scratched, wood becomes a *śalya*; by the hand, the orifices [are affected]; by that, the neck and so forth [are affected]. A chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) itself is a *śalya*.

With three cubits, or else right there at the neck, one should place the carcass—the skeleton—belonging to a cat, from a pit measuring half a man's height. Regarding the words "pravāla" and so forth: on the two ears—that is, the pair of ears—one should place coral (*pravālaka*), which is either red coral (*vidruma*) or gold, or else silver, [taken] from a pit dug from half a man's height.

"Like a pearl," and so forth; "a pearl for the eyes" means like that. "Of the measure of half a man" and so forth; "the elbow of a boar" refers to what is under discussion, namely, the part called the knee belonging to a boar, which is a splinter [used for measurement] from three cubits.

The following passage beginning with "in the nose" (ghrāṇe) should be understood as yet to be explained. "In the nose" means that within the nasal cavity, a fragrant substance is the foreign object (*śalya*); it is generally located between the eyebrows at a distance of three finger-breadths. It has been stated here that the phrase "at three finger-breadths" applies to both of the two previously mentioned [locations]. Regarding "in the teeth" (*daśaneṣu*).

When there is a distortion of the teeth, one should recognize the presence of mica (*satyabhra*). Likewise, [the presence of a foreign object] is known from a depth of three cubits. A bone of the arm belonging to a human being is a splinter (*śalya*) [to be extracted] from a pit measuring the width of the waist.
In the chest or the breast, a bone belonging to an animal should be extracted from a depth of one cubit. A splinter located in the side or between the ribs [is to be removed from a similar depth].
From two cubits [in height]: a bone splinter originating from the region of the heart in the chest should be extracted from half a cubit [of depth].
Below one cubit is the "paryāṅka" (bed-frame); in the hip region of a bed-part, it is "āvāma" due to its deformity;
and the "caimara" is scattered.
One should extract a splinter resembling a stake from a distance of three cubits. Regarding "black iron":
one should identify a splinter made of *caimara* wood as being at a distance of three cubits. Regarding "three metals" beneath a pit measuring one cubit:
one should extract a splinter consisting of gold, silver, and copper from the buttocks—that is, from the posterior part of the back.

The *vayava* is denoted by the word *sphik*. Scratching that [spot] results in a dart consisting mostly of tin, shaped like a hook and measuring half a man's height. In the two thighs, there is a core of wood; from a hand and a half above the knees, it is a pillar-like structure, just like a pillar.

"Like a wooden razor, etc. means that one should lift up from beneath the hand— either a barber's tool, a razor, or by the inclusion of "etcetera," a pair of scissors or a knife— alternatively, as the remainder [of the sentence] indicates, from the wrist, which is three parts less than the length of the hand.

One should understand that "turaṅga" refers to the horse; one should designate its foot as "turaṅgapāda. "Dvirada" refers to the elephant; "dvairada" refers to this [elephant's] tusk and so forth—the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes the trunk and other parts. In this manner, one should observe some foreign object (śalya) generally below the hand. This applies when there is itching of the foot, according to the context.

"Regarding the thumb": since that very foot is the subject under discussion, "impurity" (*śalya*) refers to lead, tin, or iron. Likewise, one should remove impurities such as a skin scab, a leather thong, or similar items used for scratching or for the foot, rather than for mere contact. "With the hand" means while remaining in that very position until an exception occurs; when there is a deformity of the little finger, [one uses] "the sound."

One should understand that a bronze splinter (*kāṃsya-śalya*) is located in the middle; [the text] says "the thumb is deformed. When a splinter of brass (*ārakūṭa*) and so forth is mentioned as being in the thumb, that very same [splinter] is called a "foot-splinter" (*padya*); it is a leather splinter (*carma-śalya*) placed in the sole of the foot, hence it is called *padya*.
Those limbs which have been mentioned, those parts of them which are situated above or below and are proximate are the "subsidiary parts" (*upāṅga*).

When those [wounds] have been scratched, one should extract the types of foreign bodies (*śalya*) mentioned as being composed of those [materials], which were described according to their constituent parts. Alternatively, it may be asked: how can gold, silver, and so forth be called "foreign bodies" (*śalya*), as was stated previously? To this it is replied: because the nature (*tattva*) and other qualities of foreign bodies cannot be determined by name alone; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), they are included among those already mentioned.

Whatever has been stated regarding specific locations, that alone constitutes the "spear" (*śalya*) there; thus, even if other measurements are mentioned, they are not considered defects. This rule concerning jewels, gold, and so forth—stating "only that much," and so on—refers to digging to the extent of the stated measurement until the sight of the spear occurs.
