That much [is the limit].

Immediately after that, one should purify the ground. Or else—this indicates recourse to an alternative view—the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of providing an option, meaning up until the sight of water. Regarding the phrase "that stone," and so forth: that ground is filled by the hand; thus, it is "karāpūra. By those measures, eight [handfuls] equal eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*).
"By those with soft interiors" means having completed [the altar] with a very level interior. "Likewise,
with desirable slopes" means that since in all the *Saṃhitās* it is stated that the eastern and northern slopes are the most excellent,
one should construct it in that manner according to the reasoning to be explained immediately hereafter.
One should worship the deities whose names will be mentioned later, who reside within the layout of the site (*vāstu*), beginning with "Shadow" (*chāyā*) and so forth.
The sphere (*gola*) is marked at its central region; that which is situated there, being the *saṃku* (the gnomon), is brought [as the result] by means of it as an instrument.

Having understood the direction from the two marks of the shadow produced in the eastern and western directions, [one proceeds] by means of the "piercing of the pole star" (*dhruvavedha*). Since this verse likewise depends upon the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), we do not know its true meaning. It is stated for the sake of thoroughly understanding the nature of reality: "of the subjects," and so forth.

The offspring of Cakṣus is Cākṣuṣa, the son of Brahmā; "his ill-health" refers to that. "Bhūtakṛt" (the creator of beings) refers to Umāpati (Śiva), who is the benefactor of the world and the performer of universal welfare. Regarding the phrase beginning with "by a rope" (*rajjvā*): the eightfold rope itself is a great noose;
by that, or by the two lineages whose names will be mentioned below, his body was tormented.

Immediately after performing that [square], Śaṅkara himself made it four-cornered. Regarding this, for those who raise the objection as to how the worship and other rites of the Vāstu-deities should be performed during the division of the ground-plan (vāstudevatā-pada-vibhāga) for the temples whose names will be mentioned here— such as the circular, hexagonal, octagonal, and so forth— it is by this very [method] that [the answer is given].

The answer is given in a verse: having first worshipped the body of Vāstu belonging to whichever temple it may be, one should then proceed with the construction of the desired temple. Furthermore, the manifestation of other fields is seen from a square field alone; and so it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇa: "Of all..."
"A field that is square is a field on all sides. Regarding "its body" (*tadvapuḥ*) and so forth: it "remains awake" (*jāgarti*), meaning it stands firm.
To demonstrate the etymological significance of the term *vāstu*, he says "the gods" (*deva*) and so forth. Because the gods dwell (*adhivasanti*) upon its body, it is therefore called *vastu*.
Furthermore, because [the deity] always remains present in the house where one dwells (*vasati*), [it is so called]. Regarding "desired" (*iṣṭa*) and so forth...

For the sake of protecting the vital points (*marmans*) and manifesting the intended qualities, [the body] becomes otherwise through non-protection or piercing. Regarding the phrase "those bodies" and so forth: those twenty channels (*nāḍīs*) in that body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the wind (*vāyu*), and its deity—[this applies] when there is indeed that very [deity] of the house and the site (*gṛhavāstu*).

By the word "sannidheḥ" (from proximity), because it is required first; "īritaḥ" means uttered, as in "manoratha" and so forth. And those [directions] beginning with Manoratha and ending with Śānti are the ten eastern ones. "Pūrvānanāḥ" refers to the directions starting from the north of the lunar portion. "Antakāntam" refers to the southern direction.

Indeed, as long as they remain established—beginning with *bhā* and ending with *hiratādaśottarānanā*—these twenty [syllables] become the causes for the destruction of the objects corresponding to those who are afflicted. When protected, they perform their virtuous functions. Regarding "Agnīṣoma" and so forth: among these twenty that have been enumerated, those which are to be accomplished...

Thus, there are six channels in the center; in the middle of those is the Suṣumṇā. According to the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), there are ten channels, while according to the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), there are three primary channels.
Thus, there are six [channels] in the region of the directions, specifically in the quarters of the compass.

Regarding the phrase "the head of Vāstoṣpati has six faces": according to the statement to be made later, there are six *sauṣumṇa* [bricks] in the eastern portion (*vāsabhāga*), seven *aiḍya* bricks in the southern portion, and seven *paiṅgalya* bricks in another location; furthermore, this will be clarified during the time of the arrangement (*prastāra*) of the other *vāstu* at the beginning of the fire-altar (*agniciti*).
When the *sīrā* is pierced, eleven *sauṣumṇa* vessels emerge as before;
there are eight *aiḍa* and eight *piṅgalā* great vessels.
By this [statement], he explains that among these ten channels, six—beginning with Suṣumṇā—are set aside, while the remaining four are Aiḍa and Piṅgalā; furthermore, these belong to those same ten.
Thus, due to ignorance regarding their true nature, one might think they reside within a single body.

The two bodies, situated between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, are made known by the pair of *suṣumṇās*. Furthermore, the consistency of the meaning with the words to be spoken hereafter is demonstrated. Moreover, [the phrase] "only for those who possess the [correct] view" is a qualifying attribute of the proponent; there is no [such qualification] merely by name, having already stated the twenty-fold system of channels (*nāḍī*).

From among all these [qualities], because of their inclusion therein—whatever has been stated by the author of the Sūtra, let that dear-to-the-gods (the fool) explain exactly according to his own fancy. Regarding the phrase "of these" and so forth: of these twenty enumerated [qualities], due to the application of the excellence of the cloth, there are many great benefits and transformations.

Regarding what will be stated, "contraction" and so forth: even when the site (*vāstu*) is very small, provided that the number of squares (*pada*) is few, the nature of being composed of the *pitṛs* (ancestors) remains; that is to say, its nature as consisting of the *suṣumṇā*, *iḍā*, and *piṅgalā* channels does not cease. Regarding the term "transverse": the second portion named Durjaya is situated in the southeast and northwest corners, while [the third] is situated in the northeast and southwest corners.
"Difficult to sustain," "Brahman," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in any place whatsoever":

whether it be the placement of pillars in a house, or the placement of the Brahma-stone in a temple, and so on, one must certainly avoid even a portion as small as a mustard seed by means of the *aṇu* [mantra].
And it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
Having understood this connection of the sutras, that would be the vital point (marman);
one should know that the vital point is situated in the middle, and therefore one should avoid it with effort.
Having divided that [area] into sixteen parts, one should again divide one of those vital points (marman) into sixteen parts; one should avoid that very portion which remains deficient.

Thus, regarding the passage beginning with *samasta* and so forth: through the complete descents (*samyak-pātaiḥ*) of all the channels (*nāḍī*), specific configurations arise; these are called "joints" (*saṃdhi*). And as for the phrase "in the dwelling" (*vasatau*): when they are situated within the house, they become the cause for the contraction of the joints of the limbs of any one among the agent, the architect, or the master.

"Of the Sūris" means of the Ācāryas. Regarding "in the mouth," etc.: among these [mantras] beginning with the Pravaktṛ, one should understand the four cords (*rajjus*) starting with Kīlakī; and among those beginning with Hṛd, the four beginning with Sadbhāva will be explained later. Regarding "the Parās": those which were first mentioned are the three-footed ones (*tripadāḥ*). Afterwards...
It is established that they are called "six-footed" (*ṣaṭpada*). Regarding "rope," etc.: "conjunction" (*saṃpāta*) means a friction;

"eight-limbed lotus" (*aṣṭāṅgapadma*) refers to a lotus characterized by eight parts, which is to be inferred from its defining marks. "Adorned" (*upaskṛta*) means pressed. Regarding "trident," etc., in those locations there is, by implication, a pair of bamboo tubes.
The trident is characterized by three half-devas. "That very [thing]" and so forth:

one should know that very trident to be a vajra due to its presence on both sides. "By walls and so forth" refers to the primary materials; "bamboo and so forth" means it is joined precisely at the corner regions by means of bamboo and rope—that is, its connection takes the form of a triangle.
"Half of that," and so forth: by means of half of the *saṃpuṭa*, there shall be a vital point (*marman*) in the form of a balance.
"The square," and so forth: the meaning is that by means of the two cords alone, there is a group of four in the middle of the square, which are the vital points known as the respective *svastikas*.
"As stated for the cords and the bamboo," and so forth: it arises from the cords and the bamboo in that very same form.
The only distinction is that it is called the "Great Svastika" (*mahāsvastika*), as indicated by the passage beginning with "great fear" (*mahābhaya*). Regarding the term "pure" (*śuddha*):
it refers to that which, being square, serves as the dwelling place for the feet at midday. As for the passage beginning with "at the end of sleep" (*svapnānte*):
the junction of the channels (*nāḍī*) at the end of sleep constitutes the vital point (*marman*) known as *trikaṭa*. For this reason—

That [hand] consists of three [parts], because it is produced from the form of a trident; thus, through the birth of the offspring, it is said to be fivefold, and so forth. "That very same" means that by means of the three-fold [structure] itself, it is fivefold, consisting of five parts known as the wrist-joint (*maṇibandhana*). By the word "sheath" (*kośa*), the moving [organ] is expressed. "These," and so forth.

"These" refers to the twelve known as the vital points (*marmans*), namely: the great vital point-junction (*mahāmarmasaṃdhi*), the lotus-vital point (*marmapaṅkaja*), the trident-vajra-impact (*triśūlavajrasaṃpāta*), the plow (*hala*), the svastika, the great svastika (*mahāsvastika*), the pure foot (*śuddhapada*), the triple-angle (*trikaṭa*), and the wrist-joint (*maṇibandhana*). If the practitioner avoids these, together with the performer of the rite, [he shall succeed].
One obtains what is desired. Regarding the passage beginning with "of that," etc.: "of that" refers to the body; "prāgbhāvam" means the southern [side];
"ayyam" means the western; "udbhavam" means the northern. Having "viṣṭabhya" means having presided over [the directions]. Regarding "in the east," etc.:
although one part of the bamboo has been halved by the cords, nevertheless...

That [deity] is indeed the totality, because it will be described as being a part—as half of a single temple, half of the site of that temple, or half of the feet of certain deities. Regarding the phrase "in the center of Brahmā":
the peripheral deities are thirty-two, situated in the enclosure of the outer cells starting from the northeast (Īśāna), while in the center—

"Brahmā, Marīci," and so forth. "From this" refers to Brahmā himself; in the eastern direction is Marīci, who is six-footed. This connects with what is to be said later. Regarding "Mṛtyujit in the southern quarter" and "Āpavatsa," and so on, in the case of "Rākṣasakṣma in Nābhasvatī," the meaning takes precedence over the order of recitation.

The sequence should be followed accordingly: having first placed Indra in the southeast corner (Agni), one should thereafter place Rājayakṣmā in the northwest corner (Vāyu). "In that very same way" means that just as there are two two-footed deities beginning with Apavatsa, so too are there four deities beginning with Jayā and Śūlin—namely, Indra, Jaya, Rudra, and Dāsa.

The meaning is that these four [lines] belong to her in the remaining squares immediately following those [already mentioned], starting from Āpavatsa and proceeding by placing groups of four, beginning with Śaṅkara. "Outside the enclosure" means in the corners starting from the northeast (Īśāna); there are four Rākṣasīs. "Mahāntam" means old. "Arbukam" means...

To dispel the doubt as to how many deities reside in the fields (*kṣetra*), he says "in the field," and so forth. "The group of five" means forty-five. If one asks how that is so, it is because there are thirty-two starting from Īśa and ending with Brahmā, Marīci, Vivasvat, and Mitra.

The *pṛthavīdhara* [plan] consists of the *pāpa*, *vatsa*, *savitṛ*, *sāvitra*, *indra*, *aindra*, *jaya*, *yara*, and *rudra*; with *rudradāsa* added, there are thirteen, and thus forty-five in total. "In any place whatsoever" means that for all the houses to be described hereafter, such as the four-winged (*catuḥśālā*) and others, there is a pair of quadrangles situated on the exterior.

"Forty-five together with the divine pillar and the Brahma-stone"—this verse is a restatement of what was previously mentioned; it describes the layout of the temple site (*devagṛhavāstu*). "Nine in the east," and so forth: "nine in the east" means they are included within the eastern [direction].
Thus, the end of one [measurement] is included within another, and that [end] is likewise included within yet another, and so on.

And it has been said: "Sixty squares are produced in the field. This refers to all the palaces to be described hereafter, such as Meru and others, as he stated: "The field consists of sixty-four squares in all the abodes of the gods. In that regard:

"Caditi," "Ceśa," "Khakṛṣāṇu"—these are the eight [deities] residing in the corners of the intermediate space (antarikṣa); "Strīmṛga," "Pitṛnāman," "Rogāḍhya," and "Vāyu"—these are the eight residing in the half-corners (ardhakoṇa).
The remaining twenty-four are single-footed (padika) in the outer enclosure. This is the subject at hand. And it has been said:
In the venerable Kiraṇa [Tantra].
Diti, Īśa, Antarikṣa, Agni, Mṛga, and he known as Pitṛ;
Pāpa, Yakṣman, and Roga—these are the deities residing in the corners and the intercalary day (Āsyā).
If Parjanya and the others are said to be joined with [their consorts], they should nevertheless be known as single-padas;

that is to say, Koṇabhṛt, Oṣṭha, and so forth—namely Āpavatsa and the rest, eight in total—are like the outer deities, meaning Parjanya and the others are each one-pada. Just as before, Marīci and the others are likewise six-padas as previously described; however—
Through the variety of the four positions, by means of the function of Parjanya and the others, there are four feet below;

beneath those, there are two feet. In this form, Marīci consists of six feet. Likewise, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Payodhara—thus, there are eight one-footed [deities] occupying the corners, forming the two *vaṃśas*.

The eight feet are the eight *pada*s; the goal is accomplished by means of the sixty-four *pada*s of the site (*vāstu*). Now, the person of the site (*vāstupuruṣa*) is to be understood as inferable through his symbolic form (*rūpaka*) based on his abiding state as a deity; for that purpose, it is said:
"Brahmā’s navel," and so forth, meaning that which has Brahmā’s navel. And it has been stated: "Brahmā is in the center, consisting of four *pada*s."
And the navel is indeed the central location; this is also stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*.

It is said that he has attained the state of Brahmā. "The feet of the Father" refers to those situated in the south-western corner (Nairṛtakoṇa); for there, the deity named Pitṛ resides at his feet. This is also stated in the venerable Kiraṇatantra.
"Two feet in the southwest" means that in the northeast corner (Īśāna), there is the head;

"of whom the head is [there]" refers to the head of the deity Īśāna in the Vāstu diagram. Furthermore, "the calves" refers to the mouth, which is located in the position below the northeast corner of the Lord of Devas (Deveśāna).

Regarding the phrase "with that [hand] likewise possessing the neck" (*sakaṃdharā*), it means "by him whose neck (*kaṇṭha*) possesses the earth along with the calves (*sapavatsakam*)," thus forming a pair of hands holding the two corners. Consequently, the remaining two—the Savitṛ and Sāvitra [hands], as well as Rudra and Rudradāsa—are designated as the right and left hands respectively. This is also stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "Savitṛ is his hand."
"Diti and Parjanya are the meanings of the word. This means that Diti and Parjanya are the ears, and sound is the purpose (*prayojana*) of those two ears.
Jayāditya is the one with the pair [of ears], known as Jaya; Aditi is his two shoulders.
"The Ṛgveda and Indra, etc. refers to the six beginning with the Ṛgveda and the six beginning with Indra, respectively.

"By the pair situated in the directions of the north and south arms"—meaning that pair situated in the direction of Nairṛta (the southwest) consists of two corners; their lords are those who are in the secret place (guhya) of him who is called "Disease" (roga) and "Pūṣan. The meaning is that he whose limbs are the knees is called "Disease" and "Pūṣan"; thus, "Disease" and "Pūṣan" refer to the knees. Marīci... [text fragment]

"Vanibhṛt," "Marīci," and "Pṛthivīdhara"—these are his two shoulders; "Mitra" and "Vivasvān" are his hips; and "Ruru" is his region of the groin. Thus this Vāstupuruṣa is to be known as facing downwards. Regarding his limbs, "savya" and "asavya" refer to his left and right sides respectively. Of this Vāstu, that which is the *savya* limb is the left, and that which is the [other] is the right.

"Left and right, situated there in their own [positions]" means that the deities remain well-established without abandoning their respective directions. Regarding "the vital points" (*marman*) and so forth: one who desires the highest good, having identified those subtle vital points (*marmasthāna*) not explicitly mentioned, should avoid them; another type of site (*vāstu*) is now described.
Of this [field], there are eleven channels facing east and eleven facing north, which are *sauṣumṇya* as before;

"as before" means that from the eleven, three each are *sauṣumṇya*, while the remaining eight each are *vaiḍa* and *paiṅga*. Thus, the field becomes one of a hundred squares. For what reason is this so? It is said: [to explain].

Regarding the phrase "on the grounds of the watchtowers of a fortress": the term *kheṭaka* refers to a small village, as the word "village" (*grāma*) is already implied by its own mention [in the preceding rule], according to the maxim of the oxen and the yoke (*balīvardanyāya*). Because of the inclusion of the phrase "in dwellings and so forth," the installation of the deity (*devatānyāsa*) is to be performed there even in pleasure groves, gardens, outer walls, and the like.

"The planets are fourfold givers" means that the four beginning with the *skandha* [spirits] are as previously described; the meaning is that they are indeed in the cardinal directions. However, within the outer row, there is this other distinction for the *vāstu*: "the five parts are the leaders of the spirits," namely Carakī and the others.

In the corners are the five-footed deities beginning with Brahmā; these are the portions of the divine abode mentioned in the Vāstu-śāstra, including the cords and so forth, as well as the beams, because they are included in the phrase "and so on. Thus, having excluded the outer enclosure which is caused by the Graha-Rākṣasīs, that inner field consisting of sixty-four squares is the divine abode.
The Lord who has divided the Vāsūs [into] hymns. Now, the site-plan (*vāstu*) is described, beginning with "thirty-four," and so forth.
When a field is laid out with thirty-four [units] facing east and north, there is an excess of ninety-eight *aṃśakas*. As it has been said:

That "it arises from exactly a thousand *aṃśakas*" is the very subject under discussion. Regarding that, he speaks for the purpose of arranging the deities: "There, with half... and so forth. Why are there two rows and a half-row? If one asks why they are omitted, he says:
"From the *rakṣas* and *graha*, *ka*. This refers to those connected with the *rakṣas* and *grahas*, such as Carakī and others, Skanda and others.

Regarding the phrase "separated by half a square" (*padārdhāntaritaiḥ*): it is understood that, for the purpose of entering the intervening space between the rows, nine parts are abandoned; these abandoned parts are separated [from the next] by those very nine parts. Then, "by nine parts tripled" means by twenty-seven parts. By those [twenty-seven] being tripled again, this very same [result follows].
The Lord of the Corners (Koṇeśa) specifies that Brahman occupies a single square, while the six Lords of the Kṛtis occupy six squares.

This refers to their being multiplied by six; the meaning is that, according to the previously mentioned description of the site-plan (*vāstu*), the lords of the corners—Āpavatsa and the others—are the presiding deities of thirty-six squares, while the fifty-four Īśas are the presiding deities of the [remaining] squares.

As for Parīcya and the others, even though there are fifty-four lords, they are ninefold each. Regarding the phrase "the other [lords] situated in the directions up to Īśatodit," this refers to the two rows that remain after setting aside the six rows immediately following the row of Brahmā; in each of those, there are nine.

The meaning is that he is the presiding deity of the nine compartments (*navakoṣṭhaka*). One might ask: what is the distinction between this [deity] and the deities of forts, cities, and so forth, such that while Skanda and others are mentioned there as belonging to other specific fields (*kṣetra*), they are not mentioned here? To this he says: "The distinction consists in pervasion (*vyāpti*).
There is no other distinction; those very same deities are present here, but only by virtue of their pervasion.

The gods partake of many syllables, but there it is otherwise. Now, regarding the *citā-vāstu* (the site for the funeral pyre) which is prepared at the place of cremation for those who have failed their initiation (*vipanna-dīkṣita*), as he will state:
"For those initiated, [the rite] is performed"—for what purpose is this? He says: "What has occurred? To that end, he speaks.
Regarding the phrase "in the group of elements" (*bhūtavarge*): it refers to that which is characterized by twenty-five squares. Therein, in the center of that field, are the "five groups.

"In the center" means situated in the middle; the meaning is that [the five groups] are in the four directions starting from the east, as well as in the very central square. Therein, "earth" (*kṣmā*) is *sa-ka*, together with Brahmā.

"One should place him together" (*sahavītyasyet*)—by this division of the sentence, there is the supply of a verb (*kriyādhyāhāra*). Regarding "the *nairṛta* [deity] in the group of four": that which belongs to *ninṛti* is *nairṛta*; in that group of four, one should place Varuṇa, accompanied by Viṣṇu, in his own two directions.
"Whichever direction is his own, in that same way. In the very same group of four, Rudra is supported by Īśa; according to their respective numbers.

The meaning is that one should place Vyoma together with Śambhu in the northeast direction (Īśānī), forming a group of four; that is, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma are situated in the positions marked by the Vedas—that is, indicated by the number four. Furthermore, this is done by pervading each position with a single *pada*. "Having sacrificed thus" means in this manner.

When the deities have been assigned according to their indicated portions and worshipped with the mantra "of the kingdom and of beings," there occurs the increase of all six classes of beings; for their deficiencies are their misfortunes. Thus, by not performing this, misfortune is certain; now follows the purification of the ground along with its defects.
Thus, the internal arrangement is described: "The ninefold," and so forth. Regarding the term "ninefold":

when worship is performed in a field marked with nine squares, beginning from the position of Brahmā and proceeding in order to the east and ending at Īśāna, by worshipping the world-sustainers—the world-protectors headed by Brahmā—the earth becomes free from defects.

The meaning is that it becomes a source of desired results for the master. On this very point, he states two alternative options in a verse beginning with "grahān" (the planets). Having worshipped these planets—beginning with the Sun and ending with Ketu—in these [nine] locations, the ground becomes purified; the meaning is that within these very positions, [the ground is divided] ninefold.

The meaning is that one should assign those very planets individually according to their respective divisions, starting from the center as before, in the sequence from the east to the northeast, as described in the *Śrī Pauṣkara* regarding the sacrifice of the nine-fold diagram (*navanābhayāga*). Now, the Vāstu-sacrifice: "Having performed the enclosure of the ground," etc., refers to the site for the worship of Vāstu.

In another location, having performed the ritual demarcation of the ground (*bhūparigraha*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the placement of the water-jar (*kalaśa*), the pouring of streams of water, and so forth, and having worshipped the Śiva-weapon jar (*śivāstrakalaśa*); then,
in the center of the pavilion’s altar (*maṇḍapavedikā*) at the aforementioned spot, one should worship the Śiva-mandala.

"Accompanied by mantra" means that the knower possesses the nature previously described. It is stated elsewhere as well: "One who is ignorant, deluded, full of doubt, or devoid of devotion is not a guru. Once the offering of one's heart has been made, having performed the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) and the *homa* for the purpose of satisfying the mantras, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) to fill up any deficiencies.

Having performed the *homa* and offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) of the *saṃhitā*, one should thereafter fashion the body of the site (*vāstu-deha*) according to the previously mentioned procedure by means of the division of channels (*nāḍī-vibhāga*). Regarding the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*): having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites of worship in the sequence starting from Īśāna, one should offer the sacrificial food (*bali*) according to the division as will be described hereafter.

One should give [the offerings]. By this, it is meant that the teacher [should act] according to the sequence of the directions. "With those having Īśāna as their deity" means with those mantras whose deities are Īśāna, specifically those expressive of origin. "With the general [Vedic mantras]" refers to the Vedic [mantras]:
"These [oblations] for Rudra, the wielder of the firm bow"; "To the one Rudra, the wise one"; and "We worship Tryambaka."

The meaning is: with such Rigvedic verses as these, and likewise with those recited in the Yajurveda beginning with "I make this animal [offering] for Rudra," with the Rudra-sāmans recited in the Sāmaveda, or otherwise with those prescribed in one's own ritual manual (kalpa). "Ghṛtākṣatāḥ" means clarified butter and barley grains.

"Padmā" and so forth. Regarding "in the lotuses": [offer] a lotus and water to Ghananātha (Parjanya). Regarding "canopy" and so forth: a canopy that is red, smoky-colored, blue, or brown is for Aṃśu (Arka) and the others; [offer it] to Sanya and so forth. Regarding "with the gesture of giving" (*dānamudrā*): with the hand directed toward the principal deity, [offer] honey and so forth.

"A *pala* of raw meat," "fragrances," and so forth; "fragrances" refers to all types of fragrances. "The tongue," and so forth; "belonging to birds" (*vaihagīm*) means pertaining to birds. "To the deer," and so forth; "barley sprouts," and so forth;
"to the ancestors," and so forth. "Kṛsara-rice," and so forth; "with sesame," "known as *sarā*," "accomplished," "the water-bearer," and so forth.
"Teeth-cleansing," beginning with "O Sugrīva," and so forth; "darbhaka" refers to a seat of *darbha* grass, beginning with "O Pracetas," and so forth;

"vāriruha" refers to a lotus, as previously stated; and "sumanā" [is offered] with the gesture of giving (*dānamudrā*). Since liquor is the substance [of the offering], the powder of *nāgakeśara* is well-known as the material for the serpent-goddess *Phaṇinī*.

Regarding "edibles" (*bhakṣyāṇi*) and so forth: "edibles" refers to various types of foods such as *ghṛtapūra* (butter-filled cakes), *gharikā* (sweetmeats), and others. The triad beginning with "edibles" is assigned respectively to the three [categories] beginning with the "principal" (*mukhya*), through the application of mantras.

The restatement of what was previously mentioned begins with "ṛgyāya" and so forth. "Śālūka" refers to the root of the lotus; "tallopya" and so forth means those things which are to be removed (lopya), hence they are called *lopikās*. "Pūrikās" are a specific kind of food made from flour. "Modakas" and so forth [are sweets]. "Raktacandana" is red sandalwood mixed with fragrant substances; "haritānna" and so forth refers to food mixed with turmeric (*haridrā*).
"Mantra" refers to food mixed with *dhautamudga* (washed mung beans) and so forth. "Mixed food" (*miśrānna*) means indeed that which is mixed.

"For the conquest of that," namely for the conquest of Indra, refers to rice cooked with jaggery (*guḍaudana*) and so forth. "Like meat" means that same prepared food joined with meat, [offered] to Rudra Rājayakṣman—that is, to Rudra Dāma. "Food with meat" (*sāmiṣānna*) refers to this.

The distinction is that the food for Rudra is mixed with meat, whereas [the offering] is further combined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). "Not well-cooked" means slightly cooked. To the "bearer of the earth," that is, the mountain (*pṛthivībhṛte*), [the offering is made].
Regarding "Īśa" and so forth: it is stated by the rays [of the sun] that curd and milk correspond respectively to *āpa* and *apavatsa*.

"In the northeast of the ocean and curd," and so forth; "with the five products of the cow" (pañcagavya), etc. Again, the words "ocean" (payas) and "curd" (dadhi) denote equal quantities [of substances]. "Bile" (pitta) refers to a specific internal piece of flesh;
"externally" (bāhyataḥ), etc., means having offered the oblation (bali) according to the sequence released by Carakī and the others, [one offers] another from that point.

The *bali* offering, which fulfills all desires and grants all objects of longing, should be given toward each cardinal direction to the hosts associated with the *mātṛmaṇḍala* and to those dwelling in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms by employing the word "namaḥ. This is the meaning [of the instruction]. As for the *homa*, it consists of oblations made with mantras ending in the word "svāhā," and the *argha* [offering] likewise.

"Likewise with those ending in *vaṣaṭ*"; "with those ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one offers] garlands and so forth"—by the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth," garments and ornaments are also included; all that is performed with the application of salutation (*namaskāra*), such as the recitation (*japa*) and so on.
For the purpose of paralyzing (*staṃbhanam*), the recitation should be performed while remaining in the *pārthava* seed-syllable and its forms.

*Cāṭana* (bewildering) and *uccāṭana* (driving away) are for that purpose; the letter *ya* is the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*). For the sake of accomplishment by those residing therein, [the syllables] exist together with the *visarga* (the *visarjanīya*).
With those [syllables] accompanied by the *visarga*, joined with the radiant *repha* (the letter *ra*) above and below, there is the word *chaga* for the purpose of cutting.

By their extremities, nourishment and satiation are attained; for that purpose, the letter *va* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Varuṇa, since it consists of nectar-letters: *raṃ raṃ ruṃ*. [This is] for the sake of victory over death. By means of those syllables, or else, by the specific birth prescribed for each respective ritual manual (*kalpa*), the secondary suffix (*upapada*) is formed for that purpose.
By those [means] which have such characteristics, [the phrase] "thus" and so forth means that it is "unobstructed," i.e., free from impediments.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, this is the meaning of the term *vāstupala*.
Now he speaks regarding the consecration of the water-pot (*kumbha*). "Then," and so forth.

For the completion of the house (*agāra*), there is the procedure for the square field. First, having stretched a thread extending from the eastern to the western direction and marked its center, then [of that]...

From the center, one should place two points situated precisely in the eastern and western directions; having made them equidistant, this serves as an adverbial qualification for the action. "With that in front" means that which has been described as being in front of those two points. Thus it is said: by means of two threads, one effects the intersection in the north and south.

"Two" means two fish-marks. By means of that, one should lay down a thread extending from south to north along the path of the two fish-marks—the northern and the southern. And by means of half the desired measurement, one should form a thread marked and manifested at the intersection in the intermediate directions (vidik), which is itself a fish-mark. Thus, there are four threads.

"Thus, [the ground] is equal and square on all sides," and so forth. Therein, in the square area, having avoided the location of the vital point (*marman*) and having moved slightly toward the northeast direction in the central region, that which was stated as "that which must necessarily be avoided" refers to the impurities. "In any place whatsoever" refers to the entire path of the universe (*viśva*).

"The Śaiva [power] which is the support, possessing infinite designations," means that which is the substratum of the universe. For this very reason, it is the cause of the universe—the cause of the entire world—and the teacher should install it as such, as the presiding authority. "Then," and so forth; after the installation of the Support Power (ādhāra-śakti),...

One should contemplate and place him immediately after [the previous deity], thinking: "He is the Lord of all the leaders of the world and the sustainers of the world; he who, as the sustainer of the world, is the controller of duties through his triple nature. Thus, one should place that very Lokapāla. The word "avyam" means "steadfastly for the sake of fortitude. The phrase "the support of the jar" (kalaśādhāram) serves to further specify him.

The meaning is that the *ādhāra* (support) is in the *kalaśa* (vessel). Regarding the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), although it follows the order of the recitation, it refers here to the sequence of performance;

for immediately after the mention of the body [of the deity], he will state [in the verse] beginning with "having worshipped Śiva in the center of the altar," and so forth, [describing how] one should place the vessel called *ananta* upon the *śakti*, consecrated with its respective mantra, [and likewise] the *śivamantra*.

Having uttered [the mantra] ending with "svāhā" and containing the word "buddhi," one should place it at the end of the syllable "la" along with the salutation (*namaskāra*). Then, one should invoke the imperishable power (*śakti*) known as Aiśvarī, who possesses many stones;
thereafter, having first placed the jars of the lords of the gods and others with devotion, the enemy [of obstacles] should remain present with their respective [mantras].

One should place those stones in sequence. By this [concluding] statement, the order of performance is established. Regarding the phrase "of that" (tasya) and so forth: as for the term "stone" (śilām), it is commonly known as the "foot-stone" (pāda-śilā); however, here, due to its proximity to the word *brahman*, it is figuratively designated as the "Brahma-stone" (brahma-śilā).

The study of one's own [Vedic] texts occurs precisely at the time of establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*), because the characteristics of the *saṃskāras* will be explained later. The path leading to the attainment of the state of Brahman is the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). As it is stated in the venerable *Nandīśvarakārikā*: "In the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkṛt*), intellect (*buddhi*), and the god Brahmā."

And, O Lord, he further qualifies that very stone by saying "the Lord whose form is entirely undivided" (*sarvāvibhaktamūrtīśa*). Those eight forms beginning with Earth which are to be described, as well as their respective Lords, are all indeed contained within it;
likewise, the principles (*tattvas*) and the triad beginning with Brahmā belonging to them—all this is present without division within the pit.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yasyāstataḥ" and so forth: one should install the eight slabs (*śilāṣṭaka*) as the eightfold deity, characterized by the earth and other elements according to the previously mentioned sequence, by virtue of their presiding over the ritual power (*kriyāśakti*) of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) placed upon the eight pitchers (*kuṃbha*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatsaṃskāra": for the completion of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the eight slabs, the preliminary rite of consecration (*adhivāsa*) is performed in the outer enclosure.
In the pavilion, upon the altar-mound (*vedisthaṇḍila*), immediately after the formal assignment (*uddeśa*), he speaks [the following] in order to establish the sequence of performance:

"Upon the altar," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the center of the Brahma-stone": this refers to that which was first deposited in the center of the Brahma-stone. He clarifies this very point: "One should place [the others] to the east and north of that. Those...

"Successively from the north, east, and so forth"—this refers to those [sites] and so on. "The abode of Śakra" means where Indra’s festival was held; "the ant-hill" refers to the mound of earth previously mentioned; "the supporter of cows" (*gobhṛt*) means the bull (*ṛṣabha*); by the word "horn" (*viṣāṇa*), one should understand the tips of horns, tusks, or the branches of the *bhuī āmalakī* tree and the like.

The mixed water, beginning with the *praṇava*, is for the middle [layer], and so forth. On the central stone, one should fashion the three-fold *dhvāsa* belonging to Brahmā— the presiding deity of the *buddhitattva*— as previously mentioned, according to the distinctions of the *ātmatattva* and the others, by means of what is to be described.

The connection [to the previous topic]. He states the reason for this very point: "Consciousness and the unconscious" refers to the group of consciousness, such as mantras, *mantrasvara*, and so forth;

the group of the unconscious refers to impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and so forth. Since all of this consists of the three principles (*tritattva*), he says "therein," etc., in order to demonstrate the paths (*adhvan*) within this very context, ending with the *māntra* path.

The placement of the ten principles (tattvas) belonging to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) extends thus far; thereafter, up to the principle of the mind (manastattva), there are eleven principles—including those known as the organs of action and the organs of cognition—along with the perceiver, which constitute the placement of the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva). Furthermore, in the third, the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), there is the ego (ahaṃkāra).

One should also conceive of the intellect (*buddhi*), its lords such as Brahmā and others, as well as the eight dispositions (*bhāva*) beginning with virtue (*dharma*), and the fifty misconceptions (*viparyaya*) and so forth, as it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "This evolution of the misconceptions is known as error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*); [it arises] from the differentiation of the qualities (*guṇa*)."

By way of analysis: its divisions are fifty—the five varieties of error (viparyaya), the twenty-eight varieties of incapacity (aśakti) arising from the deficiencies of the organs, the ninefold contentment (tuṣṭi), and the eightfold perfection (siddhi). Having also set forth the auspicious [factors], the phrase "the Brahman-egg" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned; then follows the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and so on.
Its function is such that it is pervasive, consisting of the nature of *ātman* and so forth; it is "unwavering" (*anamaya*), meaning it is imperishable and perfectly stable.

The *aṅguṣṭhaga-bhāntarodha-mudrā*, whose characteristics are described in the venerable *Raurava-āgama* and other texts, consists of earth, fire, and so on. Regarding the phrase "in those which have the nature of earth, fire, and *ātman*": earth, fire, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) are [designated] by the word *ka* in their respective positions.

"Varuṇaḥ dhātu" and so forth. *Dhātu* refers to minerals such as yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) and others; these, along with those whose names will be mentioned hereafter, should be placed within the jars made of gold and other materials according to their availability. Regarding "in them" and so forth: in the central jar, one should place Ananta; in the eastern [jar], Sureśa (the Lord of the Gods), who is the Lord of Indra’s world; and in this manner, [one should place the deities] in their respective [jars] in due order.

"Residing in their own places, they are to be worshipped through the sequence of mantra-yoga, relying upon *dhāraṇā*. One should cause those Lords of the Directions (*lokeśas*), who are bound by the contemplation of their respective forms, to be present in the center," and so forth. The Guru, having kindled the fire in the central hearth (*kuṇḍa*) according to the calculation of the nine parts (*navāṃśa-kalpanā*), [proceeds] from the east...
The meaning is that one should cast [the oblations] into the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) for the purpose of offering, in the same manner as the directions and the deities situated in those directions.

"To fill the gap in the ritual" means that whatever deficiency has arisen— whether caused by ignorance, impurity, or the lack of necessary materials during the performance— one should perform the homa to remove and fill that gap.
Regarding the phrase "the portion that has arrived": first, when the portion of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is obtained, there is a hundred, a thousand, or half [of that], and so forth.
This is the meaning.

Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with the root mantra according to one's capacity, and having offered the vessel of peace (śāntighaṭa) along with the remnants of the oblation using that same mantra,
one should touch the base of the stone with the root mantra and [sprinkle] with the vessel of peace.
The consecration of Brahmā should be performed, followed by that of the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) together with their respective forms.

Regarding the mantras of the forms of Śiva—namely the forms such as Earth, Fire, and so forth, whose lords are Śarva and the others—their mantras are *laṃ*, *raṃ*, *śaṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *yaṃ*, *saṃ*, and *haṃ*. One should perform the recitation (*japa*) equal in number to the fire-oblation (*homa*) for each of these.

One should perform [the rite], for it is said: "Just as with fire-offering (homa), so too with austerity (tapa) and recitation (japa). Having offered fragrance and the other [substances], one should [invite the deity] with the *sānnidhya-mudrā*.
Here, the *mudrā* is the *āvāhanī*; the *pūrva-nirodha-mudrā* is also mentioned, and its characteristics are described in the *Ruru-saṃhitā* and other texts.
Having placed both palms upward at the region of the heart, well-composed,
one should press the thumbs from the middle while the fingers are bent inward.
These should be employed during the invocation and in the worship of the God of gods;
likewise, one should press down both thumbs of both hands.
"One should turn the breasts toward [the mouth], even upon seeing a harsh woman.

When that has been done—and by the word "and" (ca), when the suppression [of breath] has also been performed—one should place the lower part against the upper; one should join them. That too is likewise [performed]; "the third"—this is the sequence of practice here. As he said:

Thus, having established the procedure for the three divisions [of the day], the meaning is that when the ascendant (lagna) is a fixed sign (*sthira*) and the house-purification (*bhāva-śuddhi*) is stable,

the houses (*bhāvas*) are as previously stated; when that purification is joined with a fixed ascendant, from among the previously mentioned movable (*cara*), fixed (*sthira*), and quick (*kṣipra*) signs, the fixed sign is appropriate to the context, specifically in the case of a Royal Yoga (*rājayoga*).

"Or indeed"—that is, when such a *lagna* (ascendant) is not obtained, or when there is a *rājayoga*. "Then one should place [the letters]"—this recourse to an alternative position refers to the *rājayogas*, which have been taught by those learned in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). For example, Varāhamihira:

If the Ascendant or the Moon— provided it is not the Moon itself— is conjoined with a Vargottama yoga and aspected by four or more planets, a lifespan of twenty years from the king (the ruler) is prescribed.

Many others have been mentioned by Yavana, Jīvaśarman, and others; however, because they are so numerous, they have not been written down here. Regarding the phrase "above Śakti": above Śakti is the jar (kalaśa) named Ananta, conjoined with its mantra.
That is, it is conjoined with the mantra of that Ananta, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ).

The meaning is "having performed. Regarding the phrase "having fully uttered the Śiva-mantra," and so forth: one should utter the mantra up to the ultimate limit (*parānta*) according to the sequence of abandoning the causal levels (*kāraṇatyāga*). Having brought it there into a state of non-differentiation (*avibhāga*), one should again, by will, behold the *anāhata* [sound] through the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and by means of another power.

Having agitated [the elements] up to the limit of the earth with the intellect (*buddhi*), one should observe the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), for that very reason the mantra is specified as "containing the word *budhyaṃta*. Thus, the mantra becomes uttered as existing within the path of the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*). Therefore: *oṃ laṃ*.

One should first install the stone itself with the formula: "Svāhā and obeisance to Brahmaśilā. In the place of Brahmā—that is, in the central position of the stone—as previously stated that "the stone in the center is Brahmaśilā" and "it is the power of Īśvara"—this is a restatement of what was said before. Then, in order from the east and so forth, [one installs] the lords of the gods; first, among these world-protectors (lokeśas):
Likewise, having placed those pitchers belonging to them with devotion and according to the prescribed arrangement for their presence,
one should duly install those stones and set them down in sequence. This is the restatement of the procedure.

The meaning is that, having joined [the breath] upwards toward the end of the crest-lock (*cūlaka*), and having joined it with flowers along the path, one should worship the tenth Lord of the World, the Brahman in the sky, with the vision of knowledge (*jñānadṛṣṭi*), and then offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*). Following that, one should give the offering.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) without weariness and without indolence for the sake of pacifying verbal, physical, and mental defects;
for it is heard [in scripture] that there is transgression due to verbal and other such defects, and the *Smṛti* also states:
"Through bodily defects of action, a man goes to the state of an immobile being; through verbal ones, he becomes a bird or a beast."
"By mental [means], one attains the state of the lowest caste. Regarding "from that," and so forth: "one should strive" means one should apply effort.

"In view of the purpose" means according to one's capacity for wealth and so on; the *liṅga* may sometimes be according to the measurement of the temple, or sometimes by the measurement of a cubit (*hasta*). Regarding that, he speaks of the temples by the measurement of a cubit.

Regarding the phrase "starting from four cubits" and so forth: for a *liṅga* of one cubit, the temple (*prāsāda*) may be four, ten, or up to thirty-six cubits—increasing by eight cubits at each step—but beyond that, one should not have it constructed; this is the meaning. Now, the division of the inner sanctum (*garbha*), the walls, and so on, for these very [temples] is according to the measurement of the temple.

"Divided by eight according to the measurement of the *liṅga* for the purpose of visualization," and so forth. When the site for the temple (*prāsāda*) intended to be constructed has been divided equally on all sides by eight—that is, when it is divided into eight parts—the phrase "by the squares of Brahmā" and so on follows.
This indicates the center; specifically, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is formed by four squares in the central location. This is the position of the pedestal.
By the phrase "with Āpavatsa and the others" (34b),
he refers to the previously mentioned deities of the celestial dwellings (*suragṛhavāstu*).
Among them, the four-footed Brahmā and Āpavatsa— who is of the nature of Brahmā— are located in the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*) of the four-square grid.

The movement [of the deity] consists of a circumambulation of the pedestal (*pīṭhaparibhrama*) by means of the first twelve [bricks], specifically within the interior (*garbha*). By the remaining [bricks], however, the walls (*bhitti*) are formed;
the meaning is that the walls should be constructed with bricks arranged in two rows.
By the word "wall" (*bhitti*), it is intended that they should measure eight [units] according to the width of the temple (*prāsādaviṣkaṃbhamāna*). It is precisely these [bricks] that are employed.

Because it is prescribed by the learned. On a wall-equivalent [base], with a height equal to the measurement of the wall, the height of the *jaṅghā* (the lower part) and the wall itself is thus established;
in this way, the building becomes square. "The spire (*śikhara*) is double" means that with a measurement double that of the *jaṅghā*, there is the form of the construction to be described above it.
Now, the characteristics of the nose.
Regarding the phrase "garbhapṛthvīśukāghra": it is broad on its sides according to the measurement of the womb (the inner sanctum), extending to half the height of the spire;

and in terms of its elevation, it projects outward by one-third. Thus, they should be made to project outward by one-third of their width. Now, as an incidental topic, the measurement of the temple is shown according to the measurement of the *liṅga*.

"Like the *liṅga*, etc. means that the location of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is established according to the measurement of the length of the *liṅga*, and the inner sanctum (*garbha*) is formed by a circumference equal to half of that. Regarding "the circumference of the pedestal": it is measured from side to side by that same dimension. "The outer walls are twice the height" means they are equal to the pedestal itself. [This applies to] the *jaṅghā* (shaft) and so forth.
As with the previously mentioned temple (*prāsāda*), the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be formed by dividing [the area] by eight;

he states this very alternative measure in the passage beginning with "sixteen parts" (*ṣoḍaśāṃśa*). When the site has been divided equally on all sides by four and again by four, such that sixteen parts are manifest, the womb-chamber (*garbha*) is formed by the four central squares.
The meaning is that one should construct it thus. Therefore, the pedestal (pīṭha) and the pedestal of the liṅga (liṅgapīṭha) are equal to half of the womb (garbha).

These two, at the entrance of the liṅga, are equal to the pedestal; the "beak-sniffer" (śukāghrā) is again equal to the womb, its exit being outside along the line from the corner of the pedestal to the corner of the womb. Alternatively, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is [constructed] with half of the womb, excluding [the previous measurement].

As for the maṇḍapa, it should be one-fourth or one-fifth [of the temple's dimensions], as it is said: "The maṇḍapa is equal to one-fourth or one-fifth [of the temple]. Now, he describes the *sāndhāra* temples.

"Outside," and so forth. According to the authority of the statement to be explained later, when the field has first been divided equally on all sides by eight parts, the outer wall is formed by one part; likewise, the inner wall is also only one square (padika) by means of the same part used for the beautiful head-projection (suśira-saṃdhārikā).
The meaning is that the "lap" (kroḍa)—the center—should consist of four squares. This is already established.
It is said to be like the interior of a *śukāghra* fruit, with its parts emerging both inside and out; it is devoid of the wall of the womb and has emerged according to the measure of the *pada*.
This is merely another variety of the *sāndhāra* [style]. "Divided by eight," and so forth.

From the pedestal (*pīṭha*) up to the outer wall, everything is measured by six units; the *śukanāsa* (frontal projection) extends outward by twice that measure. The outer *śukanāsa* is equal in width to the outer core, and the inner [core] is equal to the inner core.

And the inner nose: those two whose middle (madhya) or interior is beautiful. Likewise, there may be another distinction for me; however, in this case, it is exactly thus. This is for the purpose of referring to the measurement of the *padika*.
"Divided by the mountain" (*adribhājita*): having divided the field equally into seven parts from that point, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is [one] quarter.

"One should meditate" (*bhāvayet*). By the word "bosom" (*kroḍa*), the center is meant, as well as the surrounding area of the pedestal (*pīṭha*); that too is of that same measurement. And by the word "also" (*api ca*), the walls on the outside are included; [the inner wall] is by one quarter (*pāda*) of that, and the womb-wall (*garbhabhitti*) is by half of that. That which stands as a beautiful opening (*suśira*) by half of a quarter (*padārdha*) is also, by the word "also," half of that, namely by half of a quarter. Thus, there are exactly seven [parts].

The application of these terms is not due to their specific context [in other texts]. In the venerable *Piṅgalāmata* as well, for the purpose of showing the division of this very *prāsāda*, it is said:
"Having made the *liṅga* equal to the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the circumambulation (*paribhrama*) should be according to the measurement of the pedestal;
the wall (*bhitti*) should be like the pedestal, and the *andhakārikā* (the dark chamber) should be equal to the wall."

"The outer wall should be like a pedestal (pīṭha). As for the phrase "he who [says] 'just so'": he explains this as a reference to the statement "the square (pada) divided by eight. Since, according to the aforementioned distribution, only seven parts have been employed out of the eight, there is a need for the application of the eighth part.

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because [the definition] remains applicable even to that which has arisen; furthermore, there would be the impossibility of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as "it is exactly thus" regarding that which is separated by another definition. If this were admitted, however, there would be a contradiction with the *Piṅgalāmata*, another authoritative scripture; therefore, what has already been stated here is sufficient.

In the section concerning the construction of the temple and the palace, he states the reason: "In the case of the *liṅga*, such as the *cityā* [and others], etc. Regarding *liṅgas* fashioned from gems, gold, and the like, because of their high value, one must consider the priority of protection due to the fear of theft by thieves and others; for that reason, [the rule applies] from the left division.

Those [temples] which have twice the circumambulation path even from that division of the structure resulting from the arrangement within the walls of the palace (prāsāda) are described as such. By the word "liṅga," the inclusion of the term "etc. (ādi) implies those made of gold, jewels, silver, and so forth. By the word "liṅga"...

If it is argued that the term *arcā* (image) already encompasses the three types of *liṅga*— the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the mixed form (*miśrākṛti*)— according to the previously cited statement, then the phrase "and in images" (*tasyāpy arcāsu ca*) would be a redundant repetition;
however, this refers to images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and so forth, as found in their respective *saṃhitās*.

Since the term *liṅga* is not well-known [in this context], there is no fault; furthermore, there is another definition for the *sāndhāra-prāsāda* (pillared temple) beginning with "ten and so on, increasing by five," and so forth. Starting from ten cubits and increasing by five each time up to fifty cubits, those temples are thus [constructed].

The division will be explained below. For each of these, whatever its own hand-measure (hastarāśi) may be according to its respective number, it is "multiplied by the hands" (sakarāhata). It should be doubled; for the word *kara* is used as a technical term (*saṃjñā*) meaning "twice," so that one understands it as a designation for two. Thus, a measure of ten cubits is divided by twenty parts, and fifteen cubits by thirty; it is the same in other cases as well.

The fifty cubits are to be divided by one hundred so that a clear quotient of one part per cubit is produced. What follows from this? It is said: "The pedestal (pīṭha) is like the liṅga. Because it is the location [of the liṅga], it is designated by the word "pedestal" through metaphorical usage. The location itself is the pedestal; in that regard, a temple of ten cubits is first mentioned. Of that, [the measurement] is in cubits...

Regarding the pedestal (*pīṭha*) being two parts according to the measurement of the *liṅga* out of twenty parts in the middle: having established two parts in the center for the sake of the pedestal, he speaks of the application of the nine parts situated on the sides with the words "with half plus one" (*ardhena saikena*). Because it is not far removed [from the central part], it refers to that half which exists together with one [part] along with half of the pedestal itself.

"By that two-part [division]" means up to this point. Thus, excluding the Brahma-wall, there is the enclosure of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pariveśa*), the inner wall, and the outer wall known as the *garbhātura*; this is the northern [side]. In this way, first, from one side, the [measurement] is employed; with two additional [parts], it becomes the outer wall (*bāhyabhitti*). By that same half of the pedestal, increased by two—

The outer wall is for those remaining after the [initial] three have been employed; such is the distribution. In the same way, in the midst of the thirty parts of a fifteen-cubit [structure], four parts should be set aside for the pedestal (pīṭha) of a two-cubit linga—namely, by half of that [four]. This means it is stated to be "by two parts. By "with sprinkling" (sekena), it means as far as...

With three [units] on each side, there are likewise three [units] from the half of the pedestal; thus, thirty-nine parts are counted as unused. Then, with two and a half [parts], the outer wall is formed; subsequently, with the remaining eleven [parts], the outer wall is thus fifty [parts].
In this same manner, it should be understood for those not explicitly mentioned. Regarding "as before, such as the Śukāghra and so forth":

by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), the meaning is that everything—including the height of the legs and the elevation of the peaks—is as previously described. Now, concerning the *sāṃdhāra-prāsādas* (multi-storied palaces)...

He states the measurement of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*): "Within the womb" (*garbhāntam*) and so forth. Having taken a cord according to the measurement of the interior of the womb (*garbha*), and having placed it at half [the distance] on each side of the temple in the corner regions, by that measurement one pavilion is formed, ending at the wall of the womb. As for the womb...

The second [line] is by measuring up to that wall; likewise, on both sides, by laying down two half-threads, the second [section] is the previously mentioned *andhakārikā* for the *suśira* [type]. The third is by measuring up to that limit;
the fourth is by measuring up to the outer wall—this is the meaning. And this is of such a form as follows:

"Endowed with the division of the pavilion, [it is] 'younger' (yavīyaḥ) and gentle (saumya) here. In cases other than the smallest temple (kanyasa-prāsāda), it is situated otherwise in the larger temples (jyeṣṭha-prāsāda). The term "younger" (yavīyaḥ) is used specifically for the purpose of illustration.
According to the authority of the statement to be cited later, in those larger temples, [the measurement is taken] from the smallest temple.

How is this stated? "The width is one-third of the length. This is the meaning: having set aside one-third of the length specified for the smallest temple (kanyasa-prāsāda), the width of the pavilions (maṇḍapa) for the largest temples (jyeṣṭha-prāsāda) is established by the measurement of both sides.

"Prāsāda," etc. The meaning is that this measurement of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) has the same configuration as the temple (*prāsāda*); just as the temple has a configuration such as circular or square, so too do the pavilions. "Iti," etc.
"Sāmāsika" means concise. And "sāmānya" means common to all.
Regarding the layout of the *talacchanda* (the ground plan), he says: "Of the younger ones," and so forth.

Having set aside one-eighth of the area outside the fields for the smallest temples (*kanyasaprāsāda*) for the purpose of laying out the *talacchanda*, one should arrange it in whatever form is desired. Regarding the "portion for modification" (*vikārabhāga*), this refers to the medium-sized temples (*madhyamaprāsāda*).
The meaning is that for others, the share is one-twelfth, and for the eldest, it is one-sixteenth.

"Based on the distinction of names" means it indicates a difference in designation. Now, the designations of the *prāsādas* begin with "Meru," and so forth; [these include] Samudramanthāna, Mandara, and Gṛheśvara.

"The king of houses is sixteenfold"—this is a restrictive statement (*avadhāraṇa*) intended to limit the number of principal types to sixteen. There is no fault in this, because many other varieties of palaces (*prāsāda*) will subsequently arise alongside these, such as the *sarvatobhadra* and others. Thus, the *sarvatobhadra* is a type of palace.

The meaning is that even the fivefold *bhadra* formation is a cause for security. Regarding the phrase "encircled" (*vṛta*) and so forth: even the fourfold [formation] encircled is for the purpose of subduing enemies—that is, for the total destruction of enemies. Even the fourfold *śrīvatsa* is for the sake of increasing prosperity.

Regarding "gṛharādrī" and so forth: the half of the Gṛharāja, the Gṛharāja-kuṭhira, and the Astra—all three of these, being made of wood, should be constructed for the purpose of producing the glory of the house. Regarding the layout of the floor-plan (talachaṇḍaka), he says "meru" and so forth:
from the site of the Meru-prāsāda, that which is the sixteenth part [of the area] should be placed outside in all three directions.

Having marked out one-hundred-and-twelfth parts, and because the appearance of the external surface-level (*talacchanda*) would otherwise be untenable, when five lines are laid down in the lateral regions, there occurs a "falling away of the string" by way of the diagonal movement (*karṇagati*). This is according to the method of laying down the four corner-threads, starting from the outside at each corner.
By the entry and the visualization of the destruction of the three squares, [the structure is formed] with nine squares.

The corner-binding hangs from both sides; therefore, together with the corner square, it becomes five on each side. Then, likewise, by nine and similarly by seven, there are five wealth-squares and three at the front.

The movement (gati) is by means of squares numbering that [same amount]; the going (gamana) is again by nine; the entry (veśa) or entrance is to be performed by seven, three, and nine. At the entrance of the door in the center, it is by twelve; likewise, by ten according to the number of directions; and likewise, the entry is by six and those [six], in the interior of the variously wonderful hollows.
The phrase "whose belly is a sacrificial pit" (*khadā udare madhye yasya*) refers to the various activities such as carving and engraving.
There is one *āghāṭa* (section) by means of the five elements (*bhūta*), a second by the number of Vedas (*veda*),
a third by the number of qualities (*guṇa*), and the fourth and fifth by the number three (*tri*).

"Two by two levels" means that thus, from the back of the shank up to the pinnacle, there are five *āghāṭas*. The *śikharāvayava-viśeṣās* (specific components of the pinnacle) are those whose levels (*bhūmikās*) consist of successive divisions of the pinnacle. "By Viśvārkeśa" means all... [the worlds].
Thirteen, its doubling (twenty-six), the number twenty-six, likewise the union with the sun (the number twenty-four), and thus the union with Īśa (the number thirty-two).
Likewise, the union with the directions (the number twenty), and the union with the oceans (the number eight). From these...

In the first enclosure, there are subtle celestial abodes characterized by peaks numbering twenty-six; likewise, in the second [enclosure] they number twenty-four, and so on up to eight in the fifth. As it has been said: "Possessing a hundred peaks," where the word "hundred" [is used].
The term "horn" (śṛṅga) should be applied to both cases by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣi-nyāya*).
According to the technical terminology of artisans, these very [objects] are called *svika-kharaka*, and [the structure] is known as the "Complete Meru. As follows:
The Pādameru has been described as being twenty-five cubits in length, with each of its two sides measuring twelve and a half [cubits].
And the Khaṇḍameru is fifty cubits in length, with each of its two sides measuring twenty-five [cubits]; for this very reason, it is said: "Now, the Khaṇḍameru is elongated. And this...
Even though the Meru-palace has many enclosures (*prākāra*), it is recommended only for those images whose bodies are manifest;

therefore, the meaning is that it is not for *avyakta-mukha-liṅgas* (unmanifest-faced emblems). For those seeking supernatural powers (*siddhi*), it is likewise beneficial only with respect to that [former] subject.
Now, regarding "the field of the Mandara-rotation" and so forth: as before, one should provide the additional portion.

Having divided [the length] by eighty-four parts, and having applied four lines there at the side region, there is an exit of six and eight [parts] in the middle at the door-region. This means that from the outside,
first by six and then by eight, there is an exit in the form of a *talachaṇḍaka*.

Then, from the outside itself, the entry and exit should be made by six squares (*koṣṭhaka*) and likewise by four erased squares (*vedaiḥ lopitaiḥ*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that with as many [squares] as there are for the entry, there should be exactly that many again for the exit; that is, until the corner-square (*koṇapada*) is reached—meaning the square located at the corner.

"One should give as much as is obtained from the grain by means of fire and the four water-reservoirs. There are three fires and four water-reservoirs; by these, that [number] is produced. By this, the dual gender of the word *pada* is established.
Thus, by implication, first [one should mark] equally with the corner-square in both directions.

"Five below that, likewise, there are another five compartments"—this means they are the *kopabandhas*. Here, "by way of exit" means by way of entry into the Meru temple. "The nose for the arrival of the four directions" means that, like Meru, this [temple] also has gates and noses (*ghrāṇas*) in the four cardinal directions.
"Surrounded by the four *āghāṭas* and the Śukanāsā. This means they are completed and established at the four *āghāṭas*;

the regions are characterized by peaks as before, though not numbering one hundred, consisting of subtle temples (*devagṛhas*). Since the sequence for the application of the body has not been heard [elsewhere], it follows the division stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*.

As it is stated therein: "Twenty-three, twenty-one, nineteen, and two; excluding the 'slayer of Śuka' (the eighteenth), and minus the peaks, eighty are fashioned by Karika. Regarding the phrase "the ground of Sureśa," one should infer here that there are fourteen levels, just as in the case of the Meru palace; this [temple] is likewise.
"Maṇḍara, it is said. The previously mentioned manifest image (vyaktārcā) is established as before.
Now, regarding Kailāsa: when the additional field is divided by thirty-six parts as previously described, and five lines have been drawn across the sides;
In the middle region, there is an exit through eight squares; on the two sides, there are three and four [squares] respectively.
Regarding those two sides characterized by that group of eight, there are three and four pairs [of squares].
Thus, there is entry through four, and again exit, then entry, and then exit, as follows.
The phrase "they are to be counted" means "they are to be performed"—this is the ellipsis. Regarding "re-entry":
it refers to the abandonment (i.e., the omission) of that triad of parts which is in the middle of the entry; thus, [it is] "below and across" that.
By the process of applying the side-lines, there is the abandonment of that triad of parts; therefore, it is called "re-entry."

Just as the form and appearance of a sword-hilt are manifested, so too is Kailāsa established and perfected; its configuration and shape are such that it is the beloved of Śaṅkara. Its application is exclusively for the sake of Śiva and nowhere else. It has eighty peaks and upper terraces, possessing the forms previously described.
There are eighty peaks across the twelve levels, each according to its respective position;
likewise, there are four boundary walls.
Now, regarding the *bhadra*: "square" and so forth; this applies to all four [sides].
Because an additional portion is given according to the sequence of the directions, it is brought to a square shape;

this rule is universal for all [mandalas], and wherever it is not explicitly stated, it should be inferred. When twenty-eight parts have been marked and five lines are drawn across the side-area consisting of four times seven parts, it extends to the corners.

Just as in the layout of Mount Meru, by moving along the ears (the diagonals), one omits three [squares] at each corner; thus, with four corners, there are twelve [squares]. Together with the corner-square, the corner-binding consists of five [squares] on each side, totaling eight. In this manner, there is a set of four.

"One should accomplish" is the remainder [of the sentence]. Immediately thereafter, starting from the exit of each individual square, the first is the *Bhadraka* [mandala]. The second is by two [squares], the third by three; however, for the third, it is by six *ramās* (lines) situated in both directions, as it were.

Regarding the term *sāṃdhāra*: from that [base], a *saṃdhāra* (supporting structure) must always be constructed; by the phrase "four villages" (*caturgrāma*), the state of having four gates (*caturdvāratva*) is also implied by implication. Now, this is another variety of the *bhadra* itself: "with many *śikhara*s. This very *bhadra* is endowed with many *śikhara*s of the nature previously described.

When it is reduced, it is called *sarvatobhadra*. Furthermore, there is another *bhadra* type: when the entire extent of the field, starting from the shortest side and so forth, is divided by seven according to the measurement of the whole field; the mention of "on both sides" is intended as an illustration for all four corners, meaning that one *locana* (eye) is omitted at each corner.

The two [units] consisting of the removal of three parts in the middle are designated as the *rathaka*; it is desireless (*niṣkāma*). For each direction, another pair is to be determined by the removal of three [parts] at every corner, equal to the *kāṇakoṣṭaka* on both auspicious sides (*bhadrapārśva*). "The younger one" refers to the determination that it is indeed the *bhadra*.
The term *yavīyaḥ* [is used] when preceded by a word [denoting a building]. He speaks in order to dispel the doubt that it might be another palace (*prāsāda*).
He mentions another type of palace by means of this definition. Regarding the term *hita*:
this very same [structure], when joined with pillars on its outer perimeter, becomes what is named *nalina*. Furthermore, there is a specific distinction of this very [type].

Or, by the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "Śrīvatsa, etc.," sometimes this very [liṅga] becomes endowed with the crest of Śrīvatsa as will be described. Then, named Ānanda and Nandana, it brings supreme satisfaction to the maker;
such is the meaning.
Now follows the characteristics of the Gajaprasāda [temple].

"Vipaṃca," and so forth. This means that by excluding five parts out of ten from the field (kṣetra) on the rear or western side, and by revolving exactly half [of the remaining portion], they are produced through such a construction.
"Again, as before" means that they are to be measured as being square and very high. "Protuṅghna" means pre-eminently elevated.
The meaning is that the *śukanāsā* (frontal projection) is even greater than the previously stated measurement of the elephant. He describes what is called the *vimāna*: "In a square," and so forth.

When the area has been established as a square according to the measurement of the field provided as before, and it is subsequently divided into twenty-one parts, three lines are drawn toward the side directions.

In the middle, the exit is five parts; on both sides of that, however, the entry is with four [parts]. Then, the pillar is according to the measure of one part. Having omitted one part, the corner is equal to one part, with two [parts] in each of the two directions.
In this manner, the two sides and the middle of the palace (vimānaprāsāda) are formed by the emergence [of the structure] from the three [parts]. Now, regarding the classification of the vimāna:
"In that way," and so forth. This vimāna is likewise divided by the removal of three parts at the corner regions.

By removing the five great [obstacles] from both sides of the putrid corner, and by means of entry and exit other than those previously mentioned— namely, through a different mode of entry and exit as well as the avoidance of the pillars— this great celestial palace (mahāvimāna) serves the purpose of those seeking accomplishment (siddhi).
The learned ones have stated: "trimadhyaka" means that there are three central projections (*niṣka*) which are seen as similar;

this refers to what is called the *kesarī* palace. Regarding the phrase "square-shaped" and so forth: in this purely square field, the projection of the *śukanāsa* (frontal porch) must be made in the four directions, with the "breaking of the elephant's head" (*dvipamastakanirbheda*), meaning it is joined to the frontal globes (*kumbha*) of the elephants.

Lions should be made as ornaments for this *śukāghna* [temple], because it belongs to Hari, whose fame has increased through the destruction of the race of Daityas; therefore, it must always be made dear to the Lord Viṣṇu. He describes the *haṃsa-prāsāda*: "In a square," and so forth.
When a square field is divided into four parts, it is characterized by sixteen compartments; and regarding the sides,
by the addition of twelve [units] each—
meaning by the method of joining three groups of four compartments— the square field of Māyā is manifested.

"The abode of the Self-Existent" means the palace of Brahmā; it is circular and rounded in its expanse, with a pedestal marked by lotuses, and joined there with peaks associated with the two Śrīvatsas,
situated within the state of union between the two masses of parts on the wings, that is, on the sides.

Therein are Hara and Nārāyaṇa, and [the mark] of Śrīvatsa. Regarding the phrase "ten parts" and so forth: having divided the area of the field previously established by one additional unit into ten parts, and having drawn three lines on both sides, one should eliminate two parts in the corner region.

From the removal of four parts, six parts remain; from those, the central part consisting of three divisions is called the *rathaka*, which is the womb (*yoni*) of the exit. When it is joined with the *salagna* (the corner joint), it measures one and a half parts, and below the *rathaka*, its measurement is one part.

When its exit is situated in a specific region, this very [type] is known as *vardhamāna*. It is for those desiring prosperity (*śrī*). Therefore, it has complete walls, and so forth. Having divided the extent of the site into twelve parts, two parts separated by half a part should be made for the chariot-archway (*rathaka*).
The two *upakapolaka*s (side-ears) are as stated: "With eyes attached to half the portion, the *upakapolaka*s emerge equally.

Due to the equality of the eyes, there are exactly two portions; this is the only distinction from the *śrīvatsa*. Therefore it is said: "Likewise the corner, likewise the middle. He describes the one called *khaṇḍaśāla* with the words beginning "taraṃtat" and so forth. Of these two...
Of both those previously mentioned as well.
When there is an objection regarding the application of the *talacchandavartanā*, the specific statement is that "it becomes a *khaṇḍaśāla*";
