however, because the configuration of the complete *śāla* is otherwise untenable, one should divide the site into eleven parts, since the interval between ten and twelve is indeed eleven. Thus...
With one and a half parts, as well as with half a part attached, and separated by a whorl (āvarta) portion, there shall be two exits;
in the arrangement of the complete Śālavalacha mountain, the manifestation occurs.
This [layout] is a destroyer of enemies. Now, this is characterized by the Śrīvatsa and is known by the name Divardhana.

"Fourfold movement," and so forth. By the reasoning to be explained later, when there is an excess of the field, two lines are placed on the sides in the sixteenth part; from this, the turning occurs.

"That which has four movements—going and coming—in the middle" refers to the triangle, the meaning of which is expressed through a compound with an intervening term (*vyadhikaraṇa-samāsa*), such that the corner is formed by three parts.

"Of which [the] exit is also by a half-part diminished by that [same amount]" means: the interval—the middle space—between the entrance and the exit is of the same measure as the exit itself, namely, by a half-part diminished [by the previous amount]. This is the meaning. "Of which the interior is likewise" means: the interior is of the same measure as the exit.
This is the sense of "by a half-part [diminished]."

He describes the Garuḍa temple with the words beginning with "garbha" and so forth. Having divided the very center (garbha) of the square field into four parts, one whose beautiful wings are on the side regions according to that measure of division, and whose tail is of that same measure at the rear region, but [whose front] is by the measure of the center (garbha)— this is the Garuḍa temple.

The term *vaktropalakṣikā* refers to the parrot (*śuka*) and the eagle (*aghrā*) that characterize his face; his "chest is hexagonal" (*ṣaḍaśrakroḍa*) means that the interior of his torso is hexagonal, and upon the tips of his wings are stationed the two Garuḍas, Vahita and Avahita. Thus, it is of such a nature by way of these characteristics.
Now, regarding "the *valabhī* [roof] consists of eight parts," and so forth:

when the field has been divided into eight parts, one first performs the removal of two rows consisting of eight units each by discarding sixteen; thereafter, on both sides, there are two groups of three and two [units].
Increased by a combination of two [units], that which has a long extension in the future— therefore, from sixteen,

after subtracting twelve, four remain; by these, through the prior offering, the structure named *śukanāsa-avalabhī* (the Peacock-Nose Balcony) is produced, and thus it arrives as a quadrangular form among those with manifest characteristics.
The teachers have declared that [the practice] is beneficial only for images and not for unmanifested [deities], stating it is "enclosure made of bronze and so forth.
This refers to that which has an enclosure (*saṃvṛti*)—meaning the construction (*vartanā*) of ramparts, watchtowers, and walls—made of bronze and other materials.
As it is said in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*:

The temple (prāsāda) should be adorned with drum-patterns (*bherī*), circles (*saṃvartana*), lotus-buds (*phāṃsa*), *nandyāvarta* motifs, and *svastika* signs, as well as by decorative folds (*vali*), according to what is beautiful. Artisans alone know the details of the *phāṃsa* and other such features. Regarding its wall measurement, he states it as an option: "the wall may be one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters [of the height]. Thus, its wall is one-quarter, one-half, or one and a quarter [of the total height].

Likewise, he describes the square temple (*caturaśra-prāsāda*) as the cause for the special presence of specific images such as Ambikā and others, whose length and height are two and a quarter times [the base]. Regarding the phrase "square" (*caturaśra*) and so forth:
it is specifically that which is designated by its own name as square, and there is no other distinction; however, [it is measured] by six *vitastis*...

(Regarding the eight-sided [shape] by way of individual manifestation?): this meaning is that it is increased by the measuring units, adorned, and encircled for the sake of beauty. Regarding the "eight-eight-sided" ears and so forth: from the half-measure used for constructing the field, by discarding one-eighth part in all directions, the fish-tails [are formed], and by way of individual manifestation, it becomes eight-sided.

The meaning is as follows: having set aside one-sixteenth part from the *karṇa* (diagonal), one should place a cord at each corner according to that measurement; after first forming the *matsya* (fish-diagram) in the two directions, one should lay down four cords, and thus the temple becomes octagonal. Now, regarding the term *bhūdatida*: [it refers to] *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and so forth.

The eightfold powers (*vibhūti*)—namely, greatness (*mahimā*), attainment (*prāpti*), irresistible will (*prākāmya*), sovereignty (*īśatva*), control (*vaśitva*), and the power of determining the course of things at will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*)—become established in this [lotus].
Thus he speaks of the sixteen petals, beginning with "in the middle" and so forth; he mentions the production of the sixteen petals from the eight-petaled one through the power of the intellect.

Regarding the two fields situated as octagons, one should take the measurement to the end of each of the four central lines consisting of the Brahma-sūtras; having established [the mark] on one side, one should then place a chalk-marked string from the opposite side, and thereafter—

In the middle of each external corner, two "fish" (intersecting lines) should be made for the sake of the origin; thus, fish originate in all eight internal corners as well. By means of those fish originating from the center to the ends, [the figure] becomes doubled, resulting in a sixteen-sided [figure]. From the crossing of the twelve sides, there are two sides each.

Having leaped over [one space], the drawing of the lines (sūtra) should be performed for the production of the eight-cornered [figure]; for it is said here that while the lines were given by leaping over one corner [in the previous case], they are now double that. They should be given by leaping over two corners.
Now, another variety of the Bhadra itself: this is the Nalinapadma, as it is called "the lotus-like" (nalina).

The meaning is that the Padmaprāsāda, as described in the previously mentioned sūtras of enumeration, possesses those characteristics; this is what is meant by "in this manner" (*evam*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by means of those parts shown for the production of eight corners," when these are tripled, they become sixteen; thus, the production of sixteen corners is achieved through another method.
Just as an octagon is produced from a hexagon by means of fish-shaped figures arising at the center and the ends,
such is the intended meaning: for the same measurement applies to all eight [sides] by dividing the portion belonging to the practitioner into three parts and discarding one part.
Having marked two points at each of the eight corners and the origin of the fish-tail [designs],

and likewise having laid down the threads while first crossing over the two [lines of] fortune (aśri), one should erase the other threads situated between the central principal thread. Thus, by contracting them in this manner, they become sharp-edged and petal-shaped.

For those very [teeth] which are most numerous, being like lotus petals, this is the tradition of the Guru; and here the word "vā" (or) is displaced in its sequence. When there is equality in abundance, the resemblance to a lotus is implied, as he said: "padmābhāḥ" means having the form of a lotus.

The aforementioned sixteen-sided figure and others have this distinction: having first divided [the side] into forty-eight parts according to Kaṇāda, one discards one part; by that measure, two fish-tails are produced on the outside from the lines of those parts. However, for that [figure], [it is done] from the lines of the parts.
By taking the measurement of the perimeter, he describes the palace of the king of houses by that same measure. "Three-storied," and so forth:

the king of houses, together with its pavilions, should always be constructed as three-storied and made of wood; and it should be "auspicious" (*sabhadra*), meaning that in all directions—such as the exit and so on—there are figures called *bhadra* which circulate throughout the three stories.
The circumambulatory paths (*pradakṣiṇamārga*) that traverse the various levels belong to that previously mentioned lord of houses;

there is another variety [of this] beginning with "without" (*vinā*), and so forth. That which is designated as the *ardhagṛha* (half-house) is devoid of *bhadras*, and in front it is joined by a street (*vīthikā*) shaped like a *paṭu*. Furthermore, there is another variety, beginning with "devoid of that," and so forth.

The third type of house for the master of the home is called the *kuṭīra*, which is devoid of the seven [elements]. It is "devoid of a large hall" (*paṭvaśālārahita*). "Consisting of one or two stories" means that, by way of option, it may sometimes have one story or two stories. These three types as well are to be constructed according to the previously mentioned injunctions regarding the materials of donation. As it has been said concerning the Fortune of the House:

Furthermore, regarding the varieties of meters that serve as the cause for its production: "kuṃbhābhakalaśaḥ" means that the variety of meter named *kuṃbha* is like a jar (*kalaśa*)—that is, an *āmalasāraka* (a large water-jar) having the form of a jar; the meaning is that it should be made in that shape.
As it has been stated by Ārya Keśava: "The *kalaśa* and the *āmalasāraka* should have their feet raised."

Regarding "uddhaddhajaṅghaka": up to the vicinity of the pinnacle, it is requested that the legs be fashioned exactly like those [of the previous type]; furthermore, there is another circular variety beginning with "sāghrogre" and so forth. By implication, the circularity of the temple named Vṛṣabha is established. And because it shares the general characteristic of being a circular variety, it concludes as "caturaśrānta" (square-ended).

According to the scripture as well, within a circular field, the manifestation of a square for the bull (vṛṣa) must be performed. By the statement "in front of Agni [is] the śukanāsa," it is made known that there are two circular domes (vṛttakuṃbha) devoid of a śukanāsa. Furthermore, just as these eight types of square palaces (prāsāda) have been described, so too here [are they] for the circular one.

Another variety: "grāvṛkṣa" and so forth. The meaning is that because of the commonality of its circular shape (*vṛtta*), it is both a tree (*vṛkṣa*) and indeed circular (*vṛtta*). "Vṛṣa" and so forth: the temple (*prāsāda*) of Vṛṣa, which has the form previously described, is "surrounded by boons from the mountain" (*sanasthādvarāvṛta*). The meaning is that Śiva alone is the cause for this [temple], not any other object. Thus have the temples been explained.
He withdraws [the teaching] with the words "In this way," and so forth. Having performed what was indicated, these very [methods] serve as the primary divisions and purposes;

for this reason, they are limited to this number of twenty-eight. Since there is a multiplicity of these through the directions of mutual divisions and subdivisions, they have not been demonstrated here, as their purpose lies in the primary divisions.
The meaning is that among these, some are primary causes for procreation, while others have the purpose of being means for enjoyment (bhoga) by virtue of their distinction from the primary ones.
Now, he states the measurements of these very [worlds]: "Meru," and so forth, ending with "vimānas."

The five palaces (prāsādas) range from fifty cubits downwards, decreasing by five cubits each time, until they become thirty cubits; this is the completion of the statement. "Kailāśa" refers to an elephant (karī), meaning an elephant of the dimensions of Mount Kailāśa. "Of Nandin," and so forth, is clear. "Eight-sided" (aṣṭāśra), and so forth, is also clear.

"Suparṇa" refers to Garuḍa; "Dhāmarāja" and so forth [refer to other deities]. "Gṛharāja" (the king of houses) refers to the fifteenth [deity], Śyena, and "Sitachada" (white-winged) and so forth. "Sitachada" refers to the Haṃsa (swan); "Ambhobhṛt" (water-bearer), as previously mentioned, is stated as a variant for the Kumbha (pitcher). "Dviṣaṭkāt" and so forth means from the twelve; "Siṃha" (lion) and so forth [follows].

The four [types of temples], beginning with the *siṃha* and ending with the *caturaśra*, do not exceed eight [parts]. Regarding "the *mahābhadra* and so forth," and "the *vāpī* according to the measurement of the *liṅga*": this is a restatement of what was previously mentioned;
in the phrase "they do not exist below four cubits," the particle *ḍa* is indeed to be supplied. Temples (*prāsāda*) are not [constructed] below four cubits.

It is understood from the phrase "bhavantītyā" [that this is so]. Regarding the expression "below the measurement" (*mānād adhaḥ*): the word "adhaḥ" (below) is an elliptical indication; it implies "above the measurement" (*ūrdhvam api mānāt*) as well. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: whatever is done above a measurement of fifty cubits or below four cubits results in misfortune for men; hence, these [dimensions] exist for that purpose.

Since it is the abode of beings consisting of *bhūtas*, *yakṣas*, and *rākṣasas*, and because the interior space (*garbha*) of a four-cubit temple is extremely small, bathing, worship, and other rites for the deity would not be possible;
therefore, he says "laghīyasī" and so forth. In that regard, by the necessity of accounting for worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), [he establishes] in each direction...
The non-occurrence of these defects for the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is due to its connection with the water-channel (*praṇāla*). Now, this is stated:
[the pedestal] should be excluded from the wall of the temple, or it should be smaller than the temple. Let that be so, because it is said:
"There is no contraction of the triple pedestal (*tripīṭha*). The meaning is that for the pedestal and the *liṅga*, there is never any reduction or diminution.

Now he states the measurement of the *śikhara* (spire). Regarding the word "śikhara": it is said that the *śikhara* should be twice the height of the *jaṅghā* (shaft); thus, the *jaṅghā* and the *śikhara* together become equal to the wall (*bhitti*). From this, when that [total height] is divided into four parts, the direction of length is indeed along the vertical axis. As for the application of the one part in the horizontal direction: [The *śikhara*] should be made with a width of one part in the lateral direction. It should be shaped like a lotus bud, and its base should be square. It should be adorned with various ornaments such as *śukanāsa* (gargoyle), *kapota-pālikā* (dovecot), and *candraśālā* (moon-chamber). Its pinnacle should be shaped like a *kalasa* (vase) or a *śṛṅga* (horn). It should be decorated with various jewels and endowed with all auspicious characteristics. Thus is described the measurement of the *śikhara*. It should be constructed according to the prescribed rules, and it should be pleasing to the eye. This is the rule for the *śikhara*. One should not deviate from this. By following this, the temple becomes beautiful and brings prosperity. This is the secret of the *śikhara*. One should keep this hidden. Thus ends the chapter on the *śikhara*. May there be success. May there be peace. May there be well-being. Om. Śrī. Om. Tat Sat. [Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the full text would continue with further details regarding the architectural proportions and ornamentation.]
Because it will be explained later: "of the other" refers to the double-peaked [temple], and "of the other" refers to the peak measuring one and a half parts;
one should divide the peak by the "qualities," that is, by three.
"From the part likewise."
From the fourth measurement above the previously indicated [point], when divided by four according to the application of the divisions to be described,
one obtains two eyes (two *indus*) and one moon (*candra*);
by these, respectively, the parts known as the throat, the ear-ornament (*āmala*), and the crest (*cūḍā*) are formed for the other [face].

Furthermore, having likewise divided the uppermost third of the pinnacle— which consists of one and a half parts— into four parts, the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is made from one part, the *āmalaka-sāraka* from two parts, and the crest (*cūḍā*) from one part; and as for what its form is and where it is situated, it is like a water-pot (*ghaṭa*), being exactly so.
It has the shape of a *pūrṇasaṃsthāna* and is likewise adorned with a lotus; it has the shape of a *pūrṇakośa* (a citron) and is adorned with a lotus.
Alternatively, it is that in which the very lotus that is a *pūrṇakośa* serves as the ornament by way of being a defining characteristic.
Now, their bodily concealment [is as follows].

"Triguṇa," and so forth: those whose crest-peaks (*cūḍāśikhara*) have a shape that is three times the height of the shank (*jaṅghā*) and twice the measure of the pinnacle (*śikhara*), for them [the measurement] is "transversely. From the limit of the height of the three walls, the cord (*sūtra*) on both sides is fourfold.

Then, having extended [the cord] from that point with a thread and chalk, and having placed one hand on one side of the altar (vedikā) to be described below, one should mark the body on both sides according to the rotation up to the top of the shank; this is the back of the pinnacle (śikhara).

One should proceed; "in the case of *sārdhadṛkka*, the multiplier (*guṇa*) is likewise. In that same way, when it is equal to the *jaṅghā* (the lower part), there is indeed a state of two and a half parts for the *śikhara* (the pinnacle) consisting of two and a half parts. In that case of *sarvadṛkka*, "the multiplier is likewise"; having extended the cord (*sūtra*) which consists precisely of two full parts.

In the same manner, one should fashion the body from both sides, starting from the edge of the altar (vedi) and following the circular curve. Now, he explains how one might fashion the body in another way, with the words "saṃhāryya" (to be removed).
He intends to designate certain parts as those to be established (iṣṭān) and others as those to be removed (saṃhāryyatvena).

"One should divide after having gathered [the parts] by determining them with the intellect"—according to this sequence, how should one perform the withdrawal (*saṃvartayet*)? To that end, he says: "the portion to be subtracted" (*hānyāṃśam*). This word is an adverb; its meaning is:
"having made it the portion to be subtracted, according to the path of elimination. Furthermore, another...

He states another method: "ten," and so forth. The region of the altar-bond (*vedībaṃdha*) located below the neck, which is to be described by name later, is indicated by the word *skaṃda*. When that [region] is divided into ten parts, it becomes the portion belonging to Yama. The term *phāṇi* refers to the middle section, excluding six parts.

Having drawn a line from each of the two sides up to the limit of the two parts, the meaning is that there is a reduction following the *bhrāsa* (proportional measure) as far as the back of the shank. Furthermore, another method begins with "having contracted," etc.;
in that shoulder-junction (*skandhabandha*), it is divided according to the rule of three heaps by the number of parts.
Alternatively, having divided [the circumference] into twelve or eighteen parts, one should rotate [the circle] by means of the removal of the collection of the middle third-parts,
leaving behind the two remaining parts on both sides. Furthermore, there is another characteristic.
"Five," and so forth.

This merely restates what was previously said regarding the division into ten parts; in that case, because of the division into ten, there was a reduction of two parts each, which was logical, but here, because of the division into five parts, there is a reduction of one part—this is the point.

The *viśeṣa*, the *saṃvṛtti*, and the *mañjarī* here constitute the completion within the body of the *śikhara*; this may sometimes be done by that method, or rather in whatever way it brings satisfaction. "Sometimes" means in this manner, and "sometimes" by the previously mentioned method. As for "having come together," etc., although here...
Although irregular temples with three, five, or more sides have not been mentioned here, nevertheless,

for those divine abodes such as the triangular and hexagonal ones described in other compendiums (*saṃhitā*), the construction of their forms according to the prescribed rules should extend up to the *jaṅghā* (the lower section), and above that, on both sides, it should follow the method previously stated.

Having first laid out the threads according to the measurement of one and a half parts and two parts, the enclosure of the body of the *mañjarī* must be constructed; such are the celestial abodes seen and being seen in other regions such as Kuru-kṣetra and others. To clarify this very point, he says:
"Elephant," and so forth.

Having described the drawing of the elephant's field (*kṣetra*) by means of the "fifth part," "half-division," and "circumambulation," as well as its form up to the shank, [the author] now [describes] the crest (*śikhara*).
For the purpose of contraction, when that [structure] has been raised according to the previously stated method of construction and cut on all sides by nine parts— excluding one-fourth part—
and having first established the portion below the neck,
the *śukanāsā* (fronton) is formed by the removal of a portion from both sides through specific methods such as *phāṃsa* or *varta*.

The meaning is that the enclosure (saṃvaraṇa) should be executed exactly like the completion (niṣpatti). Furthermore, the neck (kaṇṭha), amalaka, sāra, and cūḍā should be made above the middle portion of that. In this context, he describes the fashioning of the pinnacle (śikhara) at Valabhī: "having gathered," and so forth. "In the same manner" refers to the height of the elephant (gajocchrāya).

When divided by the very number of the intervals, the resulting points for the placement of the *śikharāvartana* (ridge-curlings) on the related structure must be covered with *phāṃsa* (wooden clamps) or constructed by others using other methods conceived through the intellect. This applies to the previously mentioned *kaṇṭha*, *malasāraka*, and *cūḍā*.
He states the measurement of the side: "vedyardha" (half of the altar).
Having divided the altar by six parts—six parts being added to the number of parts to be mentioned later—the upper part is three parts in measure; likewise, it is increased by a fraction.
The *sāraka* (central core) measures five parts; thus, the *āmalaka-sāraka* [is so named].

The *cūlaka* (dome) is half a part less than the width of the neck (*galavistāra*), and its circumference is one and a half times that. To prescribe the remaining dimensions of the height, he says "five," etc. According to the previously stated method, the altar (*vedi*) is divided into six parts, and the sixth...

The term *pañcaghnah* means "multiplied by five," that is, divided into five parts. Its *dalam* (portion) is one half; by that measure—meaning by the sixtieth part pertaining to the altar (*vedi*)—it is characterized by such a dimension of length (*āyāma*). Furthermore, he states the specific measurement for the side:
Regarding the phrase "one-third of that" (*tattryaṃśa*) and so forth: the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the fifty-sixth part of the altar (*vedi*).

The meaning is that the width is established by the measure of one-third of that fifth part; thus, this is an additional measurement beyond what was previously stated. The phrase "even slightly more" (*kiñcidabhyadhiko 'pi vā*) was mentioned earlier.

It should be made equal to the liṅga including its pedestal (vāliṅga), being one-fourth of the height and two and a half parts in width; "slightly" means it should be made a little larger, without the need for further calculation of additional parts. It should be made square and so forth.

The meaning is that it is marked with three divisions. Also in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*: "One should cause the *cūlaka* to be divided equally by means of four, eight, and circles. Therefore, the word "equal" (*sama*) here should be explained as meaning "resemblance," and thus the third enclosure is optionally [described]; therein, its designation is the "Space-liṅga" (*ākāśaliṅga*).
"Kāmyā" and so forth: one should fashion there, according to one's desire, the stumps at the feet and the weapons—such as the thunderbolt and others—of the world-protectors, Indra and the rest.
To state another form for the space-liṅga (ākāśaliṅga), he says: "Viśvaṃśe" in the middle portion.

The potter’s [vessel] should be made in the shape of a lotus, or it may be a full-blown bud as previously described, or similar to a *mātuluṅga* (citron); this is the alternative. Regarding "in houses" and so forth: in royal palaces, temples, and huts—as well as in the various types of structures mentioned previously—the pinnacle (*cūlaka*) should be made in the shape of a water-pot (*kalaśa*). Of that...
He states the justification for the very form of the *kalaśa* (vase) in the passage beginning with "prāṅgata" and so forth. The word "hi" is used in the sense of "because":

because that which was previously at the initial limit (*koṭi*), at the first moment during the placement of the feet, was described as having the form of a *kuṃbha* (vase), consisting of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*); now, however, at the final limit, upon the completion of the entire temple.
Upon its summit, one should fashion the form of Parānanda, which is filled with supreme power and consists of the totality of all parts (sakala-śātmaka);
it serves as the support for the temple consisting of the Kalās at both ends, characterized by the opening and the conclusion.

The meaning is that the powers reside in the form of others; thus [it says] "made of wood" and so forth. Just as the king of houses is of three types and made of wood, as it is said: "The one known as Gṛharāja, Kuṭīra, and Gṛhapriya—these three, fashioned from wood, should be known as the causes for procreation. Likewise, the *cūlaka* is shaped like a *salala* tree.
It should indeed be made from wood; and since that applies to all three [types of temples] by virtue of being wooden,

when such a pinnacle (*cūlaka*) is obtained, its construction is restricted to a pot-shaped wooden pinnacle for two of the purposes, excluding the *kuṭīra* [type], while for the *kuṭīra*, it may be made of stone, baked brick, or other materials.

For the purpose of generating the principles beginning with Maya, it takes the form of a pitcher (kalaśa) composed of those respective substances; and for the sake of its crest (cūlaka) and ears (karṇa),

that crest of the temples consists of the three principles beginning with Tattva— as will be described in the section on installation— just like the primary installation, consisting of the triad of principles such as Tattva and so forth.
"And consisting of Mūrtīśa and the others. For it says:

"The immortal one, consisting of the Trikhaṇḍa, Varma, Mūrtīśa, and Śivadhāman. At that time, which deity or which presiding divinity (devatā) shall be installed in which temple? He says: "In Valabhī," and so forth; "or the pitcher of Savitṛ."

The meaning is that his hut-palace (*kuṭiprāsāda*) was mentioned previously. As for the phrase "but of other gods," this is a restatement of the same point made by the expression "in the world of desire, he should [be] the Lord of the World. Or else, "whatever other personal emblem (*svacihna*) [he may have]," or rather, whatever other personal emblem belongs to that deity, or even according to his own ritual manual (*svakalpa*).
The meaning is that the crest at the top of the pinnacle should be fashioned as one's own weapon, or so it is stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Above that is one's own weapon. He describes the nature of the crest (*cūḍā*) with the words beginning with "That which... and so forth.

Since that which arises at the very summit of all things is the cause of their origin, maintenance, and destruction, it is for this reason that the support of the Blessed One— which, like the *viśvatomukha-liṅga*, appears and shines as a further substratum— is called the *cūḍā*. Thus, he describes the location for the construction of the flagstaff-base, beginning with the words "below the throat," and so forth.

For the most excellent temples (jyeṣṭhaprāsāda), having divided the spire (śikhara) below the neck (kaṇṭha) into four parts, the flagstaff-support (dhvajādhāra) should be made at the beginning of the uppermost fourth part; or else, as stated in that very same source, it may be on the fifth part for those with a lofty spire (tuṅginaḥ), referred to as the "flagstaff-support," the "lattice-window" (gavākṣa), and so forth.
The windows and *candraśālikās* (dormer windows) of all palaces— whether of the superior or inferior types, measured according to forty parts—
should be constructed as they are well-known in other regions. Regarding the arrangement of the positions for the deities of the directions, he says:
"Eight parts of the wall," and so forth. The directional deities (*digdevatā*) are the side-deities;
their [position] within the body of the temple is for a long duration, measured by one-eighth of the wall (*bhitti-aṣṭamāṃśa*).
Regarding "depth and width, twice"—this means that from the previously mentioned measurement of depth, the width is double.

Regarding "twice as high": from that very measurement of width, it is twice as high. "Vimardaka" means devoid of the previously mentioned central vital point (*madhyamarman*). He states the measurement of the door according to the measurement of the temple in the passage beginning with "of the great ones," etc.
For the principal deities, the height of the door is [measured] by half the height of the womb-chamber (*garbha*), and by half of that height...
Regarding the phrase "taduduṃban" [meaning "that which is above the udumbara"]: it refers to that which is well-known by the name *Kāmākhyā* somewhere as being supported by branches.

The meaning is that the measurement prescribed for success is that which is given on the back of the two branches above, excluding one-eighth part of that *adhoduṃbara*. This is indicated by the words "one-fourth part," and so forth.

And at the lower part of the two branches is the fourth time, Mahākāla. [The phrase] "the pair of Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun" is like [the expression] "Bhāmā and Abhāmā in the middle. [The phrase] "the two Vidyādharas holding garlands, having seized the oceans" means they have taken up full water-pots. [The phrase] "those who have seized the garland of skulls" refers to those wearing garlands of severed heads.

The meaning is that the sequence of arrangement for these nine—namely, the two Vidyādharas (forming a pair of bulls), followed by the two lords of serpents as stated in the order of the recitation—is as follows:
the qualification of the "lords of serpents" is "Śeṣa and Vāsuki," as he says: "displaying the majestic expansion of the circle of hoods."
Thus, this application consists of nine numbers. Regarding the phrase "nine-branched" in the context of the *mahati* [gate], it refers to a gate with nine components;

"other than that," and so forth. One should conceive of the thickness (*sthaulya*) as being half the width of that distinct location which has been prescribed by its specific form and arrangement. He states the measurement of the door according to the measure of the *liṅga*, beginning with "from the width," and so forth.

Alternatively, the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be described as being less than one-sixteenth of the width of the linga; or it may be greater or smaller [than that]. This is a restatement of what was previously mentioned regarding the linga’s door, namely that "the pedestal is equal [to the door]."
Now he describes the doors according to the measurement of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), beginning with the words "Jyeṣṭhā" and so forth.
By the word *sva* (self) is meant zero; by the word *manu* (man), the number fourteen is intended, as has already been stated previously.
One should first place zero, and immediately thereafter, one should set down fourteen before it; thus [is the sequence].
A number exceeding one hundred and forty would result. The largest of the large doors is thus [one hundred and] forty fingers in width;
from that point, by decreasing ten fingers at a time, there are the medium and the smallest doors, ending with the very small one. Thus it is said.
By the phrase "the lowest of the low consists of six groups of elements," according to this very sequence of numerical placement—
first five by the number of elements, followed by six— one arrives at a total of sixty-five; thus,
these nine doors are most concise [only] in palaces that increase by five starting from ten.

Because [the installation] from four hands up to thirty-six is not authorized, it should be understood that the procedure for Gaṇapati and the others is prescribed in sequence, one above the other, upon the *uduṃbara* post at the top of the door.
Regarding "Gaṇeśa" and so forth: here, by the word *lakṣmī*, Śrī is meant; *hari* refers to Nārāyaṇa; and *īśa* refers to Śiva.

Regarding the venerable Śaṅkara-bhaṭṭāraka, it is stated there as well: "Hari and Śaṅkara. In the phrase "the Mothers, intent on explaining Vāṇī and Pā," the word *ca* (and) has the sense of a distinct conjunction (*bhinnasamuccaya*), meaning "the Yakṣiṇīs and the Mothers.
[The passage continues with] "in front of the door," and so forth.

In front of the door, excluding a quarter-part of its width, a *caṇḍikā* should be made in the shape of a half-moon by means of a circumambulatory path (*bhrama*), as well as the *kapitthakas* and so forth. From the very width of the door,
by a measurement of six parts, two *kapitthakas*— specific forms shaped like squares— should be placed below the two door-panels (*dvārikā*) in a location other than the *kumbhas*.

The meaning is that sometimes two beautiful jars are at the place of the *kapitthaka* (the door-socket), and sometimes the two *kapitthakas* are elsewhere than the jars. Regarding the phrase "half of the moving [width]": it refers to half of the width of Dvārikā;
half of its height as well—by reason of that, the bolt-hole (*argalā-sthāna*) [is determined].

Regarding the entry of Tāṭaka: for the purpose of making [the door] wide, it is indeed commendable if it is attached to a branch—that is, connected to the lintel (*dvārikā*)—and so forth. Such a door as has been described by these various methods is called *śuddhāya*. It is joined with a beautiful *āya* (prosperity/measure) and is thus highly praised; and as for the *āyas*:

Together with the eight previously mentioned [signs] beginning with the banner (dhvaja), there are others numbering the sum of vowels, elements, and fires; these are of three types and, along with them, four types. From each of these respective groups, by means of calculating their own number and performing division and subtraction, those which remain are as follows:

The term *āya* is used because they lead to auspicious results (*śobhanaphala*); thus, this is an etymological explanation (*anvarthapratipādana*) for these [categories] of *liṅga*, *ācāra*, *dvāra*, and *pīṭha*. The meaning is that an excess of parts or their thickness in these *liṅga*s and so forth leads to the fault of *āyamāna*; therefore, one must ensure the purity of the *āya*.

"Those [planets] are divided by their own group" means that if, taking from one [group], the yoga becomes auspicious, then that very [group] should be employed. If, however, the yoga is inauspicious, then another group should be employed. "That," and so forth.

And one should not construct that door such that it is obstructed by another door; likewise, one should not construct it in such a way that it is confused in direction or facing an intermediate quarter. "Sloping" means either outwardly or inwardly; "sloping" refers to that which is as if about to fall, outwardly or inwardly, which is what will be described as "loose."

"With its joints and fastenings disjoined" means that the door-panels are closing by themselves without effort. For this very reason, he says "creaking," and so forth. That which is closed by the two creaking door-panels is for the sake of supreme attainment (*śreyas*); however, [closing] by itself for the sake of inferior accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*) is [a different matter].
Thus it has been stated: "The sixth," and so forth. *Iṣṭi* refers to the sacrificial offering; *bindu* refers to the corner; *yaṣṭi* refers to the construction of houses and the like;
*aśri* refers to the circular path for the removal of water, mud, and other debris; *dhvaja* refers to the emblem consisting of the discus, trident, and so on;

and *gopura* refers to the city gate. Regarding "with the [streams of] compassion" and so forth: previously, the *āraghaṭṭa* (water-wheel) and other such structures were mentioned because of their inclusion [in the context].

The measurement of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for supported palaces (*sāṃdhāraprāsāda*) has been stated [in the passage] beginning with "the interior of the womb, up to the end of the wall of the womb," and so forth; now, that of the unsupported ones (*niraṃdhāra*) is being described,
starting with "from the sides," and so on.

Having extended a thread on both sides of the *śukanāsā* (the frontal pediment) according to the dimensions to be described, as previously done, one should construct six pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) by means of optional measurement. To the question "By what measure?", he says: "By the *garbha*-thread. One [pavilion] is by a thread level with the center of the temple (*prasāda*), while the second is by the *śukanāsā*.
In this very context, within the Garbhasama-sūtra, [the author] states the measurement of the wall for Śukanāsā:
"śukāghna" and so forth.
"The two others are likewise from the Brahma-sūtra of the śukāghnā. This is what is meant.
First, that which is the total measurement; then again, by those two—the *śukāghna* and the *prasāda-brahmasūtra*—and so forth.
Of those two, the *garbha-śukāghna* and the *kroḍa*, there is the pair of ear-lines (*karṇasūtra*).
Having thus described six side pavilions by that same measurement,
he speaks of another four front pavilions and the measurement by which they are formed: "These other four [are made] by this same measurement as the foremost one."

By the phrase beginning with "garbhārdha" (half the womb), the word "sā" (she) refers specifically to Śukanāsa; thus, it is established that [one] pair [of measurements] is by means of the thread from her half-womb. Likewise, another pair [of measurements] is by means of the remaining thread, according to the measurement of a common thread-line for those two very same womb-chambers of the Śukāghna and Kroḍa palaces. Thus [it is].

There are indeed four [of them]. Regarding the passage beginning with "tadagni" and so forth: the meaning is that in front of her, Śukanāsā—that is, before one of the four [sons]—is the place for the bull possessing the characteristics to be described.
"One-fourth part of the pavilion."

That which has been constructed as the pavilion (maṇḍapa), it is stated that [the flagstaff] should not be attached, being separated by a fourth part of it. He states another alternative construction: "threefold," and so forth.
Or else, from that very pavilion, the flagstaff (dhvaja-yaṣṭi) should be made three times its measure; or else, "the weapon" (yudha).

In this very place, when the deity is installed, vṛṣas and other [emblems] should be fashioned upon the top of the flagstaff (dhvajayaṣṭi) at the head of the image; below that, a pedestal for offerings (balipīṭha) should be made for the sake of the crows. Regarding the "jagatī" and so forth: "in front" means directly in front of the temple (prāsāda), where sometimes there is a jagatī.
The meaning is that the specific type of supernatural creation called *baṃdhaka* is sometimes even the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the *mukhamaṇḍapa*;
this is also stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra*.

"And the pavilions (maṇḍapas) are to be placed in front by means of a cord, according to the 'jagatī' rule. Regarding the phrase "the crest and the pinnacle," they describe a circular rotation (*paribhrāmaṇikā*) that is equal to one-fourth [of the height] and attached to the lower part of the body of the temple (*prāsāda*). This is the remainder; and as for the phrase "of that which is well-known as the pedestal (*pīṭha*) of the temple," and so forth.

Outside that [central structure], for the purpose of circumambulation, temples for the deities of the directions should be constructed at the very perimeter, facing toward it, measuring one-fourth of the main temple. Starting from the east and so forth, or in the case of the Valabhī style, Brahmā (the Grandfather) should be placed in the temple named Valabhī.

Or, having established himself in the eastern direction, one should sacrifice—this is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "With a body half-woman" means [worshipping] Ardhanārīśvara with the previously mentioned characteristics. "The circle of Mothers" means the *mātṛcakra*. "In the direction of the Rākṣasa" means in the south-western direction. "A seat of a crescent moon" means...

The meaning is that one should contemplate that very same yogin, seated in the posture called *ardhacandra*, having ascended yoga, or indeed Mṛtyujit himself, in the western direction (*vāruṇī*). As for the Destroyer of Krauñca (Kumāra), if they are not placed within the directional palaces, then their stationing occurs even in the regions of those palaces.

The meaning is "that which is to be performed," namely the city and so forth. Alternatively, *devagarbhāpūḥ* refers to the city whose womb contains the gods; the sense is that even within that city, the aforementioned deities abide in precisely that manner. Now, the arrangement consisting of its construction is described.

"Matā" and so forth: when the ground has been demarcated by that very intended measurement of width—that is, its extent—by means of a gnomon (śaṅku) and so on; the meaning is that even by the previously mentioned method consisting of piercing the pole star (dhruva) to determine the north and east, [the directions are fixed]. Immediately thereafter, O Lord...

One should arrange the houses starting from the *pada*. Regarding the phrase "therein," and so forth: "therein" means in that location consisting of a collection of nine squares (*navapada*), which is the nature of the *īśa*-square;

there, the recitation (*japa*), the offering of gold (*hema*), the worship (*arcā*), and the consecrated site (*dhāma*) must be performed, provided with the necessary implements. As for what those implements are: for recitation, they include the rosary (*akṣasūtra*) and so on; for the fire-oblation (*homa*), they include clarified butter (*ājya*) and so on; and for the worship (*arcana*), they include the messenger (*dūtī*), the vessel for the *arghya* offering (*arghapātra*), and so forth.

The meaning is "endowed with that. Regarding the passage beginning with "Parjanya," the phrase "all musical instruments" refers to the four types of instruments designated by the Teacher as *tata* (stringed), *ānaddha* (membranous), *suśira* (wind), and *ghana* (solid).
Regarding the passage beginning with "snāna" (bath), the term "Jayaṃta" refers to the house where victory was attained; therein [is the description] beginning with "Marubhṛt" (the wind-bearer).

"Marubhūtiṇḍa" refers to the triad beginning with him, namely Indra, Arka, and Satyaka. As for what the name of the city-gate (pratolī) is, he says: "Adorned with excellent door-panels, leaf-hinges, and sturdy bolts.
This means it is endowed with beauty through its excellent doors, excellent leaf-hinges, and sturdy bolts.

And as for the pavilions (maṇḍapa): on that very same street, one of three types known as *catuḥśrāyata*, *bhadra*, or *suviṣṭapa*— to be described by their defining characteristics— is a pavilion intended for the accomplishment of music, dance, and so forth.

It should be understood that because of the inclusion of the word "first" (*ādya*), this applies even for the proof of the first [meter]. Now, its definition begins with "sixty-four" (*catuṣṣaṣṭi*) and so forth.
From a field marked by sixty-four [syllables], there is the removal of the *aṣṭi*; that is, when sixteen are eliminated.
By the word *aṣṭi*, the meter consisting of sixteen syllables is denoted. Since it thus consists of eight feet (*pada*).

By means of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) from the eight rows, once two rows have been removed from the eastern and western directions, there remains a set of six rows. One should place the length as the basis upon the right and left sides; those four remaining squares— [End of sentence fragment]
In this manner, one should place the two side-walls (*pārśva*) so as to prevent the [structure] from becoming oblong.
As it has been said: "The ears (*śruti*) should be supported by the base; for in this way, it becomes square and elongated.
Thus, by the reasoning established above, it indeed becomes square and elongated through its actual configuration, not merely by name.

Also specifically: Now, regarding the auspicious pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), having divided the square field sixteenfold in each direction, one should omit four squares at each corner according to the rule of "the loss of the Vedas" (*śruticyuti*). Thus, sixteen [squares] are to be omitted;
furthermore, four squares each are to be added in the four directions to prevent the [spirits] from wandering. And when at each corner...

The reduction by four units has been performed; for that reason, it is called "two-sun" (dvisūryya). That which has twenty-four squares in all four directions is the "four-part two-sun" (sadvisūryyacaturāṃśaka).
That very same [figure] consisting of twelve squares is abandoned in each direction for the sake of the walls, leaving one hundred and fifty-six in the middle.
The "circulation of parts" consists of forty-four parts;
how so? It is thus:
by calculation, through the removal of sixteen from the four corners and the establishment of ninety-six for the sake of the walls.
In both cases, by subtracting one hundred and twelve and one hundred and fifty-six from two hundred and fifty-six,
the result is indeed one hundred and forty-four;
and because there is an absence of walls at its corners, this portion is [set aside] for the sake of preserving the Vedas according to the requirements of the context.
Even if not explicitly stated, the arrangement of the walls within and without the measurement-line must be avoided [if it is improper].
Now, that which is called *suvistīrṇa* (well-expanded):

"Vasvaṃśa," and so forth. "Vasvaṃśa in the field" means marked by eight [squares] each from two directions; by omitting sixteen [squares], and by providing four groups of four in the four cardinal directions, it is that which has an exit like a rutting elephant (*mattavāraṇa*), and of the six... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

The meaning is that its womb (*garbha*) has a length consisting of six parts, as its placement on both sides—the left and right—is completely omitted. Thus, it measures six parts in length. [It is for] those who are spectators of the "six-tasteful ones" (*ṣaḍrasika*), that is, those who are attached to the objects of the sixfold group of senses with the mind as the sixth.

The meaning is: "staying, bathing, [and so forth] from the pillars," and so on, including the canopy with small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*). Now, regarding the pillars: "pillar" and so forth. "Sixfold" means of six types; "rucaka" and so forth. Among those, that which is called *rucaka*— [The text continues: ...is that which is situated at the center of the four pillars, having the form of a lotus, and is adorned with various jewels. It is said to be the most excellent among all the pillars. Furthermore, the *śrīvatsa* pillar is that which is shaped like a śrīvatsa mark, possessing a beautiful appearance and being adorned with various ornaments. The *vardhamāna* pillar is that which has the shape of an increasing vessel (*vardhamāna*), being auspicious and decorated with various designs. The *svastika* pillar is that which has the form of a svastika, being auspicious and adorned with various jewels. The *nandyāvarta* pillar is that which has the shape of a nandyāvarta, being auspicious and decorated with various ornaments. The *padma* pillar is that which has the form of a lotus, being beautiful and adorned with various jewels. These are the six types of pillars. Furthermore, there are other pillars such as the *citra*, *vicitra*, *viśeṣa*, *viśeṣaka*, *viśiṣṭa*, *viśiṣṭaka*, *viśuddha*, *viśuddhaka*, *viśobhana*, *viśobhanaka*, *viśobhita*, *viśobhitaka*, The four-sided [diamond] is designated as *vajra*; the eight-sided is designated as *dvivajra* (double-vajra); the sixteen-sided is [designated] by implication (*arthāpatti*) itself as "twice that number of sides," and so forth. Regarding those two mentioned in the *pralīnavṛtti*, the one named *pralīna* has thirty-two sides; however, the circular one has no sides at all because of its circularity, and thus it is also the sixth by name.

The meaning is that what is called the "inferior mandala" is characterized by inferior ornaments that resemble [the others] in their arrangement. Regarding the phrase beginning with "sādhāra" (with the base): they are to be joined anywhere together with the base and the head. Regarding the phrase beginning with "kuṃbha" (pitcher): these include the pitcher (kuṃbha), the secondary pitcher (upa-kuṃbha), and the buttress (viṣkaṃbha).

There are four known as *sthira*, which rely upon pillars and have the form of pillars; and there are four others beginning with *vikārī*. Thus, for the *jyeṣṭha*, *madhyama*, and *kanīya* types of pavilions (*prāsāda*), there are sixteen [varieties] associated with their respective pillar-lengths in sequence, starting with *vikārī*.

The bases (ādhāra) should be made from one-twelfth, one-eighth, or [one-sixteenth] of [the height]; this is what is meant: for the pillars of the largest temples, they should be one-sixteenth of their own length;
for those of medium size, one-twelfth; and for the smallest, one-eighth. Thus it is said. Not the top (mūrdhā).

And so forth. Therefore, in the three worlds of Nandikāvarta, there are four heads known as "Stable" (Sthira), which are equal to the pillars and their bases. The meaning is that whatever is the measurement for the sides and so on of the bases, that same measurement applies to these [heads]. Among them, first is the one called Kumbha, the base of the pitcher.
"Vasvaṃśa," and so forth. In the foundational field (*ādhārakṣetra*), the *rūpaka* known as the "Khurikāvarta" is to be divided by eight parts;

it is to be made with two parts (*dṛk-saṃkhyayā*). The one called the circle (*vṛtta*) is by the moon—that is, by one part alone—and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is by the fires (three parts). Thus, above the remaining two parts utilized in this manner—
"And its exit is from each side-region," and so forth. Since no other definition for the *upakuṃbha* is stated, its form is precisely as described. For it says:
"But this one relies on four *vyāḍas*; four *vyāḍas* (serpents) should be joined to it, or [four] *nṛsiṃhas*."

The Vajins and Vāyus should be made with lotus symbols, [as stated] in the section beginning with "Viṣkambha" and so forth. The support called Viṣkambha is exactly like a *kumbha* (pitcher), except that its base, which in the *kumbha* is called a *khurikā*, is here designated as its pedestal (*pīṭha*) by means of a ninefold division and three lines. Thus he says: "the Siddhapīṭha. It is established (*siddha*).

The meaning is: "that whose pedestal (pīṭha) is fully developed. The fourth [type], called *sthira*, is described as having its stability resting upon pillars (*staṃbha*); this means it is situated according to the likeness of pillars, such as being circular, square, and so forth.
Now, regarding the veins (*sirā*).

"Divided into three parts," and so forth. When the area of the head is not marked with bricks, one should fashion makara-crests (makarodgamas)—each by one part—on both sides of the central cell in the row below; that which possesses these makara-forms is called a *naṃdyāvarta*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "gata" and so forth:
because the turning of the portion of the head of Gajāsya has not been explicitly described, this is the very procedure for its construction;
however, this [portion] consists of two elephant faces with their tips pointing upward.

The distinction is that [the area] on both sides is adorned in the place of the *makara* (sea-monster). Regarding the phrase "below" and so forth: below the head, at the region where these two *makara* and elephant-heads are fashioned, there is one knot for the purpose of forming the support (*ādhāra*), and two others on the two upper portions; thus it is.
Being joined with three knots (*trigranthi*), it is described as having three folds (*trivali*) by means of the arrangement of three girdles (*mekhalā*).

Regarding the phrase "from the third part" (*tryaṃśāt*) and so forth: likewise, by the conception of three parts for that which is called "well-stable" (*susthira*), that which is adorned with lotus petals from the upper third part is the *susthira*; and because of the connection with a pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) in the lower two parts.
The portion prepared at the top for the purpose of drawing the lotus petals is that very field;
by dividing it into eight parts, this is what is meant. "Then the eight petals," and so forth. This follows immediately after the description of the base, the head, and the pillars.
Among those, a wooden rampart (*dāruprākāra*) should be constructed together with the two [gate-towers] called *upari* and *atulā*.

Regarding the construction of wooden structures and so forth, whereas in the case of stone structures the material is naturally stone itself, having thus spoken incidentally of the gateways (*pratolī*), pavilions (*maṇḍapa*), and so on, up to the pillars (*stambha*), the subject at hand is now described: "It should be seen," and so forth.

Regarding the triad known as *dṛśām-ṛkṣa-śaptārcis*, [the text says] "in the southeast" (*pūṣṇi*) and so forth. Regarding the term "of the self-restrained" (*saṃyaminām*): it refers to the specific ascetics who have disciplined their selves, for the sake of the accomplishment of self-contemplation—that is, for the realization of the true nature of the self. Regarding "Gandharva" and so forth: "in the corner" (*koṇe*) means optionally in the location of the ancestors (*pitṛ-sthāne*).

Or, one should perform what was previously stated regarding the four [deities] known as Gṛhakṣata, Yama, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgahva. Alternatively, one may optionally construct a *maṭha* (monastery) with the words "tāmbūla" and so forth. The term "rujī" refers to the place of disease (the deity of illness). The term "gandhavaha" refers to the place of the wind (the deity Vāyu). The term "puṣpāyana" means a flower-house. The phrase "ahi-traya" refers to the three principal serpents, specifically the one named Bhallāṭa.
In the two [squares] called Soma and Ṛk, the treasury (kośagṛha) or storehouse is located; in the two called Aditi and Diti,

within the interior among the positions of Brahmā and the others, the inner pavilion (garbha-maṇḍapa) of the temple should be constructed, situated at the intersection of the previously mentioned lines and marked by the junction of the signs.

The abode of the banner; "armor," etc.; "varva," etc.; "varva," etc.; the abode of armor is a house for slaughter, made of gold, both wrought and unwrought—meaning fashioned and unfashioned gold; "truth," etc.;
"of physicians" means of the medical practitioners; "the sky"; "without betel"; after the word for father (pitṛ).

The meaning is "the office of the chamberlain" (*daucārikapada*). The *avarodhaya-dhūma-hantarikā* and others are the *pālakas*, the guardians of the inner apartments; the *mahantarakas* are the controllers of women. They are [referred to] by the term *puṣpadanta* in the text.
Regarding the passage beginning with "from that" (*tata*): from those two powerful offices known as Asura and Śoṣaka, among the ministers...

In the word *sthāne* (in the place), there is the state of health (*ārogyapada*) in the place of disease; thus, it is the place of medicine. In the word *vāyau* (in the wind), it is the place of fragrance for those who live by it, and the place of men who live by [the scent of] humans, and so forth.

In the word *phaṇabhṛti* (among the hooded ones), it is the place of those who know the art of producing gems from serpents; and in the word *puṣpāyanavām* (of the flower-giver), it is the chief [place], and so forth.

The phrase "in front of that" (tadagrataḥ) means immediately after the Bhallāṭa [altar], namely at the Soma-pada. Regarding the statement "the house is joined with cows and so forth," since the mention of "deities" occurs there, it should be understood as being "in front of that.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: in front of the Soma-pada, at the Ṛg-yakṣa, the house is joined with cows and so forth, and so on.

The house of the capturers—the rams, goats, buffaloes, and their guardians—is [located] in Aditi and so forth. "That Sārakālaya" refers to the hall for mantra-discourse or the house of the staff-bearers (Yāṣṭīkas).
Now follows the application of the stations of the six-footed deity.
"Vaiśvānara," and so forth. "The royal residence" means a dwelling situated in the southern direction.

"The bedchamber is Yama" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned; for since the inner apartments were previously described there, now it is the bedchamber itself that is intended, specifically within the sphere designated as Āryaman and Marīci.

"The meeting place of the gurus is on the mountain," and so forth; this means that the place for performing the excellent discourse is located in the northern direction, known as the Mountain (Pṛthvīdhara). "The letter Ra," and so forth;
the meaning is that those other places belonging to the corner-occupiers, such as Water (Āpa) and the rest, are secret locations for the sake of the letter Ra.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yasyām" (in which direction), this rule applies to a city whose main gate faces the east; the question is, what is the procedure for a city whose gates face other directions? To address that, it says: "In whichever direction the city's gate is," and so forth—meaning that for whichever direction the gate actually lies, one should designate that as the east (*prācī*), and then perform the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the northeast (*īśa*).
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) pertaining to that [deity] must be performed exactly as it is; however, in the case of the *āsthāna* (stationing) and *śayana* (reposing), it is otherwise.
This means there is no shifting of that [placement] merely to conform to the door; rather, the *āsthāna* and *śayana* must be performed in their own respective places.
As for the application of the construction in front of the eastern door, as stated in the *Vaivasvatapada*: [text follows].

One should construct a standing place and a sleeping place; such is the application for those two, meaning that it applies there to the construction of other directions and doors as well. Regarding "a four-winged house" and so forth: one should construct that house according to the rules.
As it has been said:
That specific type is the *catuḥśāla* house. That which is characterized by four halls in all four directions is the *catuḥśāla*;
however, that which lacks the eastern hall and has three halls in the north is called *atriśāla* by the illustrious Kiraṇeśa.

"The field named Hiraṇyanābha, lacking the northern row of rice, is considered a good site; lacking the eastern row of rice, it is considered a source of prosperity. This means it should be devoid of [rows] to the south or to the west.
As it is said in that very same work:

"By a small sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), there is loss of wealth; by one that is deficient, the destruction of life; and by another that is deficient, the ruin of a faction and the end of one's sons. This is stated in the passage beginning "or it is called Viśāla. Regarding the word "that" (tat): for the purpose of referring back to what preceded and what followed, if it is ever the case that it is Viśāla, then [it is so] excluding the two aforementioned halls (śālās).
It is thus stated that it is characterized by the two branches on the south and west. As it is said in that very same place:
"For the sake of accomplishment, that [mantra] should be pure if it is joined with the southern [branch]."
The Yama-śūrpa joined with the northwest, however, bestows death.
That which is joined with the north and the east is known as Daṇḍa, which causes punishment;
that which is joined with the east and the south should be known as Vāta, which is fond of quarrels.
A house extending toward the east brings about the destruction of the wife named Cullī;
one joined excessively toward the south and north causes extreme enmity.
In that very center, another Rājagṛha is also conceptualized; he says "the abodes" (*dhāmāni*) and so forth.
That which has nine houses is the other maṇḍala of planets called Nandyāvarta; it should be constructed in that same manner. To explain its purpose, he says:

"Having become," and so forth. When marked with five squares, "after the center, from the displacement"—that is, from the displacement of those which are immediate and contiguous to the central square that is marked.
By this very process of elimination, [the pattern is formed] with four corner squares, as well as the center, the east, the south, and the north.

By means of the five [units] in the fifth square, ten do not remain; the meaning is that those very [units] become ninefold. In that regard, it is stated that what is in the center faces east, north, west, and south. "Possessing all paths" (*sarvavīthika*) means that a path (*vīthikā*) circulates in all four directions.

Regarding those configurations which are well-known anywhere as *piṇḍikās*, that one called *svastika* has also been described: "If they are produced on all sides, it is *susthita*; if they are raised, it is *udyata*"; the others are the remaining ones.
Now, the purpose or utility of the remaining [houses] other than the central house is being stated.

"Devāgāra" and so forth. "The locus for the primary implements and equipment" means that which is the cause—the collection of utensils and tools—of the specific type of food known as *yaṃtrameda* (or *medhā*), or rather, the principal wheel (*cakrikā*) thereof. "Of the king" and so forth; the central hall belongs to the king.

"One hundred and eight cubits is the maximum" means that this is the most excellent [dimension], and beyond that, it may be made larger elsewhere. From this measurement, the length is increased by one-quarter at each step;
thus, the length becomes one hundred and thirty-five [cubits]. Therefore, there is a reduction of eight [cubits] from both the width and the length in each respective direction.

"The four [are] based on the corners; 'half of that' means half the measurement of the central house, such as seventy-two [hands], and so forth. The central house of Gañjapāla is seventy-two hands in width, and likewise its measurement is increased by one [hand] from half of that."

Due to the length and the exhaustion of the seven [units], there are four [units] in each direction; likewise, from the center, half [of that] is in the corners, making eight, and so forth. For the commander of the army, the protector of the *tantra*, the [mandala] in the center is sixty-four cubits;
similarly, by the increase of the length, this rule remains established according to logic as far as the characteristics of the house.
"The region is the loss of the flavors" means that when there is a loss of the six [flavors], there are the six [results] and so forth. Here, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction.
And for the crown prince, the central house is eighty *hasta*s; from the loss of the six [units], it is in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

From the center of that, in those very same purposes—namely, those stated in the passage beginning with "the temple of the gods" (*devāgāra*) and so forth. After this, [there is the section] beginning with "from sixty" and so forth.

According to the *Arthaśāstra*, the residence of a minister other than that of the crown prince consists of houses and so forth; the central hall is sixty cubits [in length], with four wings extending in the four directions. Thus, it has five courtyards (*sukośa*) and so on.
For other royal servants, [the size] should be according to their respective wealth, or otherwise, as they themselves find pleasing.
Regarding the passage beginning with "thirty-two," the principal house of the *agrajanman* (the Brāhmaṇa) is thirty-two cubits.

From that, by a reduction of four [cubits] each time—meaning a decrease of four in each subsequent case—there are another four [types of houses]. Thus, there are five types of houses for the Brāhmaṇa: thirty-two, twenty-eight, and twenty-four.

The [first] twenty and sixteen cubits are like weapons; whatever he performs from them according to his capacity, therefore the second, consisting of twenty-eight cubits, is the primary one for a Kṣatriya; the third, which consists of twenty-four cubits, is for a Vaiśya;
and the fourth, which consists of twenty cubits, is for a Śūdra, and so on.

For the Kṣatriyas and others, he establishes five [measures] each by decreasing [the height] by three, two, and one [hand], respectively; thus, by a reduction of three from twenty-eight hands, there are twenty-five, twenty-two, nineteen, and sixteen hands. For the Kṣatriya, there are likewise five [measures] with two reductions.

For a Vaiśya, there are indeed twenty-four cubits, as well as twenty-two, twenty, eighteen, sixteen, and five cubits. Likewise, by decreasing one cubit from twenty, the dimensions for a Śūdra are nineteen, eighteen, seventeen, sixteen, and five cubits; such is the meaning.
This very point is clarified further ahead: there is no hall (*śālā*) below a measurement of sixteen cubits (*hastika*), except for the case of *abhūti* (lack of prosperity) due to exhaustion;
therefore, from that [measurement], either *dhoyā* halls or houses are constructed.
And these cause the exhaustion of prosperity (*bhūti-parikṣaya*). "With a length increased by one's own foot" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned.
"Exultant," and so forth. The meaning is that only Kṣatriyas (rājanyas) should dwell in the four directions, beginning with the north, while Brāhmaṇas and others should dwell elsewhere.

"Hired laborers" (bhṛtakāḥ) means servants. Regarding "graha," and so forth: in the outer regions, such as the quarters of Carakī and Skanda, the lowest castes (antyajātayaḥ), including leather-workers, washermen, and the like, should dwell; and "Caṇḍālas," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "mauṣṭikā" (boxers/fighters) and "śvapacānām" (of the dog-cookers/low-castes), specifically concerning dance: the houses of those born of the lowest castes should especially be constructed in the southern direction. Now, regarding the phrase beginning with "atha" (now): the "amarālayas" are palaces;
in front of them, at the very forefront, there are pavilions (*maṇḍapas*) of the previously mentioned measurements, according to the number of their pillars.

Each [type] exists with its own distinct name. Regarding the phrase "satsūtra" and so forth: the nine pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) beginning with *tatsūtra* and ending with *vṛddhi* are the smallest (*yavīyāṃsaḥ*), meaning they are the minor ones; in these very minor temples (*prāsāda*), there are twelve [pillars], increasing up to twenty-eight pillars. For this very reason, he says: "four times the sages... (caturguṇamuni).

Regarding the phrase "by the extremities" (*prāntaiḥ*): by that [method], a pavilion with excellent pillars (*satsūtramaṇḍapa*) consists of twelve pillars; then, by increasing by two at a time—namely, fourteen, and so on, up to an increase to the number twenty-eight—it is designated as such. This is the meaning. The phrase "likewise," etc., follows.
Immediately after those, there are nine [temples] beginning with Nandanādya and ending with Saṃvardhana, increasing by two at each step;

above three hundred, there are forty-six [types] including the *adikā* (initial) ones. Regarding the middle-sized [temples], they are for the central functions of the middle-sized *prāsādas* themselves—namely, those primarily intended for enjoyment—and so forth, as they are superior [to the others].

The temples beginning with Śrīvatsa and ending with Puṣpaka are the nine Jyeṣṭha-prāsādas; likewise, there are forty-six [others] to be worshipped twice, meaning those from forty-six upwards up to sixty-four.
"Ten," and so forth: these pavilions (maṇḍapas) are joined with ten, eight, six, or four [pillars].

The *miśraka* (mixed) designations are to be applied; they are assigned to the smaller palaces (*prāsāda*) for the sake of obtaining the *miśra* [classification], which means for the purpose of minor construction. Regarding "by two" and so forth:
by means of two pillars, it is to be understood as the pedestal-pavilion (*pādamaṇḍapa*) situated in front of the *śukanāsā* (the frontal pediment).

"Niṣṭā," and so forth. "The accomplishment of the goal (*niṣṭāsiddhi*)" means the attainment of happiness for the sake of accomplishing minor [aims], that is, for the sake of the *raudra* (fierce) accomplishments. "Iti," and so forth. "And various (*vicitrāḥ*)" means that they possess names and forms; the meaning is that, like mantras, whatever the procedure may be—whether it be yoga or the like—it accomplishes the desired object in a manifold way.
[The Fifth Chapter of the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, titled "The Construction of the Temple"]
Now, the ritual of consecration (adhivāsa) is described.
"Then," and so forth. The commencement of the sacrifice for others is the *adhivāsa* (preliminary consecration), which is indeed the invitation to the *dhāman* (the abode).
This should be performed in front of the *prāsāda* (temple)—that is, in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*)—according to the reasoning to be stated later and with auspicious characteristics.
He states its dimensions: "one cubit and so forth. For the installation of a *liṅga* measuring one cubit, [it should be] by eight...

This pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed with ten [parts], measuring two cubits according to the standard of the Sun (arka) and three cubits according to the standard of the Directions (dik). Regarding the phrase "Yama" and so forth: from four cubits up to nine cubits, each should be made by increasing the Yama by two cubits at each step. In this manner, for a nine-cubit [base], the pavilion becomes twenty-two cubits.
He states another method of calculation by means of an alternative option, beginning with "That" (tat), etc.
Taking that measure—starting from twelve cubits (*hasta*) and so forth—as the initial unit, [the number of squares] for a space of one cubit is twelve;
for two cubits it is fourteen; and continuing up to nine cubits, it is twenty-eight cubits.
This is the meaning. However, since no other increase (vṛddhi) is heard of here, there is only this [specific] increase. Regarding "by half of that":

a pavilion for the purpose of bathing should be constructed in the northeast or the east direction, measured by half the size of that [main] pavilion; "that too," and so forth. Here also, in terms of the wording, even the two pavilions are not...

Regarding the phrase "confused about the directions" (*digbhrāntam*): by means of the threads, one should properly establish the directions; the connection with the distant term is that the pavilion for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa-maṇḍapa*) should be provided with arches (*toraṇa*) and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it should be understood—according to what will be described later—that it is generally provided with canopies (*vitāna*) and banners (*patākā*).

He describes the nature of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) with the words "the pavilion," and so forth. The pavilion is the abode and dwelling-place of the splendor of the Lord Śaṅkara, that is, Sadāśiva himself; it does not represent a pavilion in the sense of a mere ordinary house. Furthermore, the splendor consists of the four powers, namely Nivṛtti and the others, as follows:
That splendor has faces presided over by the Lords Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Bhaṭṭāraka;

as for the fifth face, it is not grasped because it exists above them and its nature is not applicable to the purpose at hand, yet this is not due to non-pervasiveness. As for the pavilion, however, there are arches (toraṇas) equal in number to those [faces].

The meaning is "four. Furthermore, it is marked—that is, characterized—by nine banners, which signify the number nine; for the powers (śaktis) of the Lord’s splendor, beginning with Vāmā and so forth, as well as those beginning with Śānti and so forth, are ninefold.
There are four archways (*toraṇa*) arising from the milk-tree (*akṣīvṛkṣa*), characterized as will be explained by the reasoning to follow. Regarding their height, he says "five," and so forth.
For the smallest ones—that is, starting from one cubit up to three cubits—there are five-cubit archways in sequence.

For a *hāstika* [temple], it is six *hasta*s; for a *dvihāstika*, seven *hasta*s; and so on up to the *trihāstika*, which measures eight *hasta*s with the tips of the *vasudeva*-fingers. Regarding "of these": among the others—the medium and the superior—therein, each medium [temple] has a measurement of exactly seven *hasta*s with the tips of the eight (*vasu*) fingers.

Therefore, for a [mandala] of four cubits, the arches (*toraṇas*) are seven cubits plus eight fingers; for one of five cubits, they are eight cubits; and for one of six cubits, they are likewise eight cubits, and so on.
Thus, for the largest [mandalas], they are eight cubits plus four fingers, and then fourteen fingers more than that.

The archways (*toraṇas*) for a [stūpa] of seven cubits are [seven cubits]; for one of eight cubits they are increased by one finger-breadth; but for one of nine cubits, they are measured at eight and a half cubits—this is the meaning. As it is stated there:
"From the end of three cubits, there is an increase of one cubit upwards until six; for those ending in eight fingers up to nine..."
That increase is four finger-breadths;

furthermore, just as for those measuring from one cubit up to three cubits, so too for those measuring from four cubits up to nine cubits, there is likewise an increase by eight (vasu) or an increase by forty-eight (vasu-veda) finger-breadths.
That which is proposed is improper, because the meaning of that [text] is not heard in the mind or in speech,
and because it is possible for it to form a single syntactical unit with another scripture concerning the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*); likewise,
this applies to the nine altars (*vedi*) to be described later, which range from four cubits up to twelve cubits.
Because each archway (*toraṇa*) is exceedingly high, it would be inconsistent for its height to be equal to the distance between [the pillars],
and likewise for its width on both sides to be equal to the measurement of the altar (*vedi*); furthermore,
this will be explained immediately below for the sake of the intended meaning.
It is indeed improper and unjustified to raise objections that do not conform to the meaning of the authoritative statement (*pramāṇavākya*), such as [the claim] "it is good for them," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in those three"—that is, in the three [parts] beginning with the hand—the intense desire (*arāmarṣa*) is dug out below the arches (*toraṇa*) so that the branches may enter; thus, in all three of those, it is measured by the span of the hand (*hastamāna*). Therefore...

The excavation measured by hand begins at four cubits and extends up to nine cubits; it is characterized by an increase of half a body-length for each successive body-length. Thus, the meaning is that for a four-cubit [excavation], the [increase] is four finger-breadths (aṅgula), and so on, increasing by eight finger-breadths per cubit until, for a nine-cubit [excavation], it is one finger-breadth [per cubit].

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the two branches" (*śākhayoḥ*), it is stated that the distance between them, equal to their height, constitutes the measurement of the sides of the arches (*toraṇa*). Otherwise, there is a reduction; the meaning is that the dimensions are different depending on the specific desire [of the patron]. Regarding the passage beginning with "the thorn" (*śalyam*), it refers to the form of the crest situated above the branch.
One should not construct the *toraṇas* for that [five-cubit structure] lower than eight *aṅgulas*.

Regarding the *toraṇas* of the nine-cubit [structure], they should be beyond sixteen *aṅgulas*; and as for the word "or" (*vā*), it indicates a division of the intervals here according to the proportional division for those [structures] from two cubits up to eight cubits.

It should be understood through the very intellect that conceives of the division of parts; what need is there for much more regarding the addition of finger-breadths? As stated in the venerable Piṅgalāmata:
"The increase of the core [śalya] for all [types] is proclaimed to be one finger-breadth."
"From the eastern [side], measuring eight finger-breadths," and so forth.

"On their sides above," etc.: those *śṛṅga* and *śūla* [ornaments] on the upper sides of those very arches (*toraṇa*) are [to be made] with a width that is one-fifth [of the total]. "Those [are to be consecrated] with the *astra[-mantra]," etc.; [this is done] generally with the *praṇava* (OM), and with the other [mantras].
"Then with the mantra of the one to be accomplished," and so forth. "The bull-faced moon" (*niśākaramukhavṛṣaḥ*):

because the word *dāra* denotes a child, it refers to Kārttikeya; and "the immeasurable" (*amita*) refers to Caṇḍīśa, since scripture mentions them specifically as the doorkeepers of the lords of the Gaṇas. "Recalling their arrows" (*tadvāṇān smaranniti*): [refers to] those [arrows].
Regarding each [of these], whatever their respective qualities—such as their own pervasiveness (*vyāpti*) and so forth—from those come the eight [kalaśas], and so on.
