*Praśānta* and the others, ending with *aiśānta*, are the names of the eight *kalaśas*. *Nyagrodha* refers to the corner compartments of the altar (*vedi*) of the consecration pavilion (*adhivāsa-maṇḍapa*). *Himendra* and so forth...

In the expression "resembling snow, a rainbow, the bandhūka flower, black, blue, and a cloud," the word *upamā* (resembling) is connected to each of the six [objects] beginning with snow: "resembling snow," "resembling a rainbow," "resembling the bandhūka flower," "resembling black," "resembling blue," and "resembling a cloud. This is according to the rule beginning with *śārva*. From the direction of Śarva (the northeast), that is, from the direction of Īśāna.

Regarding their placement: "In the center, white or variegated. Here, although the word "white" (*śveta*) has already been stated as being "like snow," there is no fault in its repetition, as it is appropriate to use synonyms such as conch, milk, jasmine, and teeth for the color white. That which was described as "cloud-like" in the west should be made white as an alternative.
The meaning is that they "come into being according to their respective functions" through distinctions such as those of desire (*kāmya*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "eight finger-breadths" and so on: in the middle portion, there are eight finger-breadths high wooden supports called *sthali-kās*; that [liṅga] which possesses such four-cubit [supports] is described as such, in the case of a liṅga one cubit in height.

For [altars] measuring from two cubits up to nine cubits, the wooden planks on the pedestal increase by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) for each increase of one cubit. Whether measured by the "cubit" (*hasta*) or by any other measurement, the smallest of the small increases by two finger-breadths, continuing in this manner until the size reaches nine cubits.
The third part is encompassed by the sight; that is to say, the second hand [of the measure] is increased by sixteen *aṅgulas*. Regarding "the altar" (*vedī*) and so forth:
"altar" (*vedī*) means a square; by the word "bhaga," a shape like a vulva is meant. This refers to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so on.

The connection is that the eight *kuṇḍas* (sacrificial pits), starting from the east in the sequence of the directions, should be located either outside the altar (*vedi*) of the preliminary consecration pavilion (*adhivāsa-maṇḍapa*) or outside the temple (*prāsāda*). Then, "another [pit] on the top of the altar" refers to that which is situated between Śiva and the Goddess. Regarding "that [is] nine or five," and so forth, it will be explained by what is to be stated later.

With the five elements, beginning with earth, as the womb, there are four [pots] in the four directions and likewise a fifth for Śiva and Īśā; or the others may be placed according to one's desire. Thus, with hands in that shape, [one should place them] within the girdle with the mouth [of the vessel].
For those [altars] whose connection to the ground consists of parts such as squares, triangles, and so forth, it is not the case that the lip (*oṣṭha*) and other features are likewise [proportioned].

In the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the lip should be made by means of twenty-four parts; therefore, in a pit measuring one cubit (*hāstika*), it is by a measurement of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and so on. The navel (*nābhi*) of all pits is likewise [to be made] by half or by a third part of its own measurement.
The girdle for all [types of sacrificial pits] is of a single form, shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
If there is a single girdle in a pit measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in size, it should be six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) wide;
if there are two, three, or four [girdles], they should be reduced successively by two, three, and two finger-breadths respectively.
In this regard, the meaning "proportionately according to what is desired" is precisely what must be understood; the remainder is explained by the rule "one should dig downwards.

This means that from the bottom of the girdle-measurement down to the base of the pedestal, the depth is fifteen finger-breadths proportionately. Regarding the phrase "twofold," etc.: the width of the pedestal should be twice the extent of the *brahmabhāga* (the upper portion) of the *liṅga*.
*Bhadrāsana* is a *bhadrapīṭha*; "bhadra" means beautiful. Now follows the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

Regarding "the *sruva* and *sruc*," and so forth: is it that the *śuka*, the *palāśa*, and the *śrīparṇī* tree are the ones prescribed by the aforementioned names, or may one use some other optional tree? As for the suffix *-kvā* [in the sense of "having drunk"], the intention is that in certain cases involving desire, [one may use] even a tree not specified in the ritual manuals (*ayājñika*). First, as for the *sruc*:

"Vahvāyāma" means "of great length"; specifically, it refers to a length of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Regarding the phrase "rasāgāṣṭavedikā," this is said with respect to the smallest (*kanyasa*) and other types of lingas. The meaning is as follows: for the smallest lingas, the *sruk* ladle has a pedestal (*vedikā*) of that same measure in finger-breadths;
for the middle-sized ones, there are four [finger-breadths] for the pedestal and seven times that number of finger-breadths for the sacrificial post (*medī*).

The altar-rim (*vedikā*) for the largest [sacrificial ladles] measures eight finger-breadths according to the measurement of a finger; their neck (*kaṇṭha*) is three finger-breadths in depth for all of them. Immediately after the receptacle for the clarified butter (*ājyādhāra*), there is the circular pit (*avaṭamaṇḍala*) whose designation will be stated later, from which [the ladles extend] three or four [finger-breadths].

Alternatively, it may be five finger-breadths wide because of its circularity; thus, by the specific characteristics seen in other *saṃhitās*, everything else such as its length and so forth is similar. In the venerable *Kiraṇa*, its width is stated to be six finger-breadths, for it is said in that very same text: "The lotus is sixfold due to its circular movement."

From the sides of the neck to the edge of the mouth, the facial region measures seven finger-breadths; having divided this by its dimensions, excluding the middle fifth part, there is a reduction of two parts on each side for the *veṇīkeśa* (the hairline). That [line] extends from the upper part of the neck as far as the sides of the back, and it is measured according to the size of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*).
Its broad beginning and its limit at the end are as follows:
the flow of clarified butter (ājya) descends from the circular pit (avaṭa-maṇḍala) through the path of the middle of the neck until it reaches the mouth;
from the pitcher, it rises up a staff six finger-breadths in measure, the tip of which is below the altar (vedi).

Another [ladle] is a subtle sacrificial altar (*vedi*) measuring four finger-breadths according to the *Śruti* and *Sāṃkhya* systems; and as stated in the *Mṛtyujid-vidhāna*: "The handle (*daṇḍa*) arising from the jar (*kuṃbha*) has a circumference of six parts. Thus, by means of long compounds and words whose connection is obscured, the *sruva* ladle is intended [to be described].
"Regarding the *sruva* and so forth:

'of that same origin' means that the thick handle, which is of the same material [as the bowl] and like a thumb in size, serves as the support for the *karṣa*-measure of clarified butter (*ājya*) in the vessel whose name is about to be described, the *puṣkara*."
The depth of the *vaṭa* is such that at its base, near the handle, a *gaṇḍikā* (socket) is fashioned,
resembling an *āmalaka* fruit; it is two fingers high in length, or one *hasta*, or twenty-two fingers,
with a tip like a cow’s hoof-print.
The *sruva* ladle is shaped like the reflection of a cow’s hoof-print, extending from the center up to the tip of the flame-mark (*śikhā*), joined by a line at the end of the creation-mark;
its sides are deep toward the northeast, its back is on the outside, and it is joined by two *kumbha* [bulbous] sections.
Such is its form, or else as described in one's own independent ritual manual (*svatantra-svakalpa*). This is the shape of both of these.

The sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) is to be understood from the completion manual (*samāpti-patra*). The sacrificial trees, such as the *aśvattha* and others, should be larger than the little finger in thickness and eight-sided, and so forth. The vessel for the *caru* offering should be made of *udumbara* wood;
alternatively, it may be copper. Likewise, the *pratisara* [cord] should be increased by one cubit (*hasta*), and the portion of the Linga, beginning with Brahma, [is determined accordingly].
"Displaying garlands, protective jars, and sleep-jars," and so forth.

"Both externally and internally" means that just as the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) and other rites were performed externally, they are likewise performed internally within what is called the *puryaṣṭaka*. "Having resorted to the supreme state" (*parāvṛttim āsthāya*).

The supreme transformation (*parāvṛtti*) consists precisely in abiding in one's own true nature by means of the withdrawal of all disturbances; it is essentially of the nature of peace. For, by relying upon that [transformation], the power of the self is indeed overcome by innate purity.
Due to being oriented toward agitation, there is delusion; and from the dissolution of that [agitation], there is the manifestation of that state.
As it was stated by the venerable teacher in the *Svacchandakārikā*:
"For one who is incapable of [removing] his own impurity, yet desires to act upon the duties..."
When agitation is dissolved, then there is the attainment of the state of vibration.
Then the dharma characterized by knowing and acting would be artificial,
because it knows and acts upon everything that is desired.
Having performed the rite called *karma-kara* according to the procedure observed in other *saṃhitās*, as stated in the *Ruru-saṃhitā*:
"Having washed both hands and having adorned them with perfumes and so forth..."
One should assign [the mantras] to Brahmā and to the five branches in successive order.
Having prepared a fragrant mandala, one should place there the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Śiva, the King of Vidyās, with the left thumb in the center.
"One should worship with offerings of water for the feet (arghya-pādya), perfumes, incense,

and sacred threads. Alternatively, having performed the placement (vinyāsa) and worship of the venerable Lord Śiva according to the independent ritual procedure (*svatantra-vidhāna*) where he resides,
one should act "as stated," namely by the previously mentioned method beginning with "the head of all foundations" (*sarvādharaśira*), which is designated as the *śikhā*.
The meaning is that one should place two *kalaśas* in the northeast direction (*īśāna*). Regarding the phrase "of the pavilion" (*maṇḍapasya*) and so forth:

from among the eight bricks (*vasukeṣṭaka*) starting from the east, north, northeast, west, and so on, [one should place them] in sequence from the east up to the northeast for Śiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, Māyā, Kāla, and Niyati.
In that [mandala], nine principles known as Puruṣa and Prakṛti are arranged as the causal agents; likewise,

the five vessels called Supratiṣṭha and the others are arranged as the functional substances (upayogadravya), and the five gems are arranged within those five vessels by means of the "pavitra" mantras and so forth, beginning with the Brahma-mantras.
Regarding what was stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata* that [the mantra] may sometimes be grasped by means of the limbs (*aṅga*),
or by the faces (*vaktra*), or by the heart and so forth— that is, by the Brahmās such as Sadyojāta and the rest in their proper order— it is like a thread of light.

One should prepare cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass, respectively, from goats and the other [animals]. Regarding "fresh cow dung" and so forth: "fresh cow dung" refers to that which has not fallen to the ground; "golden utensils" refers primarily to household articles made of gold, as well as the entire collection of ornaments.

"A multitude of ornaments made of gold alone in the *prakṛti*," and so forth; "in the place of the *prakṛti*-tattva, [one uses] saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and the like. By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (*ādi*), there is the mention of camphor (*karpūra*), clay (*mṛd*), and so on.
In the "thicket" (*gahana*), which refers to *māyā*, there is the "humanizing" (*narājana*) known by the name *nevadbhabhaka*. It is not [the case of] "the *udumbara* tree," and so forth.
The collection of barks derived from trees such as the *udumbara* constitutes the collection of astringents (*kaṣāya*).

The collection of fragrances (*gandha*) is produced by the ripening of the pieces of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*). These, along with the previously mentioned musk and others, are restricted to their respective specific scents; thus, it is "restriction" (*niyati*).
"Then, at the location of the principles (tattva), eight [vases]... and so forth. Outside of that, in the eight directions, there is a set of eight vases;

their specific qualities are described as "white," "pure," and "filled with fragrance. That is to say, they are filled with white sandalwood water, pure water from the Gaṅgā and other sources, and likewise, up to water mixed with various substances. And those...
The eight [oceans], beginning with Kṣāra and ending with Garbhoda, are indicated by their eight auspicious names in the dative case.
Those which are his own forms (nijāmūrtayaḥ) are, for example, like the three forms of the Lord Paramaśiva: the ātmamūrti, the vidyāmūrti, and the śaktimūrti; among these, the ātmamūrti...

The form of Knowledge (vidyāmūrti) consists of the Brahmans, the limbs of Knowledge, and the system of Grammar; it comprises the eight sections of the Mātṛkā, the ninth being the peak-syllable named *nakūṭa*, which is the letter *kṣa*. Through this, the worship and other rites of the Lord are performed. The form of Power (śaktimūrti), however, is as follows:
The names of these eight [energies], beginning with Vāmā and excluding Manonmanī, as well as the eight beginning with Vibhī and excluding Raudrī,
are stated in the venerable *Raurava*: as it is said—
Vibhu, Jñāna, and Kriyā, as well as Vāk and Vāgīśī, and likewise Jvālinī; Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are the supreme Navasaktis.
By this [verse], that which was stated by Umāpati and others, as well as by Kṣmāvāma and others, according to the scriptures, is as follows:

"Earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the self, the moon, and the sun—these are declared to be the eight forms of the God of gods according to their own measure. Of these, the jars should be consecrated with their respective names, ending in the dative case. And this...

The Supreme Guru shall clearly explain [the procedure] starting with the words, "O Fire, having stood at the foot of the form, one should perform the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa)," concerning the essential nature of the forms, the lords of the forms, and so forth; however, in this context,
something has been stated incidentally regarding how one should place other jars externally as well.

In the case of large images, rather than requiring bathing with abundant water, one should use the aforementioned group of astringents (*kaṣāya*), such as those from the pavilion and so forth; immediately thereafter,
one should use a paste made from the bark produced by the trees previously mentioned by name.
And so it is stated in the venerable Piṅgalāmata:
"Then, with decoctions arising from milk-trees, one should apply the bark-paste.
Now follows the extraction of the characteristics:
"having placed," and so forth. By the phrase "one should illuminate the marks," it is the Brahma-line itself that constitutes the portion for worship.

The food to be offered is marked in nine ways, because the defining characteristics are established therein. However, in the opinion of the venerable Nandikeśvara, this is clearly appropriate: "one should divide the portion for worship into three parts. This is also stated in the venerable Kiraṇatantra.
"Having divided the upper portion into three parts" means that the distinction here consists precisely in creating three parts and nine parts.

Regarding "three parts" and so forth: from the upper three parts, two lines characterized by descending downward should be brought down; there too, the aforementioned characteristic would be "consisting of three parts."
Also in the system of the venerable Nandikeśvara:

It should have the characteristic of two parts. He states the measurement for the middle of the characteristic lines: "liṅgāyāma" and so forth. Now, regarding "it should be equal": now, when the entire length (āyāma) of the liṅga is divided into sixteen parts, by discarding one part—

Regarding the phrase "by measuring two parts of the body of the *lakṣman*": when the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is made, the *viṣkaṃbha* (width) is the interval consisting of a separation; this is the meaning. Thus, by means of the twenty-fourth part of the entire *liṅga*, the width of the characteristic mark is established through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, any other *viṣkaṃbha* [different from this] would be either less or more.
Or it may be so. However, that [mark] is a calamity; it speaks of the thickness and measurement of the lines characterized by the signs of inferior accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*).

Regarding the lines and so forth: among the various types of marks, such as the most excellent (*uttamottama*), the *lakṣma-rekhā* (auspicious mark-line) is as broad as three barley grains (*yava*) and deep in proportion to that measure. Among those [other marks], such as the superior, middling, and so on, the smallest of the small is found in them.

One should conceive of the methods of calculation through the rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*). From eight barleycorns multiplied by nine, which are characterized by the number seventy-two parts, there are exactly eight parts remaining after the removal of eight-eighths of those parts.
In the case of the smallest of the small [units], they amount to the measure of one barleycorn less a ninth part; that is to say.
And so it has been stated in the venerable Kiraṇa:
The first line of the Jyeṣṭha-liṅga shall consist of sixteen parts;
for the others, however, there shall be a reduction by one part at a time in the sequence of nine.
Alternatively, one may make eight barley-corns by means of the left portion of that [measurement], or otherwise as it may be;
for it has been said: "That [measurement] divided into nine parts, with each line decreasing by one, follows the sequence of the Jyeṣṭha-liṅga."

He states the location where the two wing-lines emerge: "From three parts," and so forth. From the nine parts, below the third part, there are two suspension-lines; below those two suspension-lines again, from the third part, there are further two suspension-lines; and below those again, from the third part, is the emergence of the wing-lines.
Or it means "the line that is the support of the best," as stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata* as well.
"The descent of the wing-line (*pakṣasūtra*) is measured by half the length of the *laṃbasūtra*.

Having thus generally described the initial emergence of the wing-line— wherein that thread [of the *laṃbasūtra*] goes sometimes upwards and sometimes downwards according to the requirements of the subject matter and the dictates of one's desire— [the author proceeds].
He speaks again in detail,
beginning with "pakṣa" and so forth.
In that case, when the wing-line— which consists of the manifestation of the sūtra and is situated below the portion for worship—
is divided into eight parts, there is a rotation of six parts, excluding the two lower parts, preceded by the production of the wing-lines.
That has been stated in that very same place.
"Having divided that half into eight parts, one should join six circles at the back.

In this very context, there is another definition as an alternative, beginning with "nine," and so forth. When that side-line is divided into nine parts, by taking seven of those parts, one obtains the definition that grants all desires; this is the third [definition] in this very [section].

The method is as follows: "bhāga" and so forth. When that very same wing-area (*pakṣakṣetra*) is divided by three, it is either diminished by two and a half parts (*bhāgadvanasārdha*), or else the mark (*lakṣma*) [is placed] there. This is the meaning: when that wing-area is divided into three, excluding the lower half, from the two and a half parts [above], by means of the two wing-threads (*pakṣasūtra*).
The mark is reversed for those desiring progeny and for those who do not desire women.
It is stated in that very same place:
"The half-lamba [digit] is virtuous; it is remembered as being from the two and a half parts of the revolution."

"For those who have cultivated their selves for the sake of enjoyment and liberation. Furthermore, in that very same place, the fourth method, characterized by four divisions, begins with the word "vikāra" and so forth.
When that very region is divided into sixteen parts, as before, excluding the two lower portions, [the division] proceeds from that very point downward.

Above the *abhṛti*, one should gradually extend two lines for the petals from both sides by means of five parts numbered as arrows (*śara*). Likewise, another [line] is formed by nine parts, excluding two parts. "By the suns" (*bhānubhiḥ*) means by twelve; in the same way, another is formed.

"By Śakras" means by fourteen; the fourth is another distinct division. "Or by the sequence of parts" means that having divided that field with horizontal and vertical lines so as to manifest the grid, the two wings are formed either according to the movement of the diagonal or by projecting the wing-lines into each individual square.
"Behind," and so forth: the junction common to all types [of diagrams] should be made from behind the linga up to that Brahma [line] which lies between those two side-lines (pakṣasūtra).
This is according to the principle of excluding the two lower portions of all kinds of characteristics.
One should diligently lead the two side-lines from the back to the interior of the Brahma-line;
and this has been stated in the venerable Nandikeśvara-mata:
The intersection of the side-lines (pakṣasūtra) should be twice [the distance] from the back;
the wise man should diligently establish the location where the Brahma-line enters.
For those desiring enjoyments, there is yet another characteristic. Regarding the phrase "the sixth," and so forth, below:

by counting upwards starting from the base (abhṛti), that which is the sixth—meaning, at the top of that characteristic—is where there is a barley-corn (yava) shaped like a face; that is established as the portion of the mark (lakṣma).
The meaning is that [the reduction] proceeds from the end of the sixth part up to the end of the fifth part according to the rule for lateral reduction (*pārśvahrāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "in that very place" and so forth: in that region and above it, there is a sharp edge (*tīkṣṇāśra*) following the shape of a barley grain (*yava*); and such a [feature] is fashioned for the purpose of enjoyment (*bhukti*).
Excluding the side-line (*pakṣasūtra*), that which was previously described as being joined with the first side-line is for the purpose of liberation;

[the phrase] "transversely" (*tiryañc*) and so forth refers to that which is made for the purpose of the pillar (*stambha*) and other such elements. That which is done in the seventh part is "transverse" (*tiryak*), meaning it stands obliquely, as shown in the form of a bent barley-corn (*ānatayava*); it is likewise by way of its configuration (*saṃsthāna*).
The "elephant-eye" (hastinetra) should be made in the seventh division on the back of the characteristic [figure], supported by both sides; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "of that," etc.:
for that which is called the elephant and has such a form, there is only one line below, according to the principle of the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra).

Between the *laṃbasūtra* and the *pakṣasūtra*, there is a single line for it; by the word "straight" (*praguṇā*), it is meant to be very clear. By the phrase "obstructed by Hari," it is stated that it extends as far as the limit of Viṣṇu’s portion, reaching down to the end of the lower situated portion.
This applies generally to the emblems of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).

He states the emergence of the flank-line (*pakṣasūtra*): "In that manner, by a portion," and so forth. That which is the flank-line field for others is itself the eastern portion; the meaning is that the emergence of that line occurs in the middle part of the directions, at one-third [of that].
"In that [line] dedicated to Indra," and so forth: in the *liṅga* worshipped by Indra, it possesses the aforementioned form and characteristics.

One indicates it by means of the word "vajra" because its configuration does not arise from that [standard] configuration. Its tip is sharp and thin, like the turning of its head. It should be raised slightly from the middle region. Regarding "by the spear" (*śaktyā*) and so forth: the *liṅga* has the configuration of a spear, even because of its being configured as such.
The characteristic is called *śakti*. Regarding the phrase "the lower diameter has fallen away":

it means that from both sides of the upper diameter, there is a reduction (*hrāsa*) in the lateral dimensions; for this reason, its head becomes elevated. As for the passage beginning with "in the southern [direction]," when the western [quarter] is worshipped, the tip of the noose is the head, and it appears like that [head].

The meaning is "the head. Regarding the passage beginning with *naiśācarī*, [it refers to] the tongue of the Nairṛta [direction], which is like the edge and tip of a sword (*asi-jihvā-khaḍga-prānta-śikhā*); that [tongue] belongs to Agni. Regarding the passage beginning with *sāmānyeṣu*, those [liṅgas] other than the liṅgas of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) are the common ones; among them, as for the purpose of eating... [as follows].

The turning of the head has been performed by means of the umbrella and other such [ornaments]. It is thereby stated that the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is also marked by that very same form. Regarding the phrase "not this," and so forth: "nor even on a mobile iron [image]" means it should be made on stable iron. "Not a *bāṇaliṅga*" means the form consisting of its own [specific] *liṅga*.

He will describe hereafter the characteristics of the Bāṇaliṅga, the mountain-born, and those originating from river currents and springs, because they are eternally present and thus do not require the extraction of characteristics [through ritual refinement].
"The Bāṇaliṅga was consecrated by the ancient Siddhas and is eternally present."
Thus: "Roha" means that which arises from a self-manifested mountain stream; it is not only that which arises from the flow of the Narmadā, but from any other river current whatsoever.
It is implied that for the jeweled liṅgas (*ratnaliṅga*), their radiant splendor alone is the cause [of their manifestation]. This refers to the "opening of the eyes."

The opening of the eyes expresses the greatness of the *lakṣaṇa*. Regarding the passage beginning with "Lakṣmī," etc.: that splendorous light (*dhāmatejas*) of the Supreme Lord, which consists of knowledge and action, exists in the form of the *lakṣma*; for this very reason, without it, there can never be the presence [of the deity] in the *liṅgas*.
He specifies that very thing with the words beginning "by means of measurement, weight, and so forth" (*mānonmānādita*). [This refers to] a *liṅga* devoid of measurement and the like.
Whatever has been stated and as it has been explained, there the presence of the deity necessarily arrives.
"Pūryya" and so forth [refers to] Mṛtyujit. By this, the *siddhārtha* seeds which destroy demons are meant;
the *nairājana* rite has already been mentioned previously. Furthermore, there is another known as *śītalaka*, in which—

Preparations made from flour, clarified butter, lamps, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), sour gruel (*ācāmaka*), sacrificial cakes (*piṇḍa*), and so forth, as well as whatever flowers there may be, are designated by the term "sumanas. "Ratnakarabaka" refers to wealth consisting primarily of pearls, gems, jewels, and gold. Then, "on the altar" (*vedyām*) means in the middle of the altar.
One should prepare a bed for sleeping on one's side upon a mat made of *kuśa* grass within a small vessel filled with sand;
as it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:

[The pedestal] should be filled with sand, and upon it, a covering of *kuśa* grass should be placed; one should then lay the *liṅga* down with its head toward the east. "With their own seat-mantras" means that the seat-mantras are those observed in their respective *Saṃhitās* and other texts;
among them, there are six, of which four belong to Dharma and the others, and one to Ananta.

It means that [the deity] is sought as a unified whole through the two inseparable powers of the Supreme Goddess and the presiding power (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-śakti*), by means of the *praṇava* alone. Regarding "surpassing in qualities" (*guṇādhika*): one should seek an image made of clay that is superior in its other qualities, which is free from black marks and possesses its own proper form. As it has been said:

"Where there is form, there qualities reside. Regarding "obtained by the hundred": one should place near the head a sleep-vessel (nidrākalaśa) consecrated with a hundred [recitations], using the weapon-mantra (*astramantreṇa*) while in darkness. "The pillow" refers to the support for the head.
Regarding "the cover": it is the covering of the vessel with a lid; "the stone" refers to the medicinal container.

"Consisting of stone" refers to the vessel; that is, the receptacle for the purpose of eating. "And those household utensils" means those such as pots and so forth that have been mentioned, as well as those not mentioned. "Puṣya-pratisaras" refers to those [marks] shown on the upper part of the covering cloth according to the previously stated method, which indicate the portions belonging to Brahmā and the other deities.

"Garlands of flowers, strings of beads, and so forth; 'bhūti' refers to varieties of ash"—thus, having offered everything as prescribed in its proper place, one should subsequently arrange them according to the analogy of a moat, conjoined with the weapons of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*).
Since no other action is heard of here, the very action "one should arrange" is the command of Śiva, as indicated by the phrase "those who have been awakened [by His] command."

The command-word (ājñāpada) related to Śiva is that by which they were thus awakened; the command-word is "remain [here]. Regarding the phrase "at the place of the feet" and so forth, and "previously spoken" and so forth:
at the time of the ritual for the installation of the pitcher (kumbhapratiṣṭhā), it was performed according to the sequence beginning with "earth, fire, the sacrificer, sun, water, wind," and so on.

The installation of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) has been described; furthermore, in this context, those who seek enjoyment (bhogin)—namely Earth, Fire, and the others, each accompanied by their respective lords—are declared to be the forms for the sake of enjoyment during the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Moreover:
The serpent-beings such as Ananta and others are the leaders of mantras on the pure path, that is, above Māyā.

For those who desire enjoyment up to the limit of the Sadāśiva-tattva, there is a foundation (pratiṣṭhā) therein; in that regard, Ananta and the others are established in the measure of a barley-corn and a thumb, while Asitāṅga and others are known as Bhairavas.
They are indeed the lords of mantras.
As it is stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*: "For minor rites, [one should employ] the Bhairavas: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and likewise Unmattaka."

"Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, Saṃhāra, and Bhairaveśvara"—the meaning is that these are both *bhairavas* and *īśvaras*, and they are also the lords (*īśvaras*) of the mantras. In some places it says "lokabhṛtaḥ piba"; in that very context, it is also said "stokeśā mūrtīśāḥ" regarding the Śuddhāśuddhādhvara. Others, however, say "Śuddhāśuddhādhvara."
Some explain [the phrase] as "in the white and black consecration (pratiṣṭhā) prescribed by the Śaiva Vedamantras"; that is incorrect, because every form of consecration possesses that same nature.

Regarding "Dhārikā" and so forth: "The installation of the image of a woman" means that in the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of a female image, Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, and the others—the eight *mūrti-śaktis* (embodiments of power)—are themselves the *nṛtta-mūrtīśvaras* (lords of the dancing forms).
Regarding "five" and so forth: for one desiring enjoyment (*bhoga*), in the consecration of Sadāśiva, [the powers] beginning with Kṣmā [are employed].
The five forms extending to the limit of space, along with their presiding deities (mūrtīśas) such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others—
the word "others" including those from Gadeśvara up to Sadāśiva— constitute the five forms for one seeking liberation.
Furthermore, regarding their installation, there are five forms known as Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, Śāntā, and Śāntyatītā, as follows:

He stated that the five lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) called Sadyojāta and the others constitute the number; however, others say that the deities beginning with Sadyojāta are the "auspicious temples" (maṅgalaprāsādas) in the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the five forms. Furthermore, for one desiring liberation alone, in the consecration of a female image, [the powers] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and Icchā [are invoked].

Thus, these five are called the "Lords" (Īśvaras). These are the embodied powers (mūrta-śaktis) themselves, who, for the sake of minor rites (*kṣudra-karma*), are the objects of grace; they are the images (*arcās*) beginning with Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī and others. Within them reside the five [powers] beginning with Mahāmoha, up to [the end]. From the *Trikhaṇḍa* follows the path of the armor (*anuvartma*). The path of Mantra is of three kinds; therefore, from that *Trikhaṇḍa* follows the path.
One should contemplate [the deities] as being of the nature of Mantra, Mantreśvara, and Maheśvara within one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*). For this very reason, it has been stated:

"Ananta and the others [are established] in the Pure Path (*śuddhamārga*), as are the Maṇḍalins; the seeker of liberation (*mumuksu*) [is established] in the [levels of] Nivṛtti and the rest, and Sadyojāta and the other deities," and so forth. Thus, according to the aforementioned method, the eight [deities], including Īśvara, have been described in their respective forms.

Alternatively, one should perform the placement of the five forms (*mūrti*) while touching three points; that is, in all three points beginning with the Brahma-portion, the placement of the forms, their powers (*tacchakti*), and the lords of the forms (*mūrteśa*) is done simultaneously across the three points, not sequentially as in the *Piṅgalāmata*. This placement, along with its base, is performed with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) according to the previously mentioned method.
Because it is common [to all]. As it was said in that very same place:
Whether it be the embodied mantras, or others, or even a single imperishable syllable— He who pervades them is Maheśāna.
Since He is designated as the one who pervades from among whichever group of various forms has been assigned,
for that very reason He is both Great (mahān) and the Lord (īśāna).

"Omnidirectional power" (*sarvatomukhaśaktika*) means that, with respect to the objects pervaded by its own respective paths, it is proclaimed as the totality of the powers of the class of objects; it manifests as their innermost self (*antarātman*).
For this very reason, it is "of every form," for whatever form belongs to that which is to be presided over by contentment (*tuṣṭi*), all of that resides within its own self.

"Unmixed" means that, according to the movement of the causal [vibration], preceded by the utterance of the *nāda*, it proceeds sequentially upward as far as the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), and then again.

"By entering another power" means that one should install [the deity] either as distinct from one's own *aṇu* (individual soul) or as distinct by means of one's own mantra consisting of a collection of syllables— that is, having attained both collective and individual states. "The conjunction of the channels" refers to those [deities] installed in the directions.
For those of divided consciousness who regard the Mūrtīs and Īśvaras as distinct entities existing within intermediate states,

there is this foundation in the channel (*nāḍī*), consisting of the union of those channels, by which the entire collection of forms and form-possessors is strung upon a single channel and made manifest. But for those of undivided consciousness— the Śivas, the Self, and Brahman— [there is no such distinction].

Furthermore, for those who have been installed here without distinction as the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśas*), the connection of their respective constituent parts (*avayava*) within that [central] channel is precisely according to the method described above. This very point is clarified through the assignment of the divisions of the directions and so forth for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) by means of the non-differentiated deities whose form is consciousness (*abhinnacinmūrtipas*), starting with the words "the eastern Tattvapuruṣa" and so on.

Regarding the phrase "Viṣṇu and Ambikā," the word *ambikā* here is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all female deities. "The thousand-rayed one" refers to the Sun. In the phrase "in all [of them]," and so forth, the meaning is that they may sometimes assume their respective forms individually in each direction, or else they may all be situated together as a collective in every direction. Śiva...

Regarding the term *ekādaśikā*: although the eye (*netra*) is indeed an ancillary (*aṅga*) due to its division into Śiva, his limbs, and the Brahmās, its extraction from all the Saṃhitās is not seen because of the discrepancy in number. Its non-inclusion there is not due to non-pervasiveness (*avyāpti*), for it is seen in some places; where it is seen, its application (*viniyoga*) is separate. Likewise, in the venerable *Kālottara* consisting of three hundred and fifty [verses].

After the placement [of mantras] on the heart and other centers, he says: "Having bestowed the Eye, the external Sadāśiva is then the God of Gods. Because of the nourishment of that *vidhi*—where *vidhi* refers to the procedure prescribed by the scriptures consisting of worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and recitation (*japa*)—the presence (*sānnidhya*) of the Lords of the Forms (*mūrtīśas*) certainly occurs due to that nourishment.
"Thus," and so forth. By the word *brahman*, the causal principle of speech (*vāk-tattva*) is meant;
those who know its state as consisting of the fourfold division into the supreme (*parā*), the intermediate (*aparā*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the gross (*sthūla*) are indeed the wise.
And thus says the Śruti:

"Four are the measured steps of speech; those wise Brahmins know them. Those who are devoted to the performance of the meaning of the Vedas—meaning those committed to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) stage—are not, however, those who, having attained the goal of Śaivism, disregard Vedic conduct while reciting mantras that bear the marks of a deity. The "mark of a deity" (*devatā-liṅga*) refers to a sign or emblem.

Reciting those mantras by which [the disciple] is brought under control, and not remaining indifferent, they are "refined by Śiva and Śambaras. This means that having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities and so forth with Śaiva mantras, they are outside the enclosure; that is, those small beings (*aṇu*s) who are outside the sacrificial site (*yāgasthāna*).

Regarding "the hymns and mantras": [it means] "by means of injunction, potency, and encouragement. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "they become sufficient for the destruction of the multitude of obstacles through the arousal of power by means of injunction—that is, through the performance of the sequence prescribed in the scriptures.
He states the nature of the forms with the words "the perpetual students" (*naiṣṭhikāḥ*), and so forth. The perpetual students...

And the *bhautika* [initiates] who serve as guardians of the images (*mūrtipāḥ*) are to be appointed; the characteristic of the *naiṣṭhika* [initiates] is that they have matted hair (*jaṭila*), whereas the *bhautika* are devoid of that. There is another purpose for these very [initiates], beginning with "in their own image" (*svamūrti*) and so forth;
that is, the form of one's own image consisting of three eyes, four arms, and so on, as well as its capacity (*sāmarthya*).

The meaning is as follows: for those whose application is toward their own forms, colors, and so forth—objects within the principles (tattva) and worlds (bhuvana)—and who possess one-pointedness regarding the sound (dhvani) known as the pervasion (vyāpti) consisting of vision and action, as well as the aforementioned connection of the channels (nāḍī), they are "vigilant" for that purpose. This refers to the one who performs the yoga of all connections.

The best of teachers, who effects the unification of these [deities]—each of whom has been described as an individual manifestation—into their totality, [is described by the words] "liṅga" and so forth. [This refers to] the altar (vedī) and the pedestal (pīṭhikā), which are designated as "action" (kriyā) and the "form of the pedestal" (pīṭhavigrahā).
This is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, such as "now, the pedestal consisting of action," and so on, [located] within the cavity (randhra) in the womb (garbha).

"One whose characteristic is carved in the form of a vulva (bhaga) should be suppressed. This means that, like a *liṅga*, it should be placed separately on a bed to the left side; this is the characteristic of the *brahmaśilā* (foundation stone), beginning with "in the womb" (*gabhetyādi*).
The meaning is: by the measurement of that which is one-fourth of the interior of the temple (*prāsādagarbha*).
Also in the venerable Kiraṇa:

"From corner to corner, that thread shall be according to the measurement of the womb (garbha). However, in the *Śrīmad-divyāmata*, it is stated that for a [liṅga] of one cubit, it is increased by two finger-breadths; for other liṅgas, it is increased by one finger-breadth respectively. "The support of the universe in its particularity" refers to the power of radiance (*dīpti-śakti*) and so forth, which will be described later.
O Agni, [the deity] is filled with various supporting powers (*śakti*) that sustain all things; he will later describe her as "possessing the nature of the support" (*ādhāradharminī*).

One should place [the image] at the base of the *liṅga*. For the sake of its sleep, on a separate bed-covering, one should perform the entire ritual of installation for both the form (*mūrti*) and the lord of the form (*mūrtīśa*), just as one does for a pedestal. Thus, the placement of the form and the lord of the form must be performed for her as well.

One should install that [altar] which consists of the principles (*tattva*), which possesses the three aggregates (*skandha-traya*) known as *marmavidyā* and *śiva*, and which likewise possesses nine pits (*navagarta*)— the locations for the placement of gems and other materials. Furthermore, it should be "prepared" (*kliptām*), meaning worshipped with anointing by means of sandalwood paste and the like, and "encircled" (*samāvṛtām*), meaning surrounded by fine cloths and other such items.

"By their own mantras," and so forth. Those who are established in a particular place through the relationship of the signified and the signifier—by means of them [the teacher acts]. For this very reason, there is the qualification of the teacher as "one who knows the ritual injunctions" (*vidhiśāstravit*). An *injunction* (*vidhi*) is the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, and a *scripture* (*śāstra*) is that which concerns the application of mantras. He who knows both of these is indeed [the one who performs] these [rites] with their respective mantras.

One performs the worship. Regarding the statement "the place for the arrangement of jewels and so forth, which belongs to her," this is for the purpose of the enumeration; its application follows hereafter. "For the sake of *rocanā*, that is, for the sake of *ruci*" means for the sake of kindling the luster. Then, "as before" and so forth. "As before" means:

In the consecration of the water-pot (*kumbha*), as in the case of the [deities] seated upon their respective seats, the preceptor first performs the worship— beginning with the daily rites and so forth— upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or other substratum, preceded by the arrangement of the seats in the cardinal directions corresponding to the central portion. In that same sequence, the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) is performed in the fire, beginning with the ritual invocation of the mantras.

"One should perform [the rite] in nine ways together with the eight bearers of the forms (mūrtidhara), like one possessing manifest mastery" (vyaktaprākāmyayogavat). "Manifest" (vyakta) means evident; "mastery" (prākāmya) is pervasiveness; "yoga" is abiding in identity with that—this is the meaning of "one who is proficient therein. This is what is being said: the bearers of the forms [should perform] the oblation through their own pervasion.
"The teacher performs [this] by means of universal pervasion. This was also stated previously:

"The supreme teacher effects the union of all connections. In this context, regarding the phrase "consecrated by the descent of mantras," the consecration consisting of the placement of drops (*bindu*) is performed via the ladle (*sruva*), with the words "by one's own [fire]" and "into the fire," through the oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta-homa*).
For those [categories] in which "the peaceful" (śānta) exists as an unmanifested state, its power of proximity is internalized. As it has been said:

"That is the act of bringing about proximity to water. He describes the pervasion of the three principles beginning with the Self (ātman): starting with the word "māyā," the pervasion of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) extends up to the limit of the principle of Māyā; the pervasion of the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) extends up to the limit of the principle of Sadāśiva.

"The limit of the Śiva-principle is the Śiva-principle": this refers to the *liṅga*. Regarding the *pīṭha*, however, it should be inferred according to the reasoning to be stated later: that the *pīṭha* consists of the pervasive action (*kriyā-vyāpti*) of the Lord;
and that action, which exists as His state of possession (*parigraha*), is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), beneath which lies the pervasion of Śiva (*śiva-vyāpti*).

From the additional statement to be mentioned later, "of the Brahmaśilā, you are the one possessing the nature of the support," it follows that she possesses the form of Ananta, being presided over by the power of the Lord who is the presiding deity; since her capacity to sustain the universe [derives] from that, her nature as such extends only up to Śuddhavidyā.

The pervasion of the three principles (tattvas) should be meditated upon in this manner; having thus purified all those pervasions in sequence, then everyone together, touching the *darbha* grass, should mutter their respective mantras. The meaning is that they should touch each respective portion with the tip of the *darbha* grass while muttering [the mantra]. Each respective portion [is touched] by means of this.
It should be understood that Brahmā is the Lord of the principle of *ātman* (the individual self) within the pure category; Viṣṇu is the Lord of the principle of *vidyā*;

the supreme power (*pārameśvarī śaktiḥ*) presides over Viṣṇu; and Rudra presides over the principle of *śiva*. Thus, the "with-Lord" (*seśvara*) system is established by presenting each [category] together with its respective Lord.
Immediately after the *ātmatattva*, that *ātmatattva* is established within the supreme *vidyātattva*;
having joined them,
all [the deities] wearing crowns are placed there, and thereafter, by that same procedure, others [are likewise established].

They should purify [the elements] up to the Śiva-tattva; thus is the application of the three principles (*tattva*). Regarding the passage beginning with "the roots" (*mūlāṇi*) and so forth: the ritual procedure for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), consisting of the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed by means of the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) or else the Root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) from the Peace-pitcher (*śāntikumbha*), concludes at that point.

The ritual consisting of recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) has been taught by the supreme gurus in that same manner; indeed, the recitation should be performed as equal to the oblation, and so forth. Likewise, the three parts of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), such as the *ātmatattva* and the rest, are to be purified in that way. Just like the *liṅga*, the stone slab (*śilā*) is to be purified in that same manner; by that very same consecration, one should also purify the *brahma-śilā*. And thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"The consecration (saṃskāra) which has been described for the Liṅga must also be performed for those two [the Śakti and the Guru]. Regarding the phrase 'the substratum and its attributes' (ādhāradharmiṇī):

this is a restatement of what was previously said. The 'collection' (saṃdoha) of the paths and forms—that is, their capacity—is the defining characteristic; this is what is meant: the entire path of the Supreme Lord."

[He refers to] Śakti alone, whose characteristic is to pervade all forms. He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "icchā" (will), etc. Those who perceive reality, those who know the ultimate truth, describe [Her] as the triad of the Lord's powers of will, knowledge, and action. [The phrase] "by whose name 'Self' and so forth" refers to that power of action which constitutes the sheath of the Self.

The *vidyātattva*, whose nature consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), is called the "principle of the self" (*ātmatattva*); the *śivatattva*, whose nature consists of the power of will (*icchāśakti*), is [the principle of Śiva]. This should also be observed in the *pīṭhikā* (pedestal), starting with the word "pure" (*śuddha*) and so forth. When this triad—consisting of the *liṅga*, the *pīṭhikā*, and the *brahmaśilā*—is purified, it serves as the means for the completion of the ritual (*vidhi*) which has that very triad as its essence.

As for how the fire sacrifice (homa) is to be performed while seated, since it has not been stated here, the procedure must be sought from another *saṃhitā*, for it is said in the venerable *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara*:
"In the fire-pit situated as before, [or] in the southeast or likewise in the south..."
The preceptors who bear the forms [of the deities] should offer oblations while facing north.
In the Nairṛta, Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, Uttara, and Īśa kuṇḍas,
the offerings should be made facing east by the preceptors who maintain the forms.
In the central fire-pit, which is situated within the sacrificial pavilion,
the Guru should always perform the fire-oblation (homa) while facing the north.

"By what mantra? [The answer is] "with the words *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, etc. This means by using these words either separately, one by one, or collectively according to one's capacity, through the application of the *vyāhṛtis*. Regarding the phrase "from there," etc.:
"near the two ears" means in the vicinity of the ears; "by the mental function" means by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). As it has been said:
In the illustrious Piṅgalāmata.
And in the southern ear, one should offer this performed rite with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
Regarding the word "having restrained" (*niruddhya*): having made that karma offered to Śiva, it is self-luminous; the *Pāśupata-astra* is exceedingly luminous for him alone.
And with that [mantra] ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should expel the obstacles from the interior of the temple. Regarding the passage beginning with "the ears" (*karṇa*):

the central place of the Self-born One, Brahmā, is determined and known by means of the intersection of the ears—that is, by the laying down of the diagonal cords (*koṇasūtra*). By the word "door" (*dvāḥ*), the entrance is meant; of that [entrance], the twenty-sixth...
The meaning is that, having departed from that Brahma-sthāna by one-hundredth part and having gone a short distance toward the northern direction, one should install the Brahma-śilā.
And regarding the application of the mantra at the time of installation, he says "the Praṇava," etc.: "Oṃ, salutation to the pervasive and stable one."
Acale dhruve hrīṃ laṃ hrīṃ svāhā. [18 syllables]
By means of this eight-syllable mantra, one should contemplate all-pervasive stability;
the entire path as being mounted upon that which consists of the empowerment of the Supreme Lord’s power;
and the pedestal of the *liṅga* as the foundation, which should be firmly established and restrained.
Having gazed with the power of knowledge: "Thus you are the supreme power of the Blessed One; by his command, remain here. In this very sequence, it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
Then the preceptor should address the Goddess, who has been duly worshipped:
"You alone are the supreme Śakti; you alone are the sustainer of the throne."
"O Goddess, by the command of Śiva, you must remain here forever"—having thus restrained [her], one should deposit the gems and other items whose names will be mentioned below, beginning with "vajra.
*Heraka* is the sunstone (*sūryakānta*); *ati-nīla* is the great sapphire (*mahānīla*); *puṣpaka* is the topaz (*puṣparāga*); *abjarāga* is the ruby.
Padmarāga is the power of radiance (*dīpti-śakti*), which is none other than the supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*) that presides over all radiance.
*Hema* is pure gold; *aruṇa* is copper; *śraya* is bronze; *vamka* and *hūṃ* are lead; *phuttāra* is silver;
*ārākhya* is brass (*rīti*); *dhvani* is bell-metal (*kāṃsya*); and *patraga* is tin (*sīsa*). Of these...
The names of Hemādri and the others were previously established at the time of describing the arrangement of the *liṅgas* under the [relevant] command;

their repetition here is for the purpose of not forgetting those well-known names, and not because of redundancy, as was the case previously. At each *aṣṭaka*, there are eight [deities] in the eight directions.

Each individual [ingredient] that was cast into the womb—those very same [ingredients], taken collectively, should be explained according to this specific sequence and distinct order as "the central cavity" (*madhyagarta*). Regarding "bodily power" (*dehaśakti*): it refers to the capacity whose nature is the body; "stone" (*śilā*) refers to *manaḥśilā* (realgar), and in some places "stone" (*śilā*) is known by the name *janā* (orpiment); likewise, "copper sulfate" (*kāsīsa*) is to be heated.

One should know these as the minerals: *hemamākṣika* (copper pyrite), *sūta* (mercury), *pārada* (mercury), *agnigairika* (red ochre), and *suvarṇagairika* (golden ochre). Together with *gaṃdhaka* (sulphur), which is specifically designated by the name *gaṃdhapāṣāṇa*, and *bhṛṅga* (mica), they are known as those whose essence consists of memory and vitality (*smṛtivīryātmaka*).

The vigor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the power consisting of continuous application (*anusaṃdhāna*); it acts in that manner, meaning according to the previous sequence. *Acyutakrāntā* and *Viṣṇukrāntā* refer to red sandalwood (*śoṇa-candana*). Red sandalwood.

"Śāntavāra" refers to white sandalwood. "Śaṅkhikā" is the Śaṅkhapuṣpikā plant. "Contemplating the power of health" (ārogya-śakti) means that one should contemplate these as the powers to be presided over for the sake of attaining health; this is the intended meaning. By the word "vrīhī," grain is meant, including all others.

This is a restatement of what was previously mentioned: "these [powers] consisting of satisfaction. Because they are governed by the power of nourishment (*āpyāyana*), they are the support of the universe (*viśvadhāraṇā*); indeed, because they are the locus of manifold powers, they are the very support of the universe. As it has been said: "having meditated upon the support of the universe. These [powers] are [to be worshipped], O Lord of the World, with the mantras previously set forth which denote them.

One should place [the materials]. However, in the *Divyāmata*, the distinction is that it may be done with the *praṇava* or the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*). As it is said: "Whichever mantra is prescribed for the placement of gems and so forth, one should place them with that mantra;
or else with the *praṇava*, or with the mantra of the Lord of one's own direction, or the Guru in the heart. But in the central womb, it is golden.

"Likewise the tortoise and the earth": "the golden tortoise likewise," and "the goddess Earth is indeed golden"—this is like a qualifier [of the tortoise] through a displaced word (*vyavahitapada*). In the case of the phrase "the bull [is] golden," it is exactly so;
and it is the same even in the case of "the glorious lord of deer."

In the phrase "hemakūrma-mahī-vṛṣāḥ" (the golden tortoise, the earth, and the bull), the word *hema* (gold) qualifies all three; however, according to the venerable Nandikeśvara, one should have the tortoise made of copper. There are thus variations: the earth should be made of silver and the bull of gold. As for the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are exactly as described in the *Śaṅkhapuṣpikā*.

One should place therein the herb named Sahadevā together with that [other herb], and the herb called Ananta with the mantra that expresses Ananta. In the event that these [substances] such as gems and so forth are unavailable, there is an alternative procedure. Regarding "vajra" and so on: in the absence of metals, one uses the deity of fire. The herb *mṛgavārā* is indeed singular.
In the Śivaśāstra, these along with the one called Saha-deva are said to be the placement (nyāsa) for all the sacrificial pits (garta). As it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇatantra:
One should install a vajra, barley, gold, and sahā grass, provided that they are available;
as it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇa:
One should apply vajra, barley, gold, and sahā, provided that they are available;

if not, then mercury (rasottama) and pārada according to the previously mentioned procedure, as well as the seven seeds. Regarding the other procedure that has been stated, apart from that, all the seeds—even those few—should be firmly packed with seeds.
The meaning is "for the sake of avoiding faults. As it has been stated in that very same place:

One must not press the seed (bīja) too firmly; if it is pressed too firmly, a great fault will arise. Having made a cavity, it is described as being surrounded by water. According to the measurement of the Brahmabhāga of the Liṅga, that which is marked by nine excavations in the Brahmaśilā is known as the "white" (śubhra). And it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
One should cause nine other pits to be made in the center according to the measurement of the specific portion for Brahmā, making them deep.

"Having protected [the disciple] with the armor and weapon [mantras]" means that after performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should protect [him] with the armor and weapon mantras and offer oblations (*bali*) to the lords of the directions.

Regarding the section on the oblation (*balipakṣya*): after the foot-washing, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and so forth, and [protect him] with the weapon mantra (*astramantra*).
One should perform a hundred oblations (*homa*). He states the purpose of this: "To prevent the displacement of the thread and the occurrence of fissures in the stones.

This means that for the sake of preventing the displacement of the thread from the *brahma-śilā*, the seepage of water, and any opening that might provide an opportunity for obstacles to arise, one should perform the *homa* with clarified butter (*ājya*) or indeed with Lord Śiva himself.

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) for Vāstupati with the *astreṇa* mantra and for Brahmā, the Guru should thereafter commence the ritual to be described when the hour (*muhūrta*) possesses auspicious qualities. A *muhūrta* is a fifteenth part of a day or a night;
by that reckoning, there are thirty *muhūrtas* of Śiva and the others within the course of a day and night.
Śiva, Bhujaga, Mitra, Pitṛ, Vasu, Jala, Viśva, Viriñca, Paṅkaja-prabhava, Indra, Agni,
Niśācara, Varuṇa, Arpama, Yoni, Paścāhni, Bhadra, Ajāhi-budhna, Pūṣan, Aśvin, Antaka, Agni, Dhātṛ, Idvaṃditi, Guru, Hari, Āravi, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the one known as Anila.
The *kṣaṇas* of the night and the day constitute a fifteenth part of the night and the day respectively; these are known as *muhūrtas*.

Furthermore, these are established by the very names of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and their presiding deities (*devatā*) as recited in the sections (*anuvāka*) of the Yajurveda, such as "Agni is the deity of the Kṛttikā mansion" and so forth. Among those, the middle portion is multiplied [by the respective factor]. Moreover—
"Under a moon favorable to the sacrificer"—this means that the moon (Indu) is favorable in the manner previously explained;

likewise, it refers to the moon being "tranquil" (*saṃtāra*) and "free from affliction" (*nirupadrava*). The phrase "the grasping of the form of the moon" (*indor upagrahaḥ*) refers to its conjunction with malefic planets (*pāpagraha-yoga*); [the time] free from that is "steadfast and gentle" (*dhruvamārdava*). Steadfast and gentle...

This concerns the domain of enjoyment and liberation within the essential nature of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), which consists of four aspects, it is for the purpose of the work of the Brahmins; for that which is swift in nature, it is for the stable [rites]. Among these, the synonym is "drink" (*piba*) specifically regarding the fixed (*dhruva*) [mansions]. For the purpose of fierce rites, [it is used] when conjoined with Maghā; for the purpose of cruel [rites], [it is used] when conjoined with [the same].

"Joined by either Tvāṣṭrī or Rāmūlā" means connected with one or the other; "drink according to your desire" refers to what was previously stated regarding the nature of the *dāruṇa*, *ucara*, *kṣipra*, *dhruva*, and *sādhāraṇa* [constellations], for the sake of accomplishing the purpose inherent in that; "when the sun is situated on the northern path."

The rule regarding the time for installation applies specifically to those who desire worldly enjoyments and the like, as it is always easy for them to perform; however, it concerns those who desire liberation from the body (*tanumumukṣu*). And it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*: "The installation of the All-pervading Lord may be performed at any place or at any time."
"For liberation there is no restriction; however, for the sake of supernatural attainment (*siddhi*), it is prescribed.
Thus it is said. For one who seeks *siddhi*, [the practice may be done] at other times except during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*). As it is stated in that very same source:
"For the Liṅga installed in the north is always worshipped."
May there always be abundance, security, and health for embodied beings throughout the world.

Regarding the term "niruktitaḥ" (by definition): it refers to a time free from portents such as meteors, earthquakes, and the burning of the quarters. "Balīyasī" (more powerful) means the strength of the zodiac sign (*rāśi*) as it occurs; this has also been previously established by the statement beginning with "conjoined with or aspected by [the lord]," and so forth, regarding Mars and the others being situated in friendly signs, triplicities, or exaltations.

This is a specific qualification regarding the *muhūrta*: if malefic planets such as Mars (*bhauma*) and others occupy positions of friendship (*suhṛtsthāna*), their status as friends or enemies must be understood solely through the words of Varāhamihira, as he states in the *Bṛhajjātaka*: "The Sun, Saturn, and Venus are enemies; [Mercury] is neutral..."

Otherwise, it would be as follows: "The Moon and Mercury are friends, Jupiter is neutral, and the others [Mars, Venus, and Saturn] are enemies of Saturn.

In this context, if the intention had been to include all planets in general—rather than specifically including the malefic planets such as Mars and the rest—the statement would have been "among the Sun and the others" (*sūryādiṣu*). Furthermore, [this would apply] even to the Sun.

If it is argued that the status of being a malefic (*pāpa*) applies everywhere solely according to the opinion of Varāhamihira, and thus the use of the plural number [in the verse] is inconsistent—[we reply: no, for that is consistent in view of the malefics relative to the waning moon (*kṣīṇendu*). As they say: "The waning moon, Saturn, and Mars are malefics; a benefic is conjoined with them. Thus, even in these cases...

"Or situated in their own asterisms (*ṛkṣa*). Here, by the word "asterism," the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) is intended. As they say: "Sign, field, house, asterism, and world—these are synonymous. Therefore, it means "situated in one's own sign. The signs of the planets have been previously stated according to each; or else, [it refers to] the trines (*trikoṇa*) within those very [signs].

When the planets are situated [in their respective positions], the trines are as follows: for the Sun, Leo; for the Moon, Taurus; for Mars, Aries; for Mercury, Virgo; for Jupiter, Sagittarius; for Venus, Libra; and for Saturn, Aquarius. As it is stated in the *Sūkṣmajātaka*:

The signs beginning with Aries are known as the trines [of the planets]: Leo, Taurus, and Virgo for the Sun; Sagittarius, Libra, and Aquarius for the Moon; and so on. Now, regarding those situated in their exaltations, each has its own place of exaltation: for the Sun, the sign of Aries is the place of exaltation; for the Moon, it is Taurus; and the trines of these have been stated previously.

Capricorn is [the sign] of Mars; Virgo is that of Mercury, and its trine is said [to belong] to it; Cancer is [the sign] of Jupiter; Pisces is that of Venus; and Libra is that of Saturn. As it is stated in that very same [work]:
"Aries, Taurus, Capricorn, and Virgo are the *uchas* (natal signs) of the Sun and the others, [respectively], within the portions of Cancer, Pisces, and Libra. Among these—

It is stated that when malefic planets such as Mars (Bhauma) and others occupy any of the aforementioned positions, there is auspiciousness for the ascendant and so forth. Regarding the phrase "arise from the heart" (*hṛdottiṣṭha*),
it means "arise by means of the heart-mantra" (*hṛnmantra*).

Having addressed the Blessed One with a formal invocation, one should then cause [the deity] to rise by reciting the *Ṛgveda* verse beginning with "Do not rise, O Brahmaṇaspati, O God," and so forth. After honoring [the deity] in that very place, one should subsequently move it from that location without touching it, keeping [the hand] above the branch; for this very reason, immediately after the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Some, who are skilled in the construction of doorways, desire it otherwise; for otherwise, having touched [the base], the entry through the upper and lower branches becomes difficult to accomplish. And it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
"Without a door-bolt, one should cause the *liṅga* to enter by means of the doorway itself."
Once the door has been secured, one should cause the liṅga to enter through the sky.

One should immediately place [the deity] upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) situated right after that door, which was previously described as being in the chasm from the Brahma-stone; then, saying "Be firm," at the very moment of entering the temple, one should also utter "Be firm" in order to accomplish the *upaśruti*.

Having produced the sound, one should immediately open the pit with a weapon and cause it to be cleared; this is the demonstration of another preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*). "Supported by a machine" (*yantra*) means a specific effort in the arrangement of firm wood and so forth for the purpose of holding [the vessel]; this is the common usage. By those [threads] supported by such a machine and suspended at the proper measurements, [it is held].

Having properly straightened [the image] and brought it to a state of perfect clarity, the Guru, together with the presiding deity (mūrtipa), should lower the Blessed One into the pit. How so? To this he says: "By power" (*śakti*), and so forth. Power (*śakti*) exists in two forms, namely as the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and as the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*). Therefore, first...

First, there is the non-difference arising from the union of the foundational *brahmaśilā*, which is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the possessor of that power (*śaktimat*) in the form of the *liṅga*, whose nature is the power of consciousness (*vīdha-śakti*); this non-difference,
characterized by the dissolution of their existence in various forms, is established through meditation as the relationship of attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between the two.

The power (*śakti*) of the Blessed One, who is both the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*), is indeed identical with that attribute, consisting in their co-existence. To this extent, it is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), the support (*pratiṣṭhāna*), the primary abiding of Śiva and Śakti.
Having uttered that mantra ending in the *bindu*, preceded by agitation, through the path of the utterance of *nāda*...

The meaning is: "up to the limit of the capacity to impel the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*). By this [method], one should perform the placement (*vinyaset*) or cause the descent [of the deity] by way of the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-mārga*). Regarding the phrase "the pedestal" (*pīṭha*) and so forth: then, having performed the binding of the pedestal (*pīṭha-bandha*), which consists of the union of those two—the *brahma-śilā* and the *liṅga*—one [should worship] the Goddess whose form is the pedestal itself.

One should awaken the power called Kriyā and bring her to consciousness; having straightened her with the same threads as the Liṅga, one should install her within that [Liṅga], which consists of the power of consciousness (bodhaśakti), using the Kriyā-mantra in the dative case: "Oṃ, salutation to the power of action (kriyāśakti) known as the pedestal (pīṭhikā). Thus one should establish her.

Regarding the phrase "the offering of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) into the *liṅga* which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)," this refers to the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). By means of this performed conjunction, the installation occurs; the meaning is that the reality (*tattva*) consisting of both vision and action becomes conjoined. Previously...

At the beginning of the description of the characteristics of the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*), this was also explained: "Now, the pedestal consisting of action is the locus of the Lord whose nature is the power of consciousness; their union is that reality which consists of vision and action," and so forth. If that [power] were not present, then that pedestal would be devoid of the qualities of the day.
It should be made straight by means of moving it back and forth, and during that movement, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with either the Śiva-mantra or the Astra-mantra.

Then, for the purpose of filling the joint between the pedestal and the liṅga, he describes the application of "thunderbolt-paste" (vajralepa), beginning with the word *sarja*. *Sarja* refers to the tree known as *kunduru*.
The resin of the *lākṣā* tree, known by the names *rāla*, *sarjarasa*, *lohāmala*, and *koḍa*, which originates at the time of the emergence of *cīmara*;
and conch-powder produced from the pulverized shells of conchs and the like;
and oil known as *yavāra*, [prepared] with these specific ingredients cooked together with the resin of that very same tree.
Because it is well known in some places as being *salātaila* (sesame oil),
and also in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*.
Then, the fissures of the pit should be filled with lead, iron, dross, and so forth,
along with conch-shell powder and substances cooked in lac and oil.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tata" and so on: previously, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three principles (*tattva*) was performed individually upon the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the *brahmaśilā*.

Now, concerning their unity, the bestowal of armor (*varmādhāna*) consisting of three sections for each of the three will be described; he specifies that very [bestowal] with the words beginning with "pīṭha" and so on. From that very resonance (*dhvani*)...

The *pīṭha-mantras* are those very *vidyās* and *vidyeśas* by which they are designated as *pīṭha-mantras*; the meaning is that one should know them in the *pīṭha* as being equal to the *vidyā-tattva*. As for the *mūrti*:
the body perceived in other *saṃhitās* is endowed with thirty-eight *kalās*; one should know the *mūrti-mantras* beginning with Him (the Lord) as having Brahman as their essence.

Regarding the phrase "the supreme reality" (*para-tattva*): within that formless [reality], there is that which constitutes the essence, like the life-force (*jīva*)—namely, the nature of pure knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*). Its limbs, such as the head and the topknot, are merely constituent parts (*avayava*) for the purpose of symbolic instruction; they are indeed [merely] powers (*śakti*). And because it is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is waveless (*nistaraṅga*), being the power of consciousness itself (*cicchakti*).

By that [power], one should place the group beginning with Gaṇeśa and Lokeśa below the pedestal (pīṭha) as the principle of action (kriyātattva), equal to the principle of Śiva, which consists of peaceful consciousness. On the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), one should place this triad—consisting of the Brahma-pedestal, the Līlā-pedestal, and the Liṅga—as the principle of the self (ātmatattva), equal to the threefold division of the armor (varma). Thus, it becomes established within the three sections of the armor. Gaṇeśa...

Furthermore, for the Lords of the World (Lokeśas), the very basis (*pratiṣṭhā*) is their being presided over by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); the arrangement in the *Samuccaya* is exactly like this. As it is stated therein:
"The Lord of Gods is on the head of the Liṅga-form, accompanied by the limbs [and] the Brahmās."
Below that, one should worship the sovereigns of the wheel who are merged with Śakti.
"One should worship Gaṇeśa and the world-protectors at the base of the Liṅga.

Regarding the phrase "having restrained according to rule": it means having restrained [the breath] by means of the *nirodhamudrā*, which is characterized by the thumb being placed within [the ring finger], as observed in the scriptures. [The purpose is] for the sake of the Lord's presence, acting for the benefit [of the world] until the end of the kalpa.

"Let it be done. Having thus made the formal request (*vijñapti*), as it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*: "Then, joined with the mantra and the lord of mantras, one should request the Lord out of a desire to benefit the world."
O Mahādeva, be ever present here in this liṅga.
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, as long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains, so long should you remain here at your own will.
"Then one should perform the rite of cessation," meaning "the incense and the water offering are consecrated with *vaṣaṭ*.

This is a restatement of the procedure mentioned in the section on the worship of the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*). "Having prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness," as it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya* itself.
Then, having performed a circumambulation together with those who bear his forms, and having prostrated according to the rule, he should address Śiva as follows:
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, may all that which was not performed according to the scriptures— whether through ignorance or even through knowledge— become complete."
Also in the venerable Parākhyatantra: "Then he should inform the Lord:
'May all the siddhis come to pass for the practitioner by Your will; whatever calamities exist in the world, may they go to destruction through the power of the Lord.'"
"May there be well-being for the world, and may the king possess unsurpassed prosperity.
Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, one should say, "May you be forgiven. [The word] "iti" [is used] in this way and so forth.
All acts—worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and so on—should be performed on the very first day as well as on all four days.
And it is said in the venerable Piṅgalāmata:
One should especially offer garments, incense, perfumes, flowers, and ointments,
as well as worship, food offerings, and gifts, for a period of four days.

Thus, until the sacrifice and other rites for Caṇḍīśa have been performed, there is no fault even in consuming the food offering (naivedya) and so forth belonging to anyone. Regarding the phrase "the fourth," etc., the term "one who knows the procedure" (vidhānavid) refers to one who understands the procedure consisting of the practical performance according to the sequence of meaning, regardless of the sequence of the recitation; [specifically] that which follows the removal of the food offering, namely the fourth [rite].

The daily rites, such as bathing and so forth, should be performed. The sequence of practice here is as follows: having dismissed one's own *sādhya-aṇu* (the mantra to be accomplished), this is intended from the perspective of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). For that mantra which has been installed is to be accomplished by the practitioner alone;
[he should perform] the worship of Caṇḍeśa for one moment by means of a more specific presence (*sannidhāna*) toward it.
Having performed the dismissal (visarjana), one does not [dismiss it] by way of a specific presence, because that [power] is already established;

thus it is called the "state of the power of knowledge" (jñānaśaktipada). And in this manner, with the mantras seen at the end of the Saṃhitās, which denote Caṇḍeśa and consist of *liṅga-mūrti* and so forth, ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, they constitute the very limbs (aṅga) of the venerable Lord Śiva himself.
