And the space between Śiva and Śakti is Caṇḍeśvara, as before. Just as one performed worship on the first day, in that very same manner one should then worship him.
And it is said in the venerable Piṅgalāmata:
Having removed the food offering (naivedya) and performed the dismissal (visarjana) of the specific consciousness (cidviśeṣa),
one should install Caṇḍeśvara upon the image, [visualizing] the Wrath (Krodha) who has emerged by divine power.

"One should sacrifice"—thus it is stated. Also in another *Saṃhitā*, the one called *Parā*: "Having worshipped Caṇḍa in those lotuses as before with [mantras] consisting of the names of Śambhu. "Having recited the *veda*": having performed the recitation (*japa*) with those very mantras according to one's capacity, and having informed Him (*tam āvedya*) as prescribed.
In the Ruru-saṃhitā:

"O you who guard the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us for the sake of accomplishment; through your grace, may it abide within you. By means of this rite, one should then offer that [recitation] as a drop (*kaṇa*), a minute particle (*kaṇikā*), like a snake, a bracelet, or an armlet.

"Adorned, with an axe raised in his hand" means that one should place [the mantra] in the northeastern direction within the lotus that constitutes the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), which serves as the locus, having performed the mantra while established in the flow of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*). "With a hand occupied by an axe" means that the hand is engaged with a *paraśu* (axe); "having made the mantra abide in the self" is the intended meaning. One should deposit it in the northeast, situated upon the lotus whose nature is the foundational power.
Also in the illustrious Piṅgalāmata:
Having uprooted that which is established there, one should install it upon the *liṅga* and so forth;
for the power (*śakti*) which is the primordial support (*ādhāra*) possesses both mobile and immobile forms.

"Having first prepared that seat, one should install Caṇḍa there"—this means that [the deity] regulates the rules regarding the *samaya* and so forth; the meaning is that by accepting the *nirmālya*, it also regulates such things as stepping over it or consuming it. For this very reason, it is called "special" (*viśeṣa*).
Whether mounted on a jackal, or while eating the sacrificial offering (naivedya), or while stepping over a garland,
or even when giving a gift— even for one who is initiated— there is no prohibition whatsoever.
The meaning is "having performed the cessation. And it has been stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:

"Rudra himself, in his fierce form (Caṇḍarūpa), binds those who have violated their commitments (samayakṣatān). This was already indicated previously by the passage beginning with "Thus for four days there is no object for one engaged in worship" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "then" and so on: after the worship of Caṇḍeśa, having performed his bathing and other rites, the procedure with the common vessel (sādhāra) is as follows.

Regarding the word *vidhau*: one should worship daily that form of the Blessed One which is established as the benefactor of the entire world, for the sake of one's desired fruit. Now, he describes the installation of a movable (*cala*) liṅga with the words beginning with *calam*.
That movable liṅga which has a separate pedestal is "consecrated" (*saṃskṛta*), meaning it is stable.
As he will state according to the very procedure for the consecration and installation of a liṅga:
"Having performed the bath as before, the mantra-syllables having been deposited, and [the image] having been perfumed."
In this context, with the exception of the conceptualization of Caṇḍa which will be prohibited by the statement to be spoken hereafter, everything else is to be observed. As it has been said:
"At the time of the ritual for the installation of a separate pedestal and *liṅga*, the placement of the path of mantras (*mantrādhva*) is performed as before."

"And the ritual should be performed except for Caṇḍeśvara"—this means that one should perform the consecration (*saṃskṛta*) upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Now, this refers to the case of a separate pedestal; "consecrated without distinction" refers to [the mantra] beginning with *pūrṇā* because of its beginningless conjunction.
From the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) onwards, up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), it is for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*).

The meaning is that the preceptor, having first dismissed his own mantra which was worshipped in another location, should then worship the installed and consecrated [liṅga]. Regarding the passage beginning with "abhinnā" and so forth: they call a stone liṅga that is not on a separate pedestal a "moving liṅga" (*cala-liṅga*), and they say that this is the "mind-Śiva" (*manaḥ-śiva*). The justification for designating it thus is that it is the "mind" (*manas*).

Regarding the term "dhātu": the verbal root *man*, meaning "to understand," is the designator of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore, by that [root], its indicative mark—by means of the reasoning to be stated later—is to be consumed for the sake of stabilizing the mind in mere awareness (*bodha*) alone by the seeker of liberation who is like a son, and not by anyone else such as the teacher and so forth. For it says:

O twice-born ones, there is no specific ritual for the path (viśeṣādhvakriyā) nor even the ritual placement (nyāsa) therein; however, for the sake of accomplishment, the Guru or the practitioner must perform worship there. As for the specific ritual for the path and the ritual placement, they are shown in their detailed form first, just as they were presented in the context of the installation (pratiṣṭhā).
It is not to be produced; rather, it is said to consist of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), by virtue of its pervading all the paths (*adhvan*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the fierce" (*raudram*): this is another [mark] for the sake of minor accomplishments (*kṣudra-siddhi*). Therefore, the fierce [mark], consisting of nine manifestations, is located on the lower part of the three sections starting from the head; the sign is indeed a barley grain (*yavaka*).
Regarding the phrase "of which the fire-portion is thus situated within the pedestal":

that [pedestal] is such that its fire-portion, consisting of one-third, is entered into and contained within the base (pīṭhikā). And in this way, the meaning is that there is a portion for each of the two *bhagas* as well as for the pedestal of the image (*arcāpīṭha*). This was also previously [stated] for this [work].

At the time of prescribing the dimensions for the *liṅgas* of the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), the characteristic was indicated as being "fierce" (*raudra*) for fierce rites, consisting of one, two, or three barley-grains; and at the time of extracting the proportions, beginning with the statement that its worship consists of three parts, the pedestal cavity (*piṇḍikāvaṭa*) is one-third of that, and so forth, it was further stated therein that the mouth [of the liṅga] should be sixty barley-grains in width.
The meaning is that it has the form of wind (*vāyu*), being devoid of two sides. "In a divine abode" means in a palace;

those desiring welfare should not install [the deity] even in such a house. Here, "in an open space" (*avakāśaka*) means in a place without shelter, that is, in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). This concerns the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of a *bāṇaliṅga*.
He states the reason for not performing the prescribed consecrations (*saṃskāra*) with the words beginning "by the Brāhmaṇas," and so forth.

Since it has already been established that the ground was consecrated by other inhabitants of Tripura, the subsequent consecrations to be described are performed—or rather, not performed—by him due to his constant presence there; as he says: "In that regard, the path... (*tatrādhva*).
Whether the conceptualization of the embodied and the lord of the embodied is performed or not, he states the places of its origin:

"The well-known," and so forth. The meritorious mountains are Śrīparvata, Pāriyātra, and others; the sacred fields (*siddhakṣetra*) are Puṣkara, Kedāra, Karkhala, and so on; and the meritorious rivers are the Gaṅgā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī.

The goddesses beginning with Devīkā have already been mentioned. Thus, regarding those places where [the Liṅgas] originated from such locations, the Purāṇikas maintain that at the time of the burning of Tripura, the falling of the Liṅgas worshipped by the inhabitants there was caused by the arrows of Śiva; however, the common people say they came from the Narmadā.
Just as in that case, because the earthen lingas were carried away by the arrow, they are indeed those very same [lingas]; yet,

since it is possible for them to disintegrate at that very moment due to being carried into the current of a river, and because their persistence until another time is not established, there is merely a matter of conventional renown.
"One should not carve a mark there"—this is a restatement of the fact that there is no growth in a *bāṇaliṅga*.

"Its own configuration" (*svasaṃsthāna*) means "deformed configuration" (*visaṃsthāna*). The meaning is that while the entire form of the *liṅga* is deformed, [only] one part has been fashioned into the shape of a *liṅga* from a stone otherwise joined together. Even though it is of such a kind...

One should fashion this [liṅga] as containing all palaces and liṅgas; this is also a restatement of the principle that "in a Bāṇaliṅga or a self-manifested (svayambhū) one, it is the support for all seats and houses. It is never subject to doubt as to whether "this is for the sake of enjoyment or for the sake of liberation"; and thus, it is not fit to be an object of such deliberation.

Since it accomplishes all desires and goals precisely because of prior grace, a fire-oblation (homa) of that same number has been prescribed; however, those desiring prosperity should perform it or not as they wish. But the "Caṇḍakalpanā" ritual is never to be performed, for there is never a mixing of mantras due to their connection with the general or the particular.

This [verse], beginning with "puṣpa," is not a restatement of the phrase "never indeed consciousness" (na jātu cit), even though the subtle atoms (aṇu) previously established as the object to be accomplished (sādhya) are intermingled therein.

This [offering] of flowers and so forth is for the purpose of that means of worshipping Maheśa on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) which was mentioned earlier; that is, upon that sacrificial ground which is the imagined seat (pīṭha).

On a pedestal (pīṭha) or other support (ādhāra) prepared for the Śiva-sacrifice with flowers and so forth— the word "and so forth" (ādi) including perfumes, white mustard seeds, or the dust of a cow— on which the mind and other faculties are [conceived]; or else, as an alternative (athavā), on that very sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), when flowers and such are unavailable, on a support mentally conceived.

The meaning is "in the pure stage" (*viśuddhāyāṃ bhūmau*). Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "in one's own form" (*svamūrti*): by means of the ritual procedure of mental sacrifice (*manoyāga*), these [offerings] such as flowers—which are mentally constructed and worshipped within one's own form—[are offered]; the meaning is that one moves toward any one of these, such as the *kālimga*, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, [this being] the invocation (*āvāhana*) through the sacrificial limit-mantra (*yāgāvadhimantra*).

The dismissal (*visarjana*) is not, however, like the dismissal of those [deities] who are firmly established, which is merely the withdrawal of their specific presence; this dismissal is also described as such. The accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the intended Śiva-sacrifice is its completion.
"Free from the hole of an arrow" (*bāṇecchidravivarjita*) means that the Bāṇaliṅga has been consecrated by the ancient Siddhas and possesses eternal presence (*nityasannidhi*).

The meaning is that this [statement] is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that "success occurs even when there is a flaw," by means of the aforementioned words of praise. Regarding "unsteady" (*cala*) and so forth: success is achieved not only with an arrow possessing a flaw, but also with other things that are unsteady, fallen, or afflicted by injury and the like; in some cases, it occurs even there.

Regarding the phrase "sthiratām" (stability): [it refers to] worshipfulness, because [the deity] cannot be present in its entirety due to the vastness of its manifestation. Regarding "na arcet" and so forth: it is stated that one should worship [the deity] upon a pedestal, flowers, cloth, or other supports, but not on the bare ground.
This is also stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*:
Having first established a seat covered with flowers and leaves as appropriate,
one should worship the liṅga upon it, and never upon the ground.
"Or else, [the image] should be placed above a cloth, or in a casket.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding "sādhya" and so forth: that which has been consecrated by a perfected mantra should not be brought within the sight of everyone.
Regarding "ordinary": the entire procedure that has been taught—such as the ritual for an image—is [applicable] even without the sacrifice to Caṇḍīśa.

The pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) is established by the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). Within that pedestal, there is the placement of the fivefold group consisting of jewels and so forth, as well as the elements, metals, medicinal herbs, and seeds;

likewise, above that, there is the quartet designated as the tortoise, the lotus, the bull, and the earth. Thus, following the arrangement of the pedestal, the placement occurs specifically within the interior of the pedestal.

Regarding the term *brahmapīṭha*: it refers to the *brahmaśilā* (the foundational stone), the river, and so forth. If, at any time, those devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* install stone images in the form of *liṅgas* from the current of a river, then for those mobile *liṅgas*, the procedure that was prescribed at the time of their installation applies exactly as it is.

"For the sake of presence, the station is on the pedestal"—thus it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhās* with mantras and so forth. Regarding "the lotus of one's own path": to whatever extent the pervasion of the *adhvan* (path) extends for any [deity], to that same extent the three-sectioned (*trikhaṇḍa*) [lotus], consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, is the lotus of the abode (*dhāmapaṅkaja*), because it is that which is to be presided over; and thus, within that very extent of the *adhvan*, there are those *tattvas* (principles) which...
Just as with the Mūrtīśas; as it has been said:

"Whether in the pure or impure path, or even in some cases in the world-supporting [realm], the installation accompanied by those [deities] is to be accomplished," and so forth. The Sādhyas are the inhabitants of Janaloka.

The specific classes of deities and the *siddhas* who have attained powers such as *aṇimā* through the practice of knowledge and yoga; the serpent chiefs and others who are indeed divine beings, characterized by images in the form of serpents with their heads adorned by hoods— by this, [the text refers to] the *nāgas*, Śeṣa and the rest.
Regarding the phrase "as indicated for the sages," other great seers (*maharṣis*) who have attained the state of being presided over by Śiva are also indicated therein; or alternatively,
those indicated by the description "the seven sages (*saptarṣis*), indifferent [to worldly affairs], wearing sacred threads, carrying water-pots and rosaries"— for them, as well as for their rivers.

The rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā flow with water and remain within the water; by this [statement], the meaning is that for those [beings] previously mentioned, ending with the Piśācas, there is no pervasion beyond the path of the earth-element (pṛthivī-tattva). Regarding the phrase "of the other Lords of Worlds" (pareṣāṃ bhuvaneśānām), this refers to other deities through their own respective mantras.
The establishment (*sthāpana*) of this [deity] is called "reiteration" (*anubhāṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "as stated," etc.:

one should worship the [deity] residing on the cloth, which is endowed with the form free from the defects of the explained [procedures]. "Consecrated by mantras according to the rule" means by the ritual procedure (*samaya*) prescribed for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

One should worship her who has been consecrated by the preceptor—the agent—through the ritual procedures and mantras which serve as the causes, and who has thus been brought into presence by means of the placement of mantras (*mantravinyāsa*) and so forth; by worshipping her in such a manner, one attains what is desired. Furthermore, in that context, even the mere offering of incense (*dhūpa*) is faultless, since the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes flowers and other offerings.

One should perform the bathing, the offering of water (argha), and the anointing with unguents using those [substances]; however, out of fear of destroying the form, the worship should be performed upon the reflection in a mirror placed on the ground, not upon the physical image itself.
And it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
The purification of those [images] that have undergone plastering or painting is performed through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās);
likewise, mental bathing and other rites should be performed for [images made of] precious gems, stone, and so forth.
Here too, the procedure beginning with the opening of the eyes and the placement on the seat should be performed again with waterless flowers, so that the painting does not perish.
Thus [it is said]. He states the consecration of the door, beginning with the words "at the door" and so forth.

The two door-posts, the lintel above, and the threshold below—these four constituent parts of the door should be smeared with astringent substances, myrobalan (*harītakī*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and pieces of wood-apple (*śakala*); by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," clay and ashes are also understood.

Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances suitable for the installation and bathing rites, and having clothed it in garments, one should place it upon the bed; then, on the path known as the "Three Realities" (*tattvatraya*), one should install the appropriate *mūrti-mantras*. As it has been said: "And those [mantras], beginning with Ananta, [are placed] in the pure [space]."
On the path, whether by means of the Maṇḍalī or indeed on the pure or impure sacrificial paths, one should drink [the offering] somewhere in the world-maintaining [realm].
Then, having performed the oblation according to one's capacity for each part within the triad beginning with the *ātmatattva*, one should worship Vāstoṣpati.
"Below" (*adhaḥ*) refers to the lower portion of the door-component, specifically the substance located below the fourth part known as the *ūrdhvodumbara*.

Because there is no possibility of a place for insertion; with the mantra consisting of infinite expressive words, one should [place] the fivefold jewels and so forth—namely, the minerals, gems, medicinal herbs, metals, and seeds—as previously described;
and the two medicinal herbs known as *krāntā* (Viṣṇukrāntā) and *ṛddhi*, which were mentioned before.

That which is known abroad as *mohanavṛhatpatrikā* is called *gomṛd* [cow-dung-earth]; the earth produced from the horns of a bull is known in other regions by the name *darada*, while it is famous among horses as *śuṅguka*.
Indeed, in other countries, it is called *hiṅguluka*. *Rogeṃdra* is *kuṣṭha*, and *auragvadha* is a specific medicinal herb.

The maiden Lakṣaṇā herself shall extract the medicinal herb. Then, he should bring it from the place of the bed to the place of installation. Then, with the words "praṇavekamala," that wise preceptor should place it upon the lotus—which is of the nature of the Praṇava, presided over by the three measures (mātrās), and consists of the three principles (tattvas). This very point is stated as follows:

"Below that is the *māyātattva*, etc."— one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) by means of pervading the lower *udumbara*. Immediately thereafter, regarding the "collection of actions" (*kriyājāta*) produced through performance,
which is the collection of the movement of the thread and so forth, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) known as *kriyām* with a fire-oblation (*homa*) joined with the *astra-mantra*.

Having pacified the preceptor and others— the bearers of the forms (mūrtidharas) and the bearers of the jars— who have been initiated by means of sacrificial fees and other offerings, and having fully satisfied them, they, being entreated and requested,
shall speak thus: "Now," and so forth, regarding the installation of the door in the self of the temple-body.
The ritual procedure for the connection is indeed that same one called the installation of the heart-enclosure;
and it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
And it is said, "the heart-base" (*hṛtpratiṣṭhā*). This means at the completion of the *śukanāsā* (the frontal pediment) and the half-peak (*śikharārdha*).

For it was stated previously: "and the parrot [statue] reaching the half-peak. Therefore he says: "at the head of the womb of the eastern altar," meaning that which is the womb of the first floor (*bhūmikā*), [is placed] upon its head, the second [floor].

This refers to the commencement of the altar (*vedikā*). There, upon that empowered lotus which has the *ādhāra* (support) and *āsana* (seat) [consecrated] with the *praṇava*, one should place the jar representing the deity's form. Having performed the protection according to one's means—meaning having secured it by means of the *astra* and *varma* [mantras] against the elements—one should surround it.

Having performed [the ritual], one should invoke the *aṇu-tattva* (the principle of the individual soul) and join it within the *payas* (the fluid). "That procedure is the material cause" (*tad-vidhānam-upādānam*):

here, "that" (*tat*) refers specifically to the *ātma-tattva* (the principle of the Self), while "procedure" (*vidhāna*) means that which ordains or brings forth action and so forth; thus it is the "material cause" (*upādāna*). Therefore, it is the cause for the arising of both conceptual (*savikalpa*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*).
This term "appropriation" (upādāna) is used figuratively; otherwise, the consequence would be that [the self] undergoes transformation, which would lead to its lack of sentience.
And so it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇatantra:
"The transformation of consciousness is not tenable. Regarding the phrase "the locus of manifestation":

the locus or support of manifestation, which is called "light," is light itself by virtue of its very nature. As they have said: "There are three lights that illuminate both self and other; namely, this fire (jātavedas), and that which is within men."
"Light," "the supreme and the non-supreme"— that which consists of the two forms, the pure and the impure, is non-different from all selves,

because of the scriptural teaching of the lack of distinction among the selves that have no beginning, middle, or end. For when that [Light] is deposited, since there is no distinction for each of all the selves, everyone is indeed deposited within it.

The meaning is "they become. Having thus reflected— that is, having reflected that [the disciple] is both an atom (*aṇu*) and a portion of consciousness (*cidaṃśaka*)— the teacher, by means of the vitalizing power (*anuprāṇa-śakti*) alone, according to the direction of the impulsion of the wind, fully awakens the command of Śiva by means of the ritual mantras (*prayoga-mantra*) promulgated by Śiva.

Having withdrawn the breath and performed *kuṃbhaka*, he, through the vision of knowledge, enclosed [the object] with a handful of flowers; she remained in the form of a waveless state, situated within the *kuṃbha*. As it has been said:

Regarding the phrase "one who contemplates something": because by that very power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*), it exists in the state ending with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*. Having extracted that which is situated within the enclosure of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, the radiant body of Tārā, being thus brought forth, is compared to that [power].

Having withdrawn [the soul] by means of the principle of perfect wisdom (*saṃpaṇḍitattva*) and led it to the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), one should then, through the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), place it in the *ghaṭa* [vessel] as the *tattvātivāhika*. In that [vessel], one should place what is called the *puryaṣṭaka*, whose characteristics will be described later. It is said to be "that which makes known its own group," meaning it is the cause for the manifestation of its specific openings, beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*dharaṇī*).

The nature of the *vāhika* [conveying] is with its Lord (*seśvara*) by means of its own words and atoms (*svapadāṇubhiḥ*). For whichever principle (*tattva*), whichever Lord, whichever name-word (*nāmapada*), and whichever atom-mantra (*aṇumantra*) there may be, for the application of these very things here, one says: "Oṃ, obeisance to the *kalā*. Following this method, the teacher who perceives the principles (*tattvadarśin*) should perform the application of all purposes through the path of the intellect (*dhīvraja*).
Thus: the aggregate of intellects and actions, the modifications, and Māyā should be joined as the "filler" (*pūrakatva*), since she is well-known as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Time (*kāla*), which effects the performance of what was not yet done and the increase of what has come to be, should be joined as the "entirety" (*sakala*) by means of its instrumentality in the reckoning (*kalana*) and so forth that are its own effects; it is designated by the term "the regulator" (*niyāmaka*).

The principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*) is its own objective: the fixed rule regarding the experience of the fruits of karma. As the means for accomplishing that [experience], it is to be joined with this [principle]. By this, regarding the impelling nature of the principles, the guardians of the mantras are to be joined with their respective mantras, [visualizing] the deity as the one expressed by the root mantra, together with his limbs, as all-pervasive—namely, as the form of the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), and so forth.
Having joined all these together by way of pervasion, one should restrain them with the previously mentioned *nirodhamudrā*.
This has also been stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata*:
Abiding in the nature of all beings, he is the Lord of the Quarters who transcends calamity; through the grace of his own action, he remains unchanging and endowed with the sacrifice.

"Having thus placed [the mantra] conjoined with *māyā* and *prakṛti*, one should cause it to cease"—this means having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) for these [mantras]. For when the mantras have been fully satisfied, they become present. Regarding "a deficiency in the rite": this refers to whatever deficiency has arisen due to the incomplete performance of the prescribed procedure.
"One should bring about the cessation of the space originating from obstacles and so forth"— this means that one should perform a *homa* for the sake of fulfilling those [obstacles].

Having dismissed the mantra with "Forgive me," meaning the mantra which was worshipped in the mandala and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should dismiss it according to the ritual procedure with the words "O Blessed One, forgive [me]," and then honor the twice-born [brahmins].

One should make them well-satisfied with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), food, and so forth, so that they may depart unasked, as previously described. Then, and so on; following that, the construction of the altar (*vedikā*) shall be completed, having prepared either the neck (*kaṇṭha*) or the *malasāraka* within the space-liṅga (*ākāśaliṅga*) known as the crest (*cūḍā*).

In the previously mentioned installation of the *liṅga*, whatever was stated— all that should be performed, with the exception of the extraction of the marks (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*), the fourth-day oblation (*caturthī-homa*), and the sacrifice to Caṇḍa (*caṇḍayāga*). Regarding that *cūḍā* (the top-knot), its placement (*saṃveśa*) or entry (*praveśa*) consists of placing the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) upon its own base, and [installing] Brahmā above the forehead (*alaka*) by means of the *dhenā* (the sacrificial cow).
"By a sixth part of its own length"—meaning up to that point—thus its stability is established.

Otherwise, according to the description of the "space-liṅga," stability is possible through its placement in a location free from obstructions. And that very installation is the rite of *pratiṣṭhā*; furthermore, there is the *mūrti* [form].

This [rite] should be performed as one that is devoid of the specific placement of the faces and limbs (*vaktrāṅgavinyāsa*) and the ritual of the paths (*viśeṣādhvakriyā*). In that case, neither the ritual of the placement of the form (*mūrtivinyāsa*) nor the ritual of the paths should be performed, provided that the characteristics of the placement of the form (*mūrtinyāsalakṣaṇa*), the extraction (*uddhāra*), and so forth, are not performed during the consecration of the crest (*cūḍāpratiṣṭhā*). How then is everything prescribed for the *liṅga* to be practiced?

It may be so. With the exception of this, having considered the embryo, the signs of purity, the measurements, and so forth, there is no fault in stating that it was said [by him]. Having thus explained the consecration of the heart (hṛt-pratiṣṭhā), which is also designated as the "consecration of movement" (saṃcaraṇa-pratiṣṭhā) mentioned in other *Saṃhitās*, he now describes the consecration of the temple (*prāsāda-pratiṣṭhā*).

"Prāsāda," etc. When the completion of the entire body of the temple (*prāsāda*) has been accomplished, then it is said that this [deity] is to be installed (*kārya*). How so? To this he says: "In the lower, middle, and upper paths of the *jaṅghā*.
This means the installation of the *ātmatattva* at the base of the temple’s *jaṅghā*; above that, in the middle and at the top, the *vedi*.

At the end [of the sequence] is the *vidyātattva*; the "northern path" (*uttarādhvā*) is the essence of the *kaṇṭhāmalaka*, and therein lies the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *śivatattva*—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "together with the forms" (*mūrtisahitān*): one should remember these [deities] together with the forms previously mentioned, such as Earth (*kṣmā*), Fire (*vahni*), and so forth. This refers to the ritual of mantra-placement (*mantravinyāsa*) performed during the consecration of a *liṅga*.

The distinction, however, is that while recollecting with the mind during the ritual application for the consecration of a temple, the presence-homa and so forth are the same; others [state] that one should install the supreme pervasive [deity]. Having intended the placement of all the principles (tattvas) through the state of being [the self], starting from the self and extending through the three principles, thereafter—

One should install the Supreme Lord by virtue of His all-pervasiveness; this is the distinction from other *saṃhitās*, because in those [other texts] the *Prāsāda* is said to consist of all the *tattvas*. As it is stated in the venerable *Piṅgalāmata* and the *Parākhya*:
Since the temple is the Supreme Lord, consisting of all reality,
whatever exists there in whatever manner is described accordingly.
Earth is established in its capacity as a supporter, water in the gathering of stones and the like,
fire in their digestion, and likewise wind in touch.
In this [world], space resides in cavities; sound resides in that which is called a palace;
touch resides in its hardness; and form resides in white and other colors.
Sound is perceived through hearing; touch brings delight; fragrance resides in smoke and the like—such are the examples.
All such [verses] have not been written here out of consideration for the bulk of the entire work.

Now, the consecration of the banner (*dhvajapratiṣṭhā*). Regarding the passage beginning with "Then" and ending with "for the protection of prosperity": this is for the purpose of guarding the abundance of the fruit.

This is further specified by the phrase "the protection of the field and the moon," and so forth. Just as the protection of an extremely abundant harvest is carried out in a field, so too here [is the protection] of that which consists of enjoyment and liberation.
A great flagstaff should be erected for the sake of the glory of the fruit; and it is stated in the venerable Piṅgalāmata:
Just as a field well-sown with grain is fruitless without protection,
so too is it said that the installation of the presiding deity is incomplete without the consecration of the banner.
Also in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
"Since worship, fire-offerings, recitations, and so forth, performed in a temple from which the banner has been removed,
are destroyed by obstacles, for that reason the banner should be raised."

Thus [it is said]. Here too, he will state: "The destroyer of the multitude of obstacles"—by this, he expresses its measurement. "Characterized by the height of the temple" means by the measure of the temple's elevation. Such is the alternative regarding its measurement: by the term *dhvaja* (banner), the strength of the *jaṅghā* (the lower part) and the *dugūla* (garment) and so forth are denoted; and that—

From the back up to the knees, or else by the measure of the shank— that is, with a staff of that same length— as it has been stated that [the image] is beneficial only when endowed with a staff of that specific measurement and not otherwise, or else according to a measurement based on aesthetic beauty.

It should not be made otherwise; "soft, smooth, and firm" means that which is soft (*mṛdu*), smooth (*ślakṣṇa*), and likewise smooth to the touch (*snigdha-arūkṣa-sparśa*), as well as firmly established (*tathārūḍha*) and capable of withstanding the impact of the wind (*vātāhati-saha*). Furthermore, it must be entirely free from defects at all times. All others [should also be] likewise.

It should be free from the defects of wood; whether it be made of bamboo or from some other wood, this pair—consisting of a cloth and a staff—should be thickly covered and draped with a cloth while reciting the Kavaca mantra. On the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), having worshipped the Deity, one should place [the image] in the northern direction of that [shrine].

One should place [the deity] upon a soft, well-covered bed with the mantra "Trikhaṇḍavarma. Then, within that pair consisting of the staff and the silken garment, there is the threefold nyāsa of the nature of Self, Vidya, and Śiva. As it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
One should assign the *ātma-vidyā* [tattvas] to the staff and the *śiva-tattva* situated on the banner.

In that same manner, the assignment of the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśa*) should also be performed upon it. Regarding the statement "the fire-oblation and so forth as before," by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), the gem-bath, the assignment-bath, and the anointing are intended. However, the recitation is to be done with the *astra-mantra*.

"Japa" means recitation with any one of the three that will be mentioned hereafter, and "prokṣaṇa" means sprinkling again and again. Regarding the phrase "in the pure support of the banner of sound": having performed the purification of the path (*adhva-śuddhi*) by means of gold and *japa*, then [one uses] that previously mentioned "support of the banner," which is measured from the throat down to the feet.
This has been stated with specific detail. Also, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
"The flagstaff is [placed] on the roof of the house in the northeast or sometimes in the northwest;
for the smallest [temples], it is prescribed at one-third of the height of the spire."

"In the fourth [layer] for the middling [deities], and in the fifth for the superior ones. Therein, one should place the lotus consisting of the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti). Upon that, one should place the staff (daṇḍa) located at the top, having performed the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa) by means of the weapon-limbs (astra-aṅga) alone. "The banner as well" [is also to be placed].

Having joined [the weapon] made of *dugula* with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) which denotes the partless (*niṣkala*), as it has been stated in that very same place: "One should place the *sakala* [form] on the staff (*daṇḍa*), but one should place the *niṣkala* on the banner (*dhvaja*). Following that, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra "Aghora" or "Athava. *Āghora* means belonging to Aghora; or else, that which pertains to Śiva.

"The Pāśupata weapon is supreme. Its specific qualification is "Brahmaśiras," by means of the *śiromantra*, and "by the Lord of Knowledge" (*vidyādhipa*). The armor (*kavaca*) is preceded by the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Now follows the meditation on the deity of the banner (*dhvajadevatā*).

Having meditated upon him thus— his mouth as a cave and his tongue as a flash of lightning— one should perform the ascent and the ritual service (upacāra) there with a tongue of that same form. Furthermore, for the one who has been installed,
the bathing, as well as the anointing, adorning, and worship consisting of the Nyāsa of the Lords of the Tattvas, are also prescribed therein.
The remainder of this is as before, but that which is additional is now described: those principles (tattvas) which have been enumerated, and the lords of those principles (tattveśvaras).
Having meditated upon the Āṇavas, Śāmbhavas, and Śāktas, with their hands occupied by their own weapons,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the sake of destroying all obstacles and for the attainment of perfections (siddhis).

Thus: with mantras ending in *phaṭ* belonging to Śiva—or sometimes with weapon-mantras (*astramantra*), meaning mantras ending in the syllable *phaṭ*—there arises no confusion caused by the arrival of enemies (*parāga*) in that kingdom; that is, no delusion resulting from the approach of adversaries occurs there.

"The rain-cloud rains in its own season" means it rains at the proper time; "the peaceful ones" refers to those devoted to tranquility; "milk-yielding cows" means they possess abundant milk and livelihoods;
[the king] should also enable his servants, such as artisans, to cross over [their difficulties] even while subsisting on their wages and livelihoods;
"the Rudras" means that when they die, they become *rudra-aṇus* (subtle particles of Rudra); [this applies to] the "worn-out" and so forth.
This merit is not established only now; rather, it remains so even when the conditioned thing has decayed.

Therefore, since the merit from repairing what is decayed is equal to that from the initial establishment, for this reason one should exert effort toward the restoration of what is decayed. He speaks of the restoration of the decayed: "The decayed..."
With much time having passed, his body was mostly worn out and his limbs were impaired; and as for that embryo within him,

at the time of its formation it was not recognized as an embryo in any way whatsoever, but after some time it became manifest— [this being] appropriate for one who has been led to a wound-defiled opening by that measure of height.
Whatever is joined with that very same excess, or likewise with such a measure consisting of a steady nature, or joined with various additional amounts, and whatever conforms to its own function—
that which has been measured for that purpose is supported by the stability of its own function, such as the feet and so forth.

That mantra should not be propitiated by one who practices another mantra, because the mantra of one whose self is decayed and so forth does not grant its presence; furthermore, it becomes a refuge for piśācas and the like, and therefore it must not be propitiated. Having extracted that [mantra], one should install another. And it has been said:
According to the tradition of the venerable Nandikeśvara and that of Pitāmaha:
just as an embodied being, seeing his body shattered or burnt, abandons it and takes up another, so too the trident, having moved and seeing its place devoid of the deity, abandons that location.
Piśācas, grahas, rākṣasas, pretas, vetālas, and bhūtas undoubtedly take up residence there;

therefore, their removal must be performed according to the rules, preceded by mantras. To explain how that task is to be done, he says "outside," and so forth. Here, at the time of commencement, that which is stated in other *pratiṣṭhā* scriptures [should be followed].
It should be expected that food, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth must be given to the Brahmins and others, as it has been stated in that very same place.
Therefore, the extraction [of the image] should be performed according to the rules, preceded by mantras;
first, one should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice and ghee.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity, the rite for pacification and subjugation should be performed according to the rules;
thereafter, the extraction [of the image] should be carried out by the preceptor who knows all the Vedas.

"But if it is extracted without the proper rite by preceptors devoid of mantras, it shall strike down the kingdom and the king with disease or even through strife. Thus [it is said]. Other temples are in the southern quarter; "the lords of the directions" is an indicative mark for the [eight] primary [deities].
Having first worshipped Śiva with that [mudrā] and so forth, as it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
One should worship Śiva situated upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) within the image on the southern side;
furthermore, one should likewise worship the lords of the directions, as well as Brahmā and the others residing within the body of the Vāstu-man,
and Carakī, Skanda, and the rest who are stationed outside, taking refuge beneath the temple.

Having focused with the vision of knowledge (*jñānadṛṣṭi*) and having performed worship consisting of an offering of food (*balinaivedya*), what should one do? One should cast the *bali* offering. Then, having first generated the fire and performed the satiation of the mantras (*mantratarpaṇa*), [one should offer] "portion by portion" (*bhāgabhāga*). This is as follows in the three [sections], beginning with the portion of Brahmā (*brahmabhāga*).
"By capacity" means by no less than the measure prescribed;
as it is stated in the venerable *Nandikeśvara-mata*:
"However, the movement [of the linga] is performed with a thousand [offerings]. Also, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*:
"For the purpose of moving the liṅga, the Guru should offer a thousand oblations;
for the purpose of re-establishing it, however, a hundred-fold homa is prescribed."
Thus it is said. Having performed the *astra-mantra* homa therein, one should recite the *astra-mantra* itself while touching [the vessel] with *kuśa* grass.

Then, having sprinkled [it] with the water from the *śānti-kumbha* and offered the *arghya* in reverse order, one should offer the *arghya* with the *saṃhitā* according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), and likewise perform prostration as prescribed in other scriptures.
Having made the formal announcement (*vijñapti*), as it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*: "Then, O Auspicious One, one should announce:
'O God, this dilapidated linga brings about all manner of faults for men.'"
"When its extraction has been performed, peace shall be attained"—thus was it spoken by you.

"O Lord, by your command, I shall withdraw [the deity] presided over by that reality from here. Then he should dismiss it; that is, he should dismiss the image (*mūrti*) and the image-bearers (*mūrtipā*), who possess vision and action—that is, those stationed at the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
He should not only dismiss them, but also whatever activity or maintenance exists upon the pedestal.
Having worshipped those atoms (*aṇu*) situated in their respective positions, as well as the atoms based on the signs (*liṅga*),
the mantra-body, Śiva, the three sections of the path (*adhvan*) along with their lords,
and Caṇḍeśa— one should dismiss all that has arisen and was previously invoked as the object of this water offering (*arghya*).

Thereafter, with the mantra "With the golden spade" (*tadanu khanitreṇa haimena*), and with the mantra for the placement of weapons "With the golden plough, O Weapon" (*lāṅgalena sauvarṇenāstrayujeti nyastāstramantraṇa*), [he performs the rite] using a bull's skin tied with a rope made of cow-hide, joined to the bull Skanda with the mantra "With the rope joined to Vṛṣaskaṇḍa" (*vṛṣaskaṃdayujā rajjveti*). As it is stated in the venerable Nandikeśvara-mata:
Then one should cause the liṅga to be excavated with auspicious golden ploughs,
guided by a rope made of hair fastened to the tip of the bull's hump.
Thus it is said: "The golden noose has its point of connection [kṛtaḥ] made; one should lead [it] to the outer portion.

Therefore, from the location of the pedestal-binding (*pīṭhabandha*), the auspicious cloth and that very [portion] which is outside—that is, where the libation to the mantra (*mantratarpaṇa*) and so forth have been performed, which is in addition to the mandala and the fire-hall (*agnyagāra*)—is meant. There, of that...
The application (*viniyoga*) is consistent with the nature of what is about to be described. As it is said: "one should cast [it]," and so forth.

That which is made of gold, silver, and so on, is called "entire" (*samagra*). Having made it new again as before, and having worshipped Vāstoṣpati, one should perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) ending with the offerings to the lords of the directions, followed by the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Having performed the fire-oblation for purification and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should dedicate to Śiva that which has been accomplished in the installation of the maṇḍala; as it is stated in the venerable *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara*:
Then, for the sake of purification through expiation, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Having gone there, one should then present to Śiva whatever has been prepared.
Whatever flaw there may be in the ritual procedure, or whatever defect arises,
may there always be peace for the king, the performer, and the subjects.
"Be well-pleased with our Great Vehicle at all times!

[The text continues: "Regarding the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and so forth: if the pedestal in a linga possessing qualities should become defective, then one should remove that and install another; however, the linga itself must not be removed, even if the linga is defective."

"Having extracted by which... refers to the previously mentioned method of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); both [the *liṅga* and the pedestal] are extracted, and one should install another that possesses qualities (*saguṇa*). However, the meaning of the word "exchange" (*vyatyaya*) is not that one extracts a qualified *liṅga* and installs an unqualified pedestal (*viguna-pīṭha*). "In this manner," and so forth: the *cūlaka* is the crest (*cūlā*), as previously described, [and the *malasāraka*].
The *parivartinī* [mantra] is the *dhāmaprāsāda*. Within this very domain, the rite of restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*) is performed, preceded by the dismissal of the mantras (*maṃtravisarjana*).

As for those mantras which are in the form of *cūḍākās*, they should be deposited in a stainless and blemishless sword until the completion of the *prāsāda*; there, one should worship them, and the *liṅga* is thus protected.

"Having emerged from the palace, let him offer this three times. It is stated that wood and other materials, having been refined and consecrated through ritual application (*abhyaprāya*), should be prepared;
for it is said in the *Bharadvāja-śulba-sūtra* regarding the completion [of the structure]: "At the conclusion, there is the conjunction of mantras.
When that palace is completed, the rite involving the conjunction of mantras is performed collectively; thus it is said: "Stand here... (tiṣṭhā sā).
The meaning is: from such prohibited acts, for those who bear the insignia of the crest and the banner. Thus it is said, "the yoga of action":
practicing the previously mentioned auspicious conduct through the aforementioned type of action, one attains incomparable sovereignty.
One who seeks liberation attains the fruit consisting of the accomplishment of desired aims, or else one obtains imperishable liberation. And it is said in the venerable Kiraṇa:

By this [means], Śakra, Hutāśana (Agni), Skanda, the two Aśvins, the various Siddhas, Viṣṇu the lord of creatures, Yama, and others who are the most excellent among the devoted, having approached the Liṅga at Mahāpavitra— the foremost of sacred sites— and being endowed with devotion to Śiva, enjoy their respective positions as the foremost gods.

"Then, thereafter, they take refuge in the supreme abode. "Until the fall of the body" means as long as life lasts. "For those devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* until death, a *deśika* (spiritual teacher) is easily found," and so forth.
This refers to a case where the mantra installed in an ancient *liṅga* is not recognized and is not known at some point.

"That which is common to them" means that which is shared by the world, known as the *praṇava*; this very thing will be explained in detail later. By the passage beginning with "it should be applied to others," the author previously established himself that the self-manifested (*svayaṃbhu*) and *bāṇaliṅga* forms are not restricted to any particular *pīṭha* or house; and in that context, he incidentally [discussed] the mantra pertaining to that subject.

The prohibition of mixing [the lineages] has been stated; however, by way of incidental discussion, it is now mentioned in various contexts. Regarding the passage beginning with "prāk sthita" (previously established):

even that for whom the lineage has existed for many hundreds of years, or whose installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) was performed long ago—that too is not to be disregarded. For in such a case, the supernatural powers (*yogaiśvarya*), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, have been attained by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) through that very lineage.

"Abide, O you who have transcended the latent impressions of conceptual construction. Those mantras which have been established by those free from defects such as passion and the like are, for the reason that they serve all purposes, not subject to confusion among mantras; because those mantras, which bring benefit to all, were established therein as common to all purposes, such as "measurement and the means of measurement," and so forth.

If, from these [characteristics], that specific knowledge is inferred, then one should worship one's own mantra even without the slightest doubt regarding the placement of that very *liṅga* as the substratum. This is the meaning:
those who practice the mantras of Indra and others [should worship] those [liṅgas] characterized by Indra and others, which are endowed with the *vajra* and other [emblems].

One should worship those very [deities] beginning with Indra. Having spoken regarding the installation (*prāsika*), he now describes the subject at hand, namely the restoration of a dilapidated temple (*jīrṇoddhāra*), starting with the words "vijñāta" and so forth. The phrase "having extracted those residing there"—meaning having understood the mantras established therein—and the phrase "by the previously mentioned rite alone" are explained in both contexts according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣi-nyāya*).

One should worship one's own [deity] which has already been consecrated. "By the previously stated method" means by the method of consecration as prescribed in the *Samaya*. Regarding the passage beginning with "that," etc.: "Bhava" refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), because *bhava* is another name for that *praṇava*, according to the previously mentioned common explanation.
"His manifestation is the embodiment of the path of all mantras.

As many mantras as there are, and as many paths as there are—such as the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) and the path of words (*padādhvan*) taught in the *Svāyaṃbhuva* and other scriptures—all of these indeed reside within his body. And it has been said:
In the *Ruru-saṃhitā-mantravātika*:

"Oṃ" is the single-syllabled Brahman, characterized as the beginning of mantras and so forth; it is the imperishable state that pervades everything from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the specific elements (*viśeṣa*).

"Oṃ! This world is thoroughly woven through and through by the measures (mātrās). Having there conjoined and worshipped that [deity], and then having taken it up with the *saṃhāramudrā* using the heart-mantra as "the Supreme Reality" (*paratattva*), one leads [it] to the union of the signified and the signifier, following that to the subtle atom (*aṇu*).

One should install the intended mantra, beginning with "vatsara" and so forth. Furthermore, that which has undergone non-worship for six months should also be joined with its own mantra, according to the rule: "For Śrī, [one should use] a jewel-born [liṅga], or one touched by fire. This means a jeweled liṅga that has, by chance or through human agency, been touched by fire.

If it has not been drawn by one's own splendor, then that too should be joined with one's own mantra. Now, for the sake of ensuring the practitioner's observance of the rules, there is the consideration of the acquisition of the field (*kṣetraparigraha*), wherein he brings the four stages (*sāma*) under control through restraint.
As it has been said:
In the venerable Kiraṇa [Tantra].
"One should spend the four months of the rainy season according to the rule.

Regarding the word "having undertaken" (*parigṛhya*): it refers to an auspicious time characterized by the sun's entry into a zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*), the three days of the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, the *spṛk*, the *vilaṃbita*, the *vyatīpāta*, and so forth; and regarding the word "auspicious" (*puṇya*): it refers to a favorable moment (*lakṣaṇa*) in an auspicious place. As for those [who dwell] in holy lands...

A field that is pervaded by such qualities as the roaming of black antelopes, the abandonment of enmity toward living beings, and so forth, and which is likewise free from the defects to be mentioned later— namely, those consisting of wild beasts, *bilāṃdhaka* pits, ashes, saline soil,
husks, and stones— such a place is to be accepted. He now states what is not to be accepted:
"From afar [is the water]," and so forth.

Water, sacrificial fuel, and flowers should be far from it; likewise, that which is unpleasant, not pleasing to the mind, or of an improper form is unsuitable for sacrifice. One should avoid a tree that bears neither flowers nor fruit, or one that has been pinned or marked by Gaṇeśa and others, or where there is a linga upon another linga, or where many lingas are present.
The meaning is that it is presided over by a single *liṅga*, even according to the reasoning to be stated later;

"protected by another practitioner" means it is resorted to by another practitioner. Furthermore, it is joined with evil beings such as lions and tigers at either the southern door of the temple or the northern door.

It is appropriate to say that waking and so forth are like that; for it is said that "it is a prohibitor of what is to come. That water, when sprinkled, wards off even future obstacles. Thus, the house is free from defects; likewise, by the inclusion of the word "prāsāda" (temple), one should understand the altar (*vedī*), the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*), the interior sanctum (*garbha*), and the temple itself.

Having rendered even that outer courtyard free from defects, one should offer three oblations for those other abodes of Śiva in the form of palaces and others in the form of altars (*vedikā*) which are to be purified. Then, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with the ritual manual (*sāstra*) and its ancillaries. Following that, there is the departure for bathing and so forth in order to fetch sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), *kuśa* grass, and other materials.
Furthermore, one should meditate that as far as the field to be encompassed extends, it is completely filled with the splendor of the weapon-mantra (*astra-tejas*).

Likewise, by that very splendor, the host of obstacles is utterly consumed; thus, having become free from disease and faultless, it becomes a "hole" (*chidra*), as has already been explained previously. Then, [one should recite] the mantras of Śāstṛ and Lokeśa, and the *śaṃ* syllable.

"Prāgdigdha" means one should place [the seeds] according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east; "ito bāhyena niṣkramet" means one should exit from the outside. For the sake of identification, "carma japtena" means with [the leather] consecrated by the Kavaca mantra; "saṃdhāya" means having joined them together as one; "bahistadbāhye" means on the exterior of that; "bījāni kirennikṣipet" means one should scatter and deposit the seeds. "Śastrajajaptāni" means consecrated by the Astra mantra; "sūtracarmaneti" refers to the thread and the leather.

Then, by means of the line drawn with the cord fixed at the peg, one should fashion a radiant outer enclosure-circle using ash; and within that, on the inside, one should fashion it with the "armor" (kavaca) mantra, as indicated by the flowers, roots, and stalks. This is the general rule.

"O Rākṣasī"—thus one should offer the *bali* to the Kṣetrapāla in the southwest (*naiṛtyāṃ*). "O Abode"—thus the *bali* should be given to the Vāstu-deities in the temple. "Within the water"—this refers to bathing each object with water and with cow dung. "Honey"—this refers to applying honey (*mākṣika*) while reciting its own mantra. "Having anointed"—[refers to] having applied [the substances].
Because of ignorance regarding that which was previously established by means of the *praṇava*, it was stated earlier, "therefore," and so forth.

Having first performed the conjunction with all the mantras already established, one should purify [the object]. Then, having duly re-ascended the multitude of mantras that were previously dismissed, the practitioner, together with his assistants, should offer them as before for the sake of attaining success.

Having also disposed the mantras that depend on the *pīṭhas* according to their respective application, one should likewise dispose the *jñāna* and *kriyā* [mantras] in the very sequence previously stated. Now, regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for whatever fourfold deficiency in ritual action there may be— whether due to omission, over-performance, or performing it otherwise— in that case, by means of the fire-oblation procedure (*homavidhi*).

The meaning is "having completed [the ritual]"; one should bathe again. Although the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is separated [in the text], it should be connected with the first instance of bathing; that is, after the first bath, there is another bath. Then, having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability—preceded by the preliminary rites such as facing the east—as the cause for the presence (*sānnidhya*) of the mantra, [one should proceed].

And having offered [the oblation], one should request the presence [of the deity] according to the very procedure previously described: "O Blessed One, for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal, remain present in this *liṅga* until the completion of my observance"— thus, having been requested with such a petition, the deity is obtained as desired.

The meaning is that one should contemplate [the deity] as having attained presence; "to the beings and their own followers" means one should scatter the *bali* offering to the beings who move in their respective locations within the field (*kṣetra*), and so forth. Just as the arrangement of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*) and the weapons was made for the entire field, in the same way, during the evening at one's own small monastery (*maṭhikā*), it should be performed as part of the ritual practice (*sādhana*).

Regarding "balipūjādi" (offerings and worship, etc.): when ten stakes have been driven into the perimeter of the sacred field (*kṣettranemi*), on the festival days (*parvan*) to be described hereafter, the offering and worship (*balipūjā*) should be performed at dusk (*pradoṣa*). However, with respect to the deity, it should be performed daily during the four watches of the day—consisting of dawn, midday, dusk, and midnight—as they possess equal qualities.

He states the days for special worship and so forth for those endowed with equal qualities, beginning with "on the fourteenth," etc. Regarding the phrase "in both fortnights": this refers to the rule concerning both fortnights, namely, "on the increase of the month and on the destruction of a day. This means that within a month, on the occasions of the increase or loss of a day, as well as Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and so forth, and others such as the Yuga-ādis and the Ṣaḍaśītis.

Auspicious times such as the *mukhasaṃkrānti* and others are utilized for bathing, worship, and so forth at a sacred site (*kṣetra*) and the like. If such [an auspicious time] does not exist within the occupied sacred site, one should resort to that which is gathered from a distance by way of numerical calculation. Then, one should go outside by means of the *tattva*-self, because of the possibility of obstacles being revealed. Regarding the passage beginning with "jāti" and so forth:

"The performance of the conduct prescribed for one's own [caste] (*svacaryā*) constitutes a confusion of castes (*jātivyatikara*); the rule established therein is that which is observed in the scriptures, beginning with 'one's own conduct' (*svacaryā*) and so forth. One should perform penance (*prāyaścitta*) when there is a confusion of castes.
As it has been stated, he qualifies this by saying: "for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who follows the subtle [path], the [conduct] prescribed for his own [caste]..."

The *mātṛkās*—the powers (*śaktis*)—of that which rests upon this *vṛtti* shine forth and expand, pervading the fourfold world by presiding over the creation of beings. This is what is meant: in such a world, wherever and whatever a practitioner desires when he employs mantras, he necessarily attains it. And it has been said:
In the illustrious Jñānottara.
The mantras, assuming universal forms at the will of the sacrificer,
bestow all desires, even those difficult to obtain within the three worlds.

The "mantrin" is the practitioner (*sādhaka*) himself who, having transgressed the rule, fails to perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the section on rules; he incurs the loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*). However, the "instructor" (*deśika*), that is, the teacher (*ācārya*), becomes a partaker of disease;
the meaning is that he suffers the obstruction of the long-term fruit [of his teaching]. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of its cessation," etc., it refers to the transgression of that rule.
"The injunction to be described hereafter, known as the *pavitraka*, is for the sake of removing transgression, O Supreme Lord.

Thus, out of respect for the scripture, the venerable Lord Īśvara, whose nature is action performed with diligence, [addresses] "O Creator" to Ananteśa, the supreme Prajāpati; for he holds the primary status of the Guru at the beginning of this scripture's descent.

However, it should not be explained that [the term] "born from a lotus" (padmajanman) refers to the word denoting the Creator (vedhas) by virtue of its commonality [with Brahmā], because that Prajāpati is also mentioned in another Saṃhitā as the Lord of the entire world.
"Strengthened by the supreme power (paraśakti), this Lord of the world of the twice-born destroys, sustains, and restrains all these worlds."
And [the words] "to Skanda and Ātīkṣṇabhāsa" are intended to show the introduction of the scripture and its teachers:
"The supreme teacher Ananteśa was proclaimed as the life-force of the worlds;
that which was spoken by him was told by the Supreme Lord to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha."
Everything was recounted by the preceptor of the gods and asuras to the Goddess;
and the Goddess spoke to Nandīśa and Skanda, beginning with [the words] "Listen in brief," which means: "Hear that [account] called the Pavitra in its condensed form."
Now that is explained: "In Nabhasya," and so forth. "Nabhasya" and "nabhas" refer to the two months;

the meaning is the months of Bhādrapada and Śrāvaṇa. Since the suffix *an* is prescribed for the word *māsa* after the words *kṛti*, *tri*, and *śat*, the form *māsoḥ*—the genitive dual—is appropriate.

It should rather have been stated as "in the two months [beginning with] Āṣāḍha," meaning "on the full moon of Āṣāḍha. The fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, conjoined with the asterism Pūrvāṣāḍhā, is what is popularly known in the regional dialect as "Āṣāḍhī"; on that initial day.
Or, it may be understood in relation to each of the days specified, as being the first day of each; by this [interpretation],...
The two days known as the seventh and the thirteenth are prescribed; this should be understood. And it is said in the venerable Kiraṇa:

Furthermore, having performed worship on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should invoke Śiva in that place on that very day. Likewise, the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is also prescribed;
because it is obtained through its own [specific] designation, it is unconfused and thus consistent with the term *balakalaśa*.

The bark of a tree is mentioned; from that arises [the cord] consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), and so forth. Having made a thread with nine threads themselves and having knotted it entirely—according to the reasoning to be stated later, namely "as it goes" (*yathā-gama*)—one should bring about the purifying [cord] without transgressing the procedure seen in other scriptures (*śāstrāntara*). Thus it is established.

The term "supreme" (*param*) provides the justification for what is called the *pavitraka* (the purifier): because it purifies one from the sin consisting of transgression (*pratyavāya*) arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties; thus it is a "purifier. He clarifies this very point by stating: "One is liberated from the failure of rites performed during the year through the fulfillment of the injunction. It is precisely through this fulfillment of the injunction that it is the *pavitraka*.
"From that which is called 'bestowing,' from what is performed, or from what exists for a year"—this means one is released from the failure of ritual action performed over a year;

the meaning is that one attains purification. Regarding "twofold," and so forth: there are fourteen Indras, and twice that is twenty-eight; from that [number] of threads, one should lay out the smallest [altar], and then [an altar] two cubits larger.
From three cubits and so forth, increasing by ten at each step, there are indeed one hundred threads for the highest of the high;
this is the rule for those seeking enjoyment, or alternatively, "twelve" and so forth— the word "or" (*vā*) is used here again.
The meaning of the word "in the [lower] accomplishments such as Kanyasā" is that its cause is twelve-fold;

beyond those twelve, it increases by twelve for each subsequent stage until the reality-limit (tattvāntikā) reaches one hundred and eight—this is the meaning of the increase. "O youngest one," and so forth, refers to the minor signs (liṅgas).

Those seeking liberation should perform thirty-eight prostrations for each of the deities, beginning with Tārā and Sutārā, according to the thirty-eight digits (kalās). It is thus stated that there are fifty prostrations for the middle [deities] characterized by their phonemes; this refers to the fifty phonemes, which are the syllables of the prosodic measures (mātrās).
Because this is well-known among the elders, the number of knots is eighty-one;

that is to say, as many as there are [channels] flowing from you, those are the knots. They are at equal intervals; that is to say, having made an interval of the same measure as the knot itself, the subsequent knot is equal [to the first].
Thus, being free from deficiency or excess, [the text] is as previously indicated in its entirety.
By the term "Kāśmīraka," it refers to saffron; by the term "Gairika," a specific mineral (ore) that is red like ochre and the like;
and by the word "ādi" (and so forth), it includes *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone pigment) as well. As it has been said:
In the venerable Kiraṇa [Tantra].
All the knots have been made firm with *gorocanā* and the [five] minerals; drink this.

"Firm" means not loose. Regarding the triad and so forth: with respect to enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal, [the powers of] *Ātma-vidyā* and *Śiva* reside in the head and the region of the image (*ārcābhāga*).

The triad of purifiers (pavitra) should be prepared; furthermore, the fourth is for the pedestal (pīṭhikā). That which is the fourth purifier is "for all deities" (sārvadaivata); because it pertains to the deity residing in the image and residing in the pedestal, it is for all deities. Regarding the passage beginning with "as far as the knees" (ājānu): in the case of images, [the measure] up to the knees is threefold, and likewise [the others].

The meaning is that for mobile [liṅgas] and others, such as the *cala-liṅgas*, one should fashion the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) preceded by the triad consisting of the Self-knowledge (*ātma-vidyā*) and Śiva, joined with threads according to one's own preference and in a number as desired; "joined with threads according to one's own preference" applies even to the mobile liṅgas. For the sake of accomplishment, it should have all the knots (*samagra-granthi*), following the previously mentioned [rule] of twelve plus [the rest].

The passage beginning with "vṛddha" is a restatement; that beginning with "vidyā" refers to the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) specifically in the context of books and the like. In this very way, it is "consisting of all" (sarvātmaka). Because it pervades everything, it encompasses everything up to the end; likewise, it is "consisting of all" according to one's preference. However, as will be described regarding the bull, there is one back [part] from the tip of the horn.

Our teachers maintain that the second portion, beginning from below the neck and reaching down to the hooves, is the rite known as *sviṣṭakṛt*; here, the *balihoma* is performed when the ritual activity of the oblation has been completed at its conclusion. Others, however, hold that according to the reading *sveṣṭakṛtprānte*, it is to be offered once the rite has reached its end.

The meaning is "at the conclusion of the *homa*. Of what nature is the *pavitraka*? It is "for one's own *iṣṭakṛt*" (*sveṣṭakṛt*), which means it accomplishes what is desired or wished for by oneself. As they explain: "like the *liṅga*"; this is an extension (*atideśa*) of the rule for the fourfold *pavitraka* even to the fire of Śiva. He states that rule beginning with "three," and so forth.

At the beginning of the *Liṅga*, by way of division, three [sections] consisting of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva are presented according to the sequence required for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). The fourth [section] concerns the deities as the cause of all principles (*tattva*), starting from the Lord Kālāgnirudra up to Paramaśiva; or alternatively, from Paramaśiva down to Kālānala.

In the same manner, it should be explained according to the sequence up to the *sṛṣṭi* [stage]. Regarding the fruit seen in the *pratiṣṭhā* [stage], he says: "There is no untimely death," and so forth, until "wherein the Lord stands together with the Bull (*vṛṣa*). This implies that the installation of the *liṅga* must never be performed without the installation of the Bull.

He describes the true nature of the Bull (vṛṣa): "The Bull is Dharma," and so forth. Because he nourishes (medayati) persons with heavy fruits that pacify the burning of suffering and gladdens them, Dharma is related to the Blessed One;
for, according to both the root-meaning and the perspective of etymology (nirukti), this is a quality of the God consisting of knowledge and action.

Because of its excellence of attributes, this existent [Prakṛti] supports the aforementioned entire aggregate of sentient and insentient beings through its nature as the power of support (*ādhāra-śakti*) and likewise through its nature as the power of presiding (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-śakti*). And it is said in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Because he declares all these realms of the elements and joy to come from the Supreme Person,

he is called 'Dharma'. By this, he concludes what was previously stated at the time of the introduction to the section on sacrifice— that the worship of the Liṅga is the most excellent form of worship among these means for propitiating the Lord.

And by whatever means this goal is to be accomplished, Brahmā and the others attained that wondrous and marvelous supreme sovereignty which transcends all, having been brought about by their progeny. Even though it proceeded as a secondary method (*anukalpa*), that is, even when the person acted through a figurative conceptualization (*gauṇī-kalpanā*).

Regarding those who have attained the state of Rudra, as previously stated by the Śruti: "He shall deliver even craftsmen, singers, and servants who subsist on wages"—what learned person indeed would not place faith in this? Rather, everyone does so. As for the other [type of devotee], he is one whose vision of the supreme good is obscured and whose merit is blocked by impurity; he is primarily characterized by the root [of worldly attachment].
The meaning of "yāvat" is "up to. He states the following for the purpose of explaining that state which is said to be pure by virtue of being an auxiliary to sacrifice:

"clods of earth, ashes, balls of cow dung," and so forth. One who possesses purity, even while worshipping a *liṅga* fashioned from clods of earth and the like, attains the fruit consisting of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), even upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
The meaning is that by reciting these mantras for sacrifice, one immediately attains the desired fruit.
He states the connection regarding the manifestation of the scriptures with the words beginning "This [was taught] by the self-existent Lord... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase *jñānāvṛttottamam*: "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "the highest excellence of conduct" (*vṛttottama*) are so called because they are the cause for attaining the fourfold liberation; it is held [to be] "one part of that," meaning twelve thousand [verses] plus one thousand.
Regarding the phrase *iṣṭārthasiddhiyogasamākula*: by "desired object" (*iṣṭārtha*) is meant the foundation of what is to be longed for.

The superiority even over the scriptures belongs to those perfected ones (*siddhas*) whose nature has been described, who possess steady minds, who are wise, free from passion, and who view the world as if it were a blade of grass— by this [it is meant that] their yoga consists of the absorption (*samādhi*) which perfumes the mind with the form of the object of meditation. Through these two yogas, the attainment of desired ends [is achieved].

May there be auspiciousness and welfare for us in this world filled with turmoil. By the grace of that very Guru, who is devoted to the primordial Lord (Ādi-Śiva) and whose mind is ever-steadfast through discipline, the completion of this work has been brought about by me, Madhava, from the vessel of the Samāpātra, according to the fruit of his command. And this [work] is everywhere through the compassion of the Holder of the Crescent Moon (Candrakalādharas).
May he be forever beloved by all devotees, who perceive the singular reality through the various objects of their experience.
[Thus ends the Tantra named Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi composed by the illustrious Mahāmaheśvara. It is complete and finished. May there be auspiciousness! May there be auspiciousness!
